overview.about: The GMAT Focus Edition is a computer-adaptive test accepted by thousands of MBA and business master's programmes, including ISB and the IIMs' one-year executive programmes. chapters.title: The GMAT Focus Edition: format & scoring

cards.title: What the GMAT is for
cards.body: The **GMAT** is the admissions test most business schools use to judge whether you can handle the analytical load of an MBA. The current version is the **GMAT Focus Edition** (launched late 2023). It does not test business knowledge. It tests reasoning: numbers, arguments, and data under time pressure.

cards.title: Three sections, 45 minutes each
cards.body: **Quantitative Reasoning** (21 questions), **Verbal Reasoning** (23) and **Data Insights** (20). Each section is 45 minutes, so the test is about **2 hours 15 minutes** plus an optional 10-minute break. There is no essay. You choose the **order** of the three sections.

cards.title: What is inside each section
cards.body:
**Quant:** Problem Solving only — arithmetic and algebra, **no geometry**, no calculator.
**Verbal:** Critical Reasoning and Reading Comprehension (no grammar-only questions).
**Data Insights:** Data Sufficiency, Multi-Source Reasoning, Table Analysis, Graphics Interpretation, Two-Part Analysis — with an **on-screen calculator**.

cards.title: The score scale
cards.body:
Total score: **205–805**, in steps of 10 (scores end in 5).
Each section score: **60–90**.
All three sections count equally toward the total. Your score report also shows **percentiles** — the share of recent test-takers you beat.

cards.title: Review & edit
cards.body: Inside each section you can **bookmark** questions and, if time remains at the end, review them and **change up to 3 answers**. Review time comes out of the same 45 minutes. It is a safety net for a careless slip, not a second attempt at the section.

cards.title: Read percentiles, not raw numbers
cards.body: Focus Edition scores look lower than old-format GMAT scores for the same ability — the scale was reset. A Focus score in the mid-600s roughly matches an old 700. When you compare yourself to a school's class profile, check whether it reports Focus or old-format numbers, and use **percentiles**.

cards.q: Which statement about GMAT Focus Quant is correct?
options: It includes geometry and Data Sufficiency
It is Problem Solving only, with no geometry and no calculator
cards.explain: Focus Quant is 21 Problem Solving questions in 45 minutes. Data Sufficiency moved to Data Insights, geometry was dropped, and the calculator is only available in Data Insights.

cards.q: A candidate's report shows a total of 675. Which is impossible as one of her section scores?
cards.explain: Section scores run from 60 to 90, so 95 cannot exist. (Total scores run 205–805.)

cards.q: During the Verbal section you finish with 6 minutes left. What can you do?
options: Change as many answers as you like
Change up to 3 answers in that section
Carry the 6 minutes to Data Insights
cards.explain: You can review bookmarked questions and edit up to 3 answers per section within the remaining time. Unused time does not carry over to the next section.

notes.p:
The GMAT is a **reasoning test**, not a knowledge test. Schools use it because it predicts something they care about: can this person handle the quantitative load of first-year core courses (finance, accounting, statistics, operations) and think clearly through messy, wordy problems? An admissions committee reading 5,000 applications from engineers, commerce graduates, lawyers and designers needs one common yardstick, and the GMAT is that yardstick.

The current version is the **GMAT Focus Edition**, run by **GMAC** (Graduate Management Admission Council) and introduced in late 2023. It replaced the older 'classic' GMAT, which had an essay, a geometry-heavy quant section and sentence-correction grammar. If you read an old prep book, a lot of it no longer applies. Always check mba.com for the current format before you plan.
The test has three sections, each **45 minutes**:
points: **Quantitative Reasoning — 21 questions.** Problem Solving (five answer choices, pick one). Arithmetic and algebra word problems. No geometry. No calculator.
**Verbal Reasoning — 23 questions.** Critical Reasoning (short arguments: strengthen, weaken, assumption, inference) and Reading Comprehension (passages with several questions each).
**Data Insights — 20 questions.** Data Sufficiency, Multi-Source Reasoning, Table Analysis, Graphics Interpretation and Two-Part Analysis. An on-screen calculator is available here only.
**Total:** 64 questions in 2 hours 15 minutes, plus one optional 10-minute break that you can take after the first or the second section.
**Section order:** you choose any order of the three sections at the start of the test.

notes.p:
Each section is **computer-adaptive**: the difficulty of your next question depends on how you are doing. Your section score (60–90) reflects not just how many you got right but how hard the questions were. The three section scores combine into a **total score from 205 to 805**, reported in steps of 10. The three sections are weighted equally.

Two consequences matter for strategy. First, there is no single magic number of correct answers — two people with 15/21 correct can get different scores. Second, **unanswered questions at the end of a section are penalised heavily**, so you must finish every section (more on this in the timing chapter).

The scale was deliberately reset so that Focus scores do not look like old scores. Roughly, a Focus score in the mid-600s corresponds to an old-format 700. GMAC publishes an official **concordance table**; use it when a school's class profile still quotes old-format numbers.

A **percentile** tells you the percentage of recent test-takers who scored below you. Percentiles are recalculated periodically, so the same score can carry a slightly different percentile year to year. Admissions committees read percentiles and section scores, not just the total — a lopsided profile (say, very strong Verbal but weak Quant) raises a question about whether you will cope with finance and statistics.

Your **Official Score Report** includes performance insights at no extra cost (this used to be a paid 'Enhanced Score Report'). It breaks your performance down by section, question type and content area, and shows how you used time. If you plan to retake, this report is the single most useful diagnostic you have: it tells you whether you lost points on, say, word-problem translation or on running out of time.

notes.h: Worked example: reading a score profile
notes.p:
Two illustrative candidates apply to the same programme. Numbers are made up to show the logic.

**Ananya:** Total 665 — Quant 84, Verbal 82, Data Insights 81. Balanced, and Quant is her strongest section.
**Rohan:** Total 665 — Quant 76, Verbal 88, Data Insights 82. Same total, but Quant is weak.

Many committees will read these differently. Ananya's file shows she can handle the core numbers courses. Rohan's file may prompt questions unless his transcript shows strong maths (say, an engineering degree with good grades) or he takes a quantitative course before joining. The lesson: **aim for balance**, and do not let one section collapse because you love another.
Candidates lose points before they even start by misunderstanding the test:
points: Using an old-format book and spending weeks on geometry or sentence correction, which are gone.
Comparing a Focus score to a school's old-format average and panicking (or relaxing) wrongly.
Treating 'review and edit' as a strategy. It is limited to 3 changes per section and eats into the same 45 minutes.
Ignoring Data Insights. It counts exactly as much as Quant and Verbal, and it is the section most candidates practise least.
Leaving questions blank at the end of a section — the penalty is steep.

notes.h: How it shows up in admissions and jobs
notes.p: Your GMAT score shows up in three places. **Admissions:** it is one input alongside work experience, essays, recommendations and interviews; a strong score cannot rescue a weak story, but a weak score can sink a good one at competitive schools. **Scholarships:** many schools tie merit money partly to test scores. **Recruiting:** some consulting firms and banks ask for GMAT scores when hiring MBAs, which is a reason to keep a good score even after admission. Some Indian programmes (such as one-year executive-style MBAs and international tracks) also accept the GMAT, alongside CAT for two-year programmes.

cards.title: Diagnose before you plan
cards.body: Take a full **official practice exam** cold, before studying. It tells you your starting score, your weakest section and whether time is a problem. Planning without a diagnostic is like a doctor prescribing before examining you.

cards.title: The official materials
cards.body: Build your plan around GMAC's own material: the **GMAT Official Guide** (with the Quantitative, Verbal and Data Insights review books), the **Official Practice Exams** (the free starter kit includes two full exams), and the online question bank. Official questions are the only ones written by the people who write the real test.

cards.title: Rough time budget
cards.body:
For a 100–150 point jump, plan about **100–150 hours** over **8–12 weeks**:
• Weekdays: 1.5–2 hours
• Weekends: one 3-hour block + one full mock every 1–2 weeks
Working professionals usually need the 12-week version.

cards.title: Three phases
cards.body:
**Weeks 1–4: Foundations** — relearn concepts, untimed accuracy.
**Weeks 5–8: Speed and mixing** — timed sets of mixed topics.
**Weeks 9–12: Simulation** — full mocks in your chosen section order, deep review, error log.

cards.title: The error log is the plan
cards.body: For every wrong (or lucky) answer, write: topic, why you missed it (concept / reading / careless / time), and the one-line rule you will use next time. Review the log weekly. Most score gains come from **not repeating the same 20 mistakes**.

cards.title: Allocating by weakness
cards.body: Diagnostic: Quant 78, Verbal 83, DI 76. With 12 hours a week, a sensible split is roughly **5 hours Quant, 4 hours DI, 3 hours Verbal** — DI and Quant share skills (arithmetic, ratios, reading data), so work on one lifts the other.

cards.q: Why take a full practice test before you start studying?
options: To set a baseline and find your weakest section and timing problems
Because the first mock always gives your real score
It is required before booking the exam
cards.explain: A diagnostic gives a baseline score, shows where you lose points and whether time is the issue, so you can allocate hours sensibly.

cards.q: Which activity produces the biggest gains in the last month?
options: Doing hundreds of new questions without review
Full timed mocks plus deep review of every error
cards.explain: Simulation and review fix timing and recurring mistakes. Geometry is not tested; volume without review repeats errors.

cards.q: You have 10 hours a week and your Quant lags far behind Verbal. Which split is most sensible?
options: 10 hours Verbal to maximise your strength
Equal hours on all three sections
Most hours on Quant and DI, a maintenance dose of Verbal
No Quant — it is only one-third of the score
cards.explain: All sections count equally, so the cheapest points are in your weakest areas. Keep Verbal warm, but invest where the gap is.

notes.p:
A GMAT score is the output of a **system**, not of willpower. The candidates who improve the most are rarely the ones who study the most hours; they are the ones who (1) know exactly where they are losing points, (2) fix those causes in a deliberate order, and (3) rehearse the real test conditions often enough that test day feels ordinary.

This chapter gives you an 8–12 week plan that a working professional can actually follow. Shorten it if you are a student with more free hours; stretch it if your diagnostic is far below your target.

Before opening a book, take **Official Practice Exam 1** under real conditions: one sitting, timed, no calculator in Quant, your intended section order. Then read the performance breakdown. Answer four questions:
points: What is my **starting total** and each section score?
Which section is weakest relative to the others?
Within Quant, which topics cost the most points (ratios, algebra, counting...)?
Did I **finish** each section? If not, timing is a top-priority problem, not a side issue.

notes.h: Step 2: Set a target and a budget
notes.p:
Look at the **class profile** of the schools you want (median and middle-80% range of Focus scores, or convert old-format numbers with GMAC's concordance). Your target should sit at or above the median.

A rough rule from experience, not an official figure: a 50–80 point jump often takes 60–100 hours; a 100–150 point jump often takes 100–150+ hours. Divide by your realistic weekly hours. A consultant working 55-hour weeks might manage 10–12 hours a week, so a 120-hour plan takes about 10–12 weeks. Book the test date at the end of that window — a fixed date stops 'I'll study until I feel ready' drift.

notes.h: Step 3: The 12-week plan, built on official material
notes.p:
Official questions are scarce, so do not burn them carelessly. Use third-party questions for **early concept drilling** and save the **Official Practice Exams** for checkpoints and the final month. Do not repeat a practice exam too soon — you will remember answers and get an inflated score. Mix your sources: a good third-party course for explanations, official material for calibration.

Here is a template for ~10–12 hours a week.
points: **Weeks 1–2:** Quant foundations — number properties, fractions/decimals/percents, ratios. Verbal: Critical Reasoning argument structure (premise, conclusion, assumption).
**Weeks 3–4:** Quant — averages and statistics, rates and work, interest. DI — Data Sufficiency method. Mock 2 at the end of week 4 (any official exam).
**Weeks 5–6:** Quant — algebra, quadratics, inequalities, exponents. Verbal — Reading Comprehension. DI — Table Analysis and Graphics Interpretation.
**Weeks 7–8:** Quant — counting, probability, sets, sequences. Timed mixed sets of 10–15 questions. DI — Multi-Source Reasoning and Two-Part Analysis. Mock 3.

**Weeks 9–11:** One full official mock per week, in your chosen order, with the break where you will take it. Spend at least as long reviewing as testing. Target the top 3 error categories from your log.
**Week 12:** Light. One last mock 5–7 days before the test, then revise the error log and rest. No new topics in the final 3 days.

notes.p:
An illustrative candidate, Kavya, scores **595** on her diagnostic (Quant 77, Verbal 80, DI 75) and targets **665**. Her error log after two weeks shows three causes for 70% of misses: (a) percent-change wording ('of' vs 'more than'), (b) misreading Data Sufficiency statements as needing an actual answer, and (c) spending 4+ minutes on hard counting questions.

She does not 'study everything harder'. She drills percent-change translation for a week, practises the DS 'sufficiency, not solving' habit with 15 questions a day, and adopts a **2.5-minute cut-off rule** in Quant. Her mocks move 595 → 625 → 645 → 655, and she sits the real test at 665. The gains came from fixing three behaviours, not from covering new material.

points: **Studying without a mock for six weeks**, then discovering a timing problem too late.
**Doing questions without reviewing them.** One question reviewed deeply beats five rushed.
**Ignoring the section you are good at** until it slips 4 points on test day.
**Cramming the night before.** Sleep does more for your score than 2 extra hours of practice.
**Changing method every week** after reading a new forum post.

notes.h: How it shows up in real jobs
notes.p: A GMAT plan is your first exercise in **project management**: a goal, a baseline, constraints (hours), milestones (mocks) and a feedback loop (error log). Consultants and product managers run exactly this loop on client problems. Interviewers sometimes ask 'how did you prepare for the GMAT?' — a crisp answer about diagnosis and iteration says more about you than the score.

points: Start with a timed official diagnostic; read the section and topic breakdown.
Set a target from your schools' class profiles; budget roughly 100–150 hours for a 100+ point jump.
Three phases: foundations → timed mixed practice → full-test simulation.
Keep an error log: topic, cause, one-line fix. Review it weekly.
Spend more hours where the gap is; keep strong sections warm.
Save official practice exams for checkpoints and the last month.
Book the test date to create a deadline; rest before test day.

cards.title: Your time per question
cards.body:
**Quant:** 45 min ÷ 21 ≈ **2 min 08 s**
**Verbal:** 45 min ÷ 23 ≈ **1 min 57 s**
**Data Insights:** 45 min ÷ 20 = **2 min 15 s**
These are averages. Easy questions should take less, so hard ones can take a little more.

cards.title: How adaptivity works
cards.body: Each section is **computer-adaptive**. Answer well and the next questions tend to get harder; struggle and they get easier. Your score depends on both how many you get right and **how difficult** those questions were. So a question that feels brutal is often a sign you are doing well.

cards.title: Blanks are the worst outcome
cards.body: If time runs out with questions unanswered, the score penalty is steep — typically worse than guessing on them. **Always finish the section.** If you have 3 minutes and 4 questions left, make fast educated guesses rather than solving one perfectly.

cards.title: The 'cut-off' rule
cards.body: Set a personal limit — about **3 minutes** in Quant. If you are not close to an answer, eliminate what you can, guess, **bookmark**, move on. One stubborn question can steal the time of three easy ones. Strategic guessing on 2–3 hard questions per section is normal, even for top scorers.

cards.title: Checkpoints
cards.body: Know where you should be: in Quant, about **Q7 at 30 min left**, **Q14 at 15 min left**. Check the clock only at these points, not after every question. Being 2 minutes behind at a checkpoint means: guess faster on the next hard one.

cards.title: Smart guessing
cards.body: A question asks for a value of an odd integer expression; options are 12, 15, 18, 20, 24. Only 15 is odd. When you must guess, use **parity, units digits, sign, rough size** to eliminate. Even removing two choices lifts a random guess from 20% to 33%.

cards.q: You reach Quant question 14 with 9 minutes left. What does this tell you?
options: You are about 6 minutes behind pace
Nothing — pacing does not matter in an adaptive test
cards.explain: On pace, Q14 should arrive at about 15 minutes left (14 × ~2.1 ≈ 30 minutes used). With 9 left you are ~6 minutes behind and must guess faster on hard questions.

cards.q: Which statement about the adaptive format is TRUE?
options: Getting harder questions usually means you are doing well
Every question in a section has the same difficulty
You can return to any section after finishing it
cards.explain: The algorithm serves harder questions after correct answers, so difficulty is a rough signal of good performance. Blanks are penalised, and you cannot return to a finished section.

cards.q: Three minutes remain and you have four Quant questions left. Best move?
options: Solve one carefully and leave three blank
Leave all four blank to avoid wrong answers
Answer all four with quick, eliminated guesses where needed
Spend the time reviewing bookmarked questions
cards.explain: Blanks are penalised more than wrong guesses. Give every remaining question an answer, using quick elimination.

notes.p:
The GMAT measures reasoning **under a time limit**. Many candidates know enough maths to score well but lose 30–60 points because they spend five minutes on one question, panic, and rush the last eight. Timing is not an add-on to preparation; it is part of the skill being tested.

The winning mindset: **you are not trying to answer every question correctly. You are trying to maximise your score across the whole section.** That sometimes means walking away from a question you could solve if you had six minutes.

Each section is **computer-adaptive at the question level**. The first question is of medium difficulty. Each answer updates the system's estimate of your ability, and the next question is chosen to measure you precisely around that estimate. Over 20-odd questions, the estimate settles.

Three practical consequences:
points: **Difficulty is a signal, not a threat.** If questions feel hard, you are probably doing well. Do not let that rattle you.
**Consistency beats streaks.** A run of careless errors in a row drags the estimate down and costs more than scattered misses. Stay steady throughout instead of obsessing over the first ten.
**Finishing matters.** Unanswered questions at the end are penalised, typically more than wrong guesses, so the score falls sharply if you run out of time.

notes.p: Divide each section into thirds and memorise where you should be:
points: **Quant (21 Q):** about Q7 done by 30:00 remaining, Q14 by 15:00 remaining.
**Verbal (23 Q):** about Q8 by 30:00, Q16 by 15:00. Reading Comprehension passages front-load reading time, so the first question of a passage takes longer.
**Data Insights (20 Q):** about Q7 by 30:00, Q14 by 15:00. Multi-Source Reasoning sets take extra time to read — budget for them.
If you are behind at a checkpoint, do not panic-rush everything. Simply apply your cut-off rule more strictly on the next hard question.

notes.h: Worked example: the cost of stubbornness
notes.p:
Illustrative numbers. Suppose Arjun usually gets an easy-medium Quant question right 85% of the time in 2 minutes, and a very hard question right 40% of the time in 5 minutes.

If he spends 5 minutes on the hard question, he gains on average **0.4 correct answers**. If he instead guesses on it in 30 seconds (20% chance with five options, so 0.2 correct) and uses the saved 4.5 minutes to answer two easier questions properly instead of rushing them, he gains about 0.2 + 2 × 0.85 = **1.9 expected correct answers** from that time, versus 0.4 plus two rushed guesses (0.4 + 0.4 = 0.8). The guess-and-move-on strategy wins by more than a full question.

That is the logic of the cut-off rule: time is the currency, and hard questions are expensive.
When you guess, guess **intelligently**:
points: **Units digit:** if the answer must end in 6, drop choices that do not.
**Parity and sign:** odd/even, positive/negative eliminations are fast.
**Estimation:** if 18% of 520 is asked, the answer is a bit under 100 — choose 93.6, not 936 or 9.36.
**Plug in the choices:** start with the middle value; the choices are often in order, so one test can eliminate two more.

**Bookmark** every guessed question. If you finish with time left, revisit them — you have up to **3 answer changes** per section. Use them on questions where you now see a clear error, not to second-guess good answers.

notes.p: You pick the order. Common choices: **strongest section first** to build confidence; or **Quant first** while you are freshest, since it is the most tiring for many. Practise your chosen order in at least two full mocks, including the break position. The worst option is deciding on the day.

points: Checking the clock after every question — it wastes time and feeds anxiety.
Believing 'the first 10 questions decide everything' and burning time there.
Never guessing in practice, so guessing feels like failure on the day.
Using review time to change confident answers — first instincts on well-worked questions are usually right.
Taking untimed practice too late into preparation.
Average time: Quant ~2:08, Verbal ~1:57, Data Insights 2:15 per question.
Adaptive: harder questions usually mean you are doing well; consistency matters throughout.
Never leave questions blank — guess on the last ones if you must.
Cut-off rule: about 3 minutes, then eliminate, guess, bookmark, move on.
Checkpoints at one-third and two-thirds of each section.
Guess using units digit, parity, sign, estimation and plugging in choices.
Up to 3 answer edits per section — use them on clear errors only.

cards.title: Test centre or online
cards.body: You can take the GMAT Focus Edition **at a test centre** or **online** from home. The content and scoring are the same. Online needs a quiet private room, a clean desk, a webcam, a stable connection and a system check beforehand. At a centre the logistics are handled for you.

cards.title: ID and arrival
cards.body: Bring the exact ID you registered with — for most Indian candidates this is a **valid passport**, and your name must match your registration. Arrive about 30 minutes early at a centre; for online, log in early to finish the check-in photos and room scan.

cards.title: Your score on the day
cards.body: At the end you see your **unofficial score** on screen. The **Official Score Report**, with section scores, percentiles and performance insights, usually arrives in your mba.com account within a few days. Schools only see a score you choose to send them.

cards.title: Retake rules (check mba.com)
cards.body:
• Wait at least **16 days** between attempts
• At most **5 attempts in a rolling 12 months**
• At most **8 attempts lifetime**
• Scores are valid for **5 years**

cards.title: Sending scores
cards.body: You get a few free score reports (currently five) if you send them soon after your official score is released; later and additional reports cost a fee. You choose which attempt to send, so a weaker earlier score need not reach any school. Check current fees and windows on mba.com.

cards.title: The night before
cards.body: No new topics. Revise your error log for 30 minutes, prepare ID and route (or test the online setup), eat normally, and sleep. Your score is decided by the last 10 weeks, not the last 10 hours.

cards.q: You took the GMAT in March (585) and July (645). Applying in September, what will a school you send the July score to see?
options: Only the July score, if that is the one you send
The March score, since it came first
cards.explain: Under the Focus Edition you choose which score to send, and schools see only the score report you send.

cards.q: Your first attempt was on 1 June. What is the earliest date you could retake under the 16-day rule?
cards.explain: 16 calendar days after 1 June is 17 June.

cards.q: Which is NOT a sensible use of the final 24 hours before the test?
options: Checking ID and travel or online setup
Learning a new topic like permutations from scratch
cards.explain: New topics the day before add anxiety, not points. Consolidate, prepare logistics and rest.

notes.p:
After weeks of study, test day should feel boring. Every surprise — a name mismatch on your ID, a webcam that fails the check, a break you did not plan for — costs focus that should go into questions. The goal of this chapter is to make the logistics automatic and to explain the rules on retakes and score sending so you can make calm decisions.

Fees, windows and policies change. Treat the numbers here as the current picture at the time of writing and **confirm on mba.com** before you book or send anything.

You register through **mba.com**. Book 6–8 weeks ahead for a centre in a busy city (Delhi, Mumbai, Bengaluru, Hyderabad, Chennai and others host centres), particularly in the months before major application deadlines. The registration fee is a few hundred US dollars and differs slightly between centre and online delivery; rescheduling costs a fee that rises as the test date gets closer, and cancelling gives a partial refund that shrinks as you approach the date.

How to choose between centre and online:
points: **Test centre:** controlled environment, no tech risk at home. Better if your home is noisy or your internet is unreliable.

**Online:** no travel, more time slots. You need a private room, a clean desk, a compatible computer and webcam; a proctor watches throughout. Run the official system check days before, on the same machine and network.
Either way, practise with the **same scratch-work method** you will have on the day (a physical or on-screen whiteboard online, a provided noteboard at centres).

notes.p: A smooth sequence:
points: **Night before:** ID ready, route checked or room prepared, alarm set. Light revision of your error log only.
**Morning:** normal breakfast, water, arrive early or log in early. Centres photograph you and may take a palm-vein scan.
**During:** choose your rehearsed section order. Take the optional 10-minute break if you planned to — usually after the section you find most draining.
**After:** you see your unofficial total and section scores on screen.

notes.p:
Your **Official Score Report** usually appears in your mba.com account within a few business days. It includes section scores, percentiles and performance insights (by question type, content area and time use).

With the Focus Edition, **nothing reaches a school unless you send it**, and each report you send contains only the attempt you choose. You get a set of free score reports (currently five) if you choose schools within a short window after your official score is released; additional reports cost a fee each. Scores remain valid for **five years**, which helps if you test early and apply a year or two later.

One caution: once you send a score, you cannot recall it. Decide your target schools before you click.

Retaking is normal — many admitted students took the test two or three times. The rules: at least **16 days** between attempts, at most **five in any rolling 12-month period**, and **eight in a lifetime**.

Worked example (illustrative). Meera scores 615 against a target of 655. Her report shows Quant 81, Verbal 82, DI 77, and the insights show most DI misses on Two-Part Analysis and Multi-Source Reasoning, plus slow pacing. Retaking in 16 days with the same habits would likely give a similar score. Instead she spends **5 weeks** on DI-specific practice and two full mocks, and books the retake once her mocks are consistently near 655. The rule of thumb: **retake when your mocks say you are ready, not when the calendar allows.**

points: Registering under a name that does not exactly match the passport.
Skipping the online system check, then losing the slot to a technical failure.
Sending scores immediately to every school without a plan.
Retaking too soon without changing preparation.
Assuming old-format retake or cancellation rules still apply — the Focus Edition changed them.

notes.h: How it shows up in applications
notes.p: Admissions teams care about the **score you send**, and many say they consider your highest score. Some application forms ask you to self-report scores before the official report is verified. Keep a copy of your score report, note the date, and make sure the score is valid on the application deadline. For scholarships with separate deadlines, check whether they need the official report sent earlier.

points: Test centre or online: same test, same scoring; run the online system check in advance.
Bring the exact ID you registered with (usually a passport for Indian candidates).
Unofficial score on screen; official report in your mba.com account within days.
You choose which attempt to send; schools see only what you send.
A few free score reports soon after release; extra reports cost a fee.
Retakes: 16 days apart, 5 per rolling 12 months, 8 lifetime; scores valid 5 years.
Confirm current fees and policies on mba.com before booking.

cards.title: Why number properties matter
cards.body: A large share of GMAT Quant rests on how integers behave: **odd/even, primes, factors, multiples, remainders, units digits**. These questions reward insight over arithmetic — the right property turns a 4-minute calculation into a 30-second answer.

cards.title: Factors from prime factorisation
cards.body:
Write n = p^a × q^b × r^c (primes).
**Number of positive factors = (a+1)(b+1)(c+1)**
Example: 360 = 2³ × 3² × 5 → (3+1)(2+1)(1+1) = **24** factors.
Also: **GCF × LCM = product** of two numbers.

cards.title: Odd, even and consecutive integers
cards.body: Even ± even = even; odd ± odd = even; odd × anything even = even. Product of **k consecutive integers** is divisible by k! (so n(n+1) is always even). Sum of **3 consecutive integers** is always divisible by 3. 2 is the only even prime; 1 is not prime.

cards.title: Remainders
cards.body:
If n leaves remainder r when divided by d: **n = dq + r**, with 0 ≤ r < d.
To find remainders of expressions, **pick the smallest number that fits** (n = r) and compute.
n ÷ 6 leaves 4 → test n = 4, 10, 16…

cards.title: Units digit cycles
cards.body:
Units digits of powers repeat in cycles of up to 4.
7: 7, 9, 3, 1, 7…
Units digit of 7⁴³: 43 = 4×10 + 3 → third in cycle → **3**.
Digits 0, 1, 5, 6 never change; 4 and 9 alternate (cycle of 2).

cards.title: Test cases beat algebra
cards.body: For 'must be true' questions, try **0, 1, −1, a fraction, a big number, odd and even**. One counter-example kills an answer choice. Integers questions often hide the trap that a variable could be **negative or zero**.

cards.q: How many positive divisors does 72 have?
cards.explain: 72 = 2³ × 3². Number of divisors = (3+1)(2+1) = 12.

cards.q: When x is divided by 7 the remainder is 5. What is the remainder when 3x is divided by 7?
cards.explain: Take x = 5: 3x = 15 = 2×7 + 1. Remainder 1. (Check with x = 12: 36 = 5×7 + 1.)

cards.q: What is the units digit of 3²⁵?
cards.explain: Units digits of powers of 3 cycle 3, 9, 7, 1. 25 = 4×6 + 1, so it is the first in the cycle: 3.

notes.p:
Every integer is built from **primes** the way every molecule is built from atoms. Once you see a number as its prime factorisation, questions about factors, multiples, divisibility, GCF and LCM become bookkeeping. Remainders and units digits follow from one more idea: **patterns repeat**.

The GMAT loves these questions because they separate people who calculate from people who reason. A strong test-taker rarely multiplies big numbers here.
Know these cold:
points: **Divisibility rules:** 3 and 9 — digit sum divisible by 3 or 9; 4 — last two digits divisible by 4; 8 — last three digits; 6 — divisible by 2 and 3; 11 — alternating digit sum divisible by 11.
**Number of factors:** add 1 to each exponent and multiply. 360 → 4 × 3 × 2 = 24.
**GCF:** lowest power of each common prime. **LCM:** highest power of every prime. For two numbers, GCF × LCM = their product.
**Remainders:** n = dq + r with 0 ≤ r < d. Remainders add and multiply: the remainder of a product equals the remainder of the product of remainders.
**Parity:** odd × odd = odd; anything × even = even. A product of consecutive integers contains every smaller factor (n(n+1)(n+2) is divisible by 6).

notes.p:
**Question.** When the positive integer n is divided by 6, the remainder is 4. What is the remainder when 2n is divided by 3?

**Step 1.** Translate: n = 6q + 4.
**Step 2.** 2n = 12q + 8. Since 12q is divisible by 3, only 8 matters.
**Step 3.** 8 = 2 × 3 + 2, so the remainder is **2**.

**Fast check by picking numbers:** the smallest n is 4; 2n = 8; 8 ÷ 3 leaves 2. Try n = 10: 2n = 20 = 6 × 3 + 2. Same answer. When a remainder question has a unique answer, the smallest valid number always works.

**Question.** A metro line runs trains on route A every 12 minutes and on route B every 18 minutes. Both leave the central station at 8:00 a.m. When do they next leave together, and how many positive factors does that interval in minutes have?

**Step 1.** 12 = 2² × 3; 18 = 2 × 3².
**Step 2.** LCM takes the highest powers: 2² × 3² = **36 minutes**. They next leave together at **8:36 a.m.**
**Step 3.** 36 = 2² × 3², so factors = (2+1)(2+1) = **9** (1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 9, 12, 18, 36).
**Check:** GCF(12, 18) = 6, and 6 × 36 = 216 = 12 × 18. ✓

**Question.** What is the units digit of 7⁴³ × 4¹⁰?

**Step 1.** Powers of 7 cycle 7, 9, 3, 1 (length 4). 43 leaves remainder 3 when divided by 4, so 7⁴³ ends in **3**.
**Step 2.** Powers of 4 alternate 4, 6: odd powers end in 4, even powers in 6. 4¹⁰ ends in **6**.
**Step 3.** Units digit of the product = units digit of 3 × 6 = 18 → **8**.

No large number was ever computed. That is the point.

points: Forgetting that **1 is not prime** and **2 is the only even prime**.
Assuming 'integer' means 'positive integer' — zero and negatives are integers too, and 0 is even.
Counting only prime factors when asked for all factors.
Writing a remainder bigger than the divisor (remainder must be less than d).
Using the wrong position in a units-digit cycle when the exponent is a multiple of 4 — that is the **last** element (7⁴⁰ ends in 1).

notes.h: How it shows up in the exam and real jobs
notes.p:
On the GMAT, these appear as stand-alone Problem Solving questions and inside Data Sufficiency in Data Insights ('Is n divisible by 6?'). Typical wrappers: scheduling (LCM), packing items into equal groups (GCF), or 'which must be true' about odd and even integers.

At work the same reasoning runs supply chains and operations. A Zomato or Swiggy operations team batching deliveries, an Indian Railways planner aligning train frequencies, or a factory packing 360 units into equal cartons with no leftovers is solving GCF/LCM problems. Check-digit schemes (like ISBN or card numbers) use remainders to catch typing errors.

points: Factor count: prime-factorise, add 1 to each exponent, multiply.
GCF = lowest common prime powers; LCM = highest prime powers; GCF × LCM = product of two numbers.
n = dq + r, 0 ≤ r < d; pick the smallest valid n to test remainder questions.
Units digits cycle in at most 4 steps; 0, 1, 5, 6 stay fixed.
Product of k consecutive integers is divisible by k!; sum of 3 consecutive integers is divisible by 3.
1 is not prime; 2 is the only even prime; 0 is even.
For 'must be true', hunt for one counter-example using 0, 1, −1, fractions and negatives.

cards.title: One quantity, three costumes
cards.body: A fraction, a decimal and a percent are the same number dressed differently: **1/8 = 0.125 = 12.5%**. GMAT questions switch costumes mid-problem; fluency in switching saves minutes. Memorise eighths, sixths and the common sevenths/ninths.

cards.title: Multipliers
cards.body:
Increase by x% → multiply by (1 + x/100). Decrease by x% → (1 − x/100).
Successive changes **multiply**: +20% then −20% = 1.2 × 0.8 = 0.96 → a **4% net fall**, not zero.

cards.title: 'Of', 'more than', 'percentage points'
cards.body: 'A is 25% **of** B' → A = 0.25B. 'A is 25% **more than** B' → A = 1.25B. A rate moving from 4% to 5% rose by **1 percentage point**, which is a **25%** relative increase. Mixing these up is the most common percent trap.

cards.title: Reverse percent
cards.body: After an 18% GST is added, a phone costs ₹23,600. Pre-tax price? 1.18P = 23,600 → **P = ₹20,000**. Never subtract 18% of 23,600 (that gives ₹19,352, wrong) — the 18% was applied to the smaller base.

cards.q: A shirt is marked up 40% above cost and then sold at a 25% discount on the marked price. The overall result is:
cards.explain: Multipliers: 1.40 × 0.75 = 1.05, a 5% gain on cost.

cards.q: X is 60% of Y. Y is what percent of X?
A bank's home-loan rate rises from 8% to 10%. Which statement is correct?
options: It rose by 2 percentage points, a 25% increase
It rose by 2%, a 2 percentage point increase
cards.explain: 10 − 8 = 2 percentage points. Relative change = 2/8 = 25%.

notes.p:
Percentages are just fractions with a denominator of 100, and almost every business number you will ever read — growth, margins, market share, interest, discounts, taxes — is a percentage. The GMAT tests whether you can move between fractions, decimals and percents fluently, and above all whether you know **what the percentage is a percentage of**.

That last phrase is the whole chapter. Most percent errors are not arithmetic errors; they are **base** errors.
Three tools solve nearly every percent question:
points: **Base:** identify the original value. Percent change always divides by the original (old) value.
**Multipliers:** convert every change into a factor. +12% → ×1.12; −30% → ×0.70. Successive changes multiply; they do not add.
**Reverse:** if a value after a change is known, divide by the multiplier to get back to the original: original = final ÷ (1 + r).
**Fraction-decimal fluency:** 3/8 = 0.375 = 37.5%; 5/6 ≈ 0.833; 2/9 ≈ 0.222. Comparing fractions? Cross-multiply: 5/7 vs 7/10 → 50 vs 49, so 5/7 is larger.

notes.p:
**Question.** A company's revenue rose 25% in 2024 and fell 20% in 2025. In 2026 it rose 10%. By what percent is 2026 revenue above 2023 revenue?

**Step 1.** Multipliers: 1.25, 0.80, 1.10.
**Step 2.** 1.25 × 0.80 = 1.00 (the first two cancel exactly — a 25% rise and 20% fall are inverses, because 1.25 = 5/4 and 0.8 = 4/5).
**Step 3.** 1.00 × 1.10 = 1.10 → **10% above 2023**.

Trap answers: 15% (adding 25 − 20 + 10) and 12% are there for people who add percentages.

**Question.** Priya's salary is 25% more than Karan's. By what percent is Karan's salary less than Priya's?

**Step 1.** Let Karan = 100. Then Priya = 125.
**Step 2.** The difference is 25, but now the base is **Priya's** salary: 25/125 = 0.20.
**Step 3.** Karan earns **20% less** than Priya.

General rule: if A is x% more than B, then B is x/(100 + x) × 100 % less than A. For x = 25: 25/125 = 20%. Picking 100 for the base value is the fastest technique for any problem with only percentages and no actual amounts.

**Question.** A retailer lists a TV at ₹40,000. During a sale it offers 15% off, and then 18% GST is charged on the discounted price. What does the customer pay?

**Step 1.** Discounted price = 40,000 × 0.85 = ₹34,000.
**Step 2.** With GST: 34,000 × 1.18 = ₹40,120.
**Step 3.** The customer pays **₹40,120** — slightly more than the list price, because 0.85 × 1.18 = 1.003.

Note that the order of the two percentage changes does not matter: 40,000 × 1.18 × 0.85 gives the same answer, because multiplication is commutative.

points: **Adding successive percentages** (+20%, −20% ≠ 0%).
**Reversing with the wrong base**: removing 18% GST by subtracting 18% of the final price.
**Confusing percent with percentage points**, especially with interest rates, margins and market share.
**Misreading 'of' vs 'more than'**: 150% of X is 1.5X; 150% more than X is 2.5X.
Calculating exactly when the answer choices are far apart — estimate first.

notes.h: How it shows up in the exam and real jobs
notes.p:
In Quant, percent questions appear in word problems about sales, salaries, populations and prices. In Data Insights they hide inside tables and charts ('By what percent did segment B's share change?'), where you do get a calculator but still need the right base.

In business, the base error is expensive. When an analyst says 'margin improved by 2%', you must ask: two percent, or two percentage points? If Asian Paints' operating margin moved from 18% to 20%, that is 2 points — but an 11% improvement. Retailers like D-Mart and Amazon run discount and pricing decisions entirely on multipliers; a 'buy 2 get 1 free' offer is a 33.3% discount per unit, not 50%.

points: % change = (new − old) / old × 100; the base is always the original.
Convert changes into multipliers; successive changes multiply.
Reverse a change by dividing by the multiplier, not by subtracting.
If A is x% more than B, B is x/(100+x) less than A (25% more ↔ 20% less).
Percentage points measure differences between rates; percent measures relative change.
Pick 100 as the starting value when no amounts are given.
Memorise benchmark fractions (1/6, 1/8, 1/9, 1/12) for quick estimation.

cards.title: A ratio is a recipe
cards.body: A ratio of boys to girls of **3 : 5** says nothing about actual numbers — only that the class splits into 8 equal 'parts'. With 40 students, each part is 5: 15 boys, 25 girls. Total ÷ sum of ratio parts = value of one part. That one move solves most ratio questions.

cards.title: Combining ratios
cards.body:
a : b = 2 : 3 and b : c = 4 : 5. Make **b** match: multiply the first by 4 and the second by 3.
a : b = 8 : 12, b : c = 12 : 15 → **a : b : c = 8 : 12 : 15**.
Always scale to the common term's LCM.

cards.title: Direct and inverse proportion
cards.body: **Direct:** y = kx — double x, double y (cost and quantity). **Inverse:** xy = k — double workers, halve the time. Ask: if one goes up, does the other go up or down? That decides whether you multiply or divide.

cards.title: Weighted mixtures (alligation)
cards.body:
Mix A (value a) and B (value b) to get mean m, with a < m < b:
**Quantity of A : Quantity of B = (b − m) : (m − a)**
Tea at ₹60/kg and ₹90/kg to get ₹70/kg → (90−70) : (70−60) = **2 : 1**.

cards.title: Repeated replacement
cards.body: A 40 L can of milk: remove 8 L and replace with water, twice. Each time milk keeps 32/40 = 4/5 of itself. Milk left = 40 × (4/5)² = **25.6 L**. General: final = initial × (1 − removed/total)ⁿ.

cards.title: Ratios change when you add
cards.body: If 8 boys join a 3 : 5 class of 40, the new ratio is (15+8) : 25 = **23 : 25**. You cannot add 8 to the ratio terms. Always convert to actual numbers, change them, then convert back.

cards.q: If a : b = 3 : 4 and b : c = 6 : 7, what is a : c?
In what ratio must tea costing ₹60/kg be mixed with tea costing ₹90/kg to get a blend worth ₹70/kg?
cards.explain: Alligation: (90 − 70) : (70 − 60) = 20 : 10 = 2 : 1 (cheap : expensive).

cards.q: ₹12,000 of profit is shared among partners A, B and C in the ratio 2 : 3 : 5. How much does C get?
cards.explain: Total parts = 10, so one part = ₹1,200. C gets 5 × 1,200 = ₹6,000.

notes.p:
A **ratio** compares quantities by relative size: 3 : 5 means 'for every 3 of these, 5 of those'. A **proportion** says two ratios are equal. **Mixtures** are ratios in disguise: blending two things with different values (prices, concentrations, scores) produces an average that sits between them, closer to whichever you used more of.

The master technique is the **unit-part method**: a ratio is a set of equal parts; find the value of one part and everything else follows.

points: **Part-to-part vs part-to-whole:** boys : girls = 3 : 5 means boys are 3/8 of the class, not 3/5.
**Unit part:** actual total ÷ sum of ratio terms = one part.
**Combining ratios:** scale so the shared term matches (use its LCM).
**Cross-multiplication:** a/b = c/d ⇔ ad = bc. Useful for 'if 5 kg costs ₹350, what do 8 kg cost?' → 350 × 8/5 = ₹560.
**Alligation:** for two ingredients with values a and b mixed to an average m, quantities are in the ratio (b − m) : (m − a). It is just a weighted average rearranged.
**Replacement:** each draw-and-replace keeps a fraction (1 − x/V) of the original liquid; after n rounds, original left = V(1 − x/V)ⁿ.

notes.p:
**Question.** In a company, the ratio of engineers to managers is 7 : 2. After 10 new managers are hired, the ratio becomes 7 : 3. How many engineers are there?

**Step 1.** Engineers = 7k, managers = 2k (engineers do not change).
**Step 2.** 7k : (2k + 10) = 7 : 3 → 3 × 7k = 7(2k + 10) → 21k = 14k + 70 → k = 10.
**Step 3.** Engineers = 7 × 10 = **70**; managers were 20 and are now 30. Check: 70 : 30 = 7 : 3. ✓

The trick: the quantity that does not change is your anchor.

**Question.** How many litres of a 30% acid solution must be added to 10 litres of a 60% acid solution to make a 40% solution?

**Alligation:** (60 − 40) : (40 − 30) = 20 : 10 = 2 : 1. So 30%-solution : 60%-solution = 2 : 1. With 10 L of the 60% solution, we need **20 L** of the 30% solution.

**Algebra check:** acid = 0.30(20) + 0.60(10) = 6 + 6 = 12 L in 30 L of liquid → 12/30 = 40%. ✓

Notice the mixture's concentration (40%) is closer to 30% because there is more of the 30% solution — that is the intuition behind every weighted average.

**Question.** Three friends start a café in Pune. Asha invests ₹4 lakh for 12 months, Bilal ₹6 lakh for 6 months, and Chetan ₹3 lakh for 12 months. Profit of ₹5.2 lakh is shared in proportion to capital × time. What is Bilal's share?

**Step 1.** Capital-months: Asha 48, Bilal 36, Chetan 36 → ratio 48 : 36 : 36 = 4 : 3 : 3.
**Step 2.** One part = 5.2 lakh / 10 = ₹52,000.
**Step 3.** Bilal = 3 × 52,000 = **₹1.56 lakh**.

points: Treating a part-to-part ratio as a fraction of the whole.
Adding the same number to both terms of a ratio and assuming it stays equal.
Combining ratios without matching the shared term.
In alligation, putting the differences on the wrong ingredient (the cheaper ingredient gets b − m, the distance from the **dearer** one).
Forgetting that replacement is multiplicative, not a fixed subtraction each round.

notes.h: How it shows up in the exam and real jobs
notes.p: On the GMAT, ratios hide in recipes, mixtures, populations, investments and in Data Insights tables ('What is the ratio of 2025 to 2024 sales for region C?'). In management they are everywhere: debt-to-equity, current ratio, inventory turnover, staff-to-customer ratios at a hospital chain, and product mix. Amul's procurement blends milk from many villages with different fat content to hit a standard fat percentage — an alligation problem solved at scale every day. Partnerships in Indian law traditionally share profits in an agreed ratio, often linked to capital.

points: One part = total ÷ sum of ratio terms.
Part-to-part 3 : 5 means 3/8 and 5/8 of the whole.
Combine ratios by scaling the shared term to a common value.
Direct proportion: y = kx; inverse proportion: xy = k.
Alligation: A : B = (b − m) : (m − a).
Replacement: original left = V(1 − x/V)ⁿ.
Anchor on the quantity that does not change.

cards.title: The average is a total in disguise
cards.body: **Mean = Sum ÷ Count**, so **Sum = Mean × Count**. Nearly every average question is solved by converting averages to totals, doing the arithmetic on totals, then converting back. Average of 5 numbers is 40 → their sum is 200.

cards.title: Weighted average
cards.body:
When groups differ in size: **mean = (n₁x₁ + n₂x₂) / (n₁ + n₂)**.
30 students averaging 70 and 20 averaging 80 → (2,100 + 1,600) / 50 = **74**. The combined mean leans toward the bigger group.

cards.title: Median and mode
cards.body: **Median:** the middle value after sorting; with an even count, the mean of the two middle values. **Mode:** most frequent value. **Range:** max − min. The median resists outliers: one billionaire moves a town's mean income a lot, its median barely.

cards.title: Standard deviation, intuitively
cards.body: SD measures how **spread out** values are around the mean. The GMAT rarely asks you to compute it; it asks you to compare. {8, 10, 12} has a smaller SD than {2, 10, 18}. A set of identical numbers has SD = 0.

cards.title: How SD reacts
cards.body:
Add or subtract the same number from every value → **mean shifts, SD unchanged**.
Multiply every value by k → **mean and SD both multiply by |k|**.
Add a value equal to the mean → **SD falls** (more points at zero distance).

cards.title: Evenly spaced sets
cards.body: For evenly spaced numbers (like consecutive integers), **mean = median = (first + last) / 2**. Average of integers 11 to 59 = 35, with no adding needed.

cards.q: The average of 6 numbers is 15. When a seventh number is added, the average becomes 16. What is the seventh number?
cards.explain: Old sum = 90. New sum = 7 × 16 = 112. Seventh number = 112 − 90 = 22.

cards.q: Every value in the set {3, 5, 7, 9, 11} is increased by 10. What happens?
cards.explain: Adding a constant shifts every value and the mean by 10, but distances from the mean are unchanged, so the SD stays the same.

cards.q: What is the median of {12, 3, 9, 15, 6, 20}?
cards.explain: Sorted: 3, 6, 9, 12, 15, 20. Even count, so median = (9 + 12)/2 = 10.5. (10.8 is roughly the mean, 65/6.)

notes.p:
Statistics on the GMAT is about **describing a group with a few numbers**: a centre (mean, median) and a spread (range, standard deviation). The questions are rarely computational; they test whether you understand what these measures mean and how they respond when the data change.

The single most useful habit: **turn averages into sums**. Sum = mean × count. Once you think in totals, adding, removing or combining groups becomes simple arithmetic.

points: **Mean** = sum ÷ count. Sensitive to extreme values.
**Median** = middle value of the sorted list (average of the two middle values if the count is even). Robust to outliers.
**Mode** = most frequent value; a set can have more than one.
**Range** = largest − smallest.
**Standard deviation** = roughly the typical distance of values from the mean. Formally the square root of the average squared deviation, but intuition is what is tested.
**Weighted average** = Σ(weight × value) ÷ Σ(weights). The result always lies between the smallest and largest group means, closer to the heavier group.

notes.p:
**Question.** The average weight of 5 parcels is 40 kg. When one parcel is removed, the average of the remaining 4 is 38 kg. What does the removed parcel weigh?

**Step 1.** Total of 5 = 5 × 40 = 200 kg.
**Step 2.** Total of 4 = 4 × 38 = 152 kg.
**Step 3.** Removed parcel = 200 − 152 = **48 kg**.

**Sanity check:** removing a parcel heavier than the average should pull the average down — it did (40 → 38).

notes.h: Worked problem 2: weighted average in reverse
notes.p:
**Question.** A firm's 50 employees have an average salary of ₹74,000 a month. The 30 analysts average ₹70,000. What do the other 20 (managers) average?

**Step 1.** Total payroll = 50 × 74,000 = ₹37,00,000.
**Step 2.** Analysts' total = 30 × 70,000 = ₹21,00,000.
**Step 3.** Managers' total = ₹16,00,000 → average = 16,00,000 / 20 = **₹80,000**.

**Balance check:** the overall average (74) is 4 above 70 and 6 below 80. Distances are in ratio 4 : 6 = 2 : 3, which is the inverse of the group sizes 30 : 20. This 'see-saw' view is the same as alligation from the ratios chapter.

**Question.** Which set has the greatest standard deviation?
A {10, 10, 10, 10}  B {8, 9, 11, 12}  C {1, 10, 10, 19}  D {101, 102, 104, 105}

**Reasoning.** All sets except D have mean 10; D has mean 103. A has SD 0. B's values sit 1–2 from the mean. D is just B shifted by 93, so its SD equals B's. C has two values 9 away from the mean. **C** has the largest spread.

No formula was needed: compare **distances from the mean**.

points: Averaging two averages when the groups have different sizes.
Forgetting to sort before finding the median.
Thinking adding a constant changes SD (it does not) or that multiplying leaves it unchanged (it does not).
Assuming mean = median in skewed data. Income, house prices and startup valuations are right-skewed: mean > median.
Confusing 'average increased by 2' with 'each value increased by 2'.

notes.h: How it shows up in the exam and real jobs
notes.p: In Quant, averages appear as test scores, salaries and sales figures. In Data Insights, Table Analysis questions ask whether a column's median exceeds its mean, or which region has the most variable sales. In business, the mean vs median distinction drives real decisions. India's household income data is heavily skewed, so a mean-based 'average customer' can mislead a product team; firms like HDFC Bank segment customers using medians and percentiles. Standard deviation is the language of risk in finance (volatility) and of quality in operations — Toyota's and Motorola's quality programmes focused on cutting variation, not only shifting the average.

points: Sum = mean × count; work in totals.
Weighted average lies between group means, nearer the larger group.
Median: sort first; even count → average the middle two.
For evenly spaced sets, mean = median = (first + last)/2.
Adding a constant: mean shifts, SD unchanged. Multiplying by k: both scale by |k|.
SD measures distance from the mean; identical values → SD = 0.
Skewed data: mean is pulled toward the long tail.

cards.title: One equation for everything
cards.body: **Distance = Rate × Time** and **Work = Rate × Time**. Speed problems and work problems are the same problem. Write a small table with columns R, T, D (or W) for each person or vehicle, and fill it in.

cards.title: Average speed
cards.body:
**Average speed = total distance ÷ total time** — never the average of the speeds.
For two equal distances at speeds a and b: **2ab / (a + b)**.
40 km/h out, 60 km/h back → 2·40·60/100 = **48 km/h**.

cards.title: Relative speed
cards.body: Moving **toward** each other: add speeds. Moving in the **same direction**: subtract. Two trains 300 km apart, approaching at 70 and 80 km/h, close the gap at 150 km/h → meet in **2 hours**.

cards.title: Combined work
cards.body:
Convert each worker to a rate: job in 6 h → 1/6 job per hour.
**Rates add:** 1/6 + 1/12 = 1/4 → together **4 hours**.
A drain works against you: fill in 10 h, empty in 15 h → 1/10 − 1/15 = 1/30 → **30 h**.

cards.title: Units first
cards.body: Convert km/h to m/s by multiplying by **5/18** (72 km/h = 20 m/s). Mixed units are the most common silent error. Write units next to every number in your table.

cards.title: Train past a platform
cards.body: A 200 m train at 72 km/h (20 m/s) crosses a 300 m platform. It must cover its own length plus the platform: 500 m ÷ 20 m/s = **25 s**. Passing a pole (zero length) takes 200/20 = 10 s.

cards.q: Ravi cycles 12 km to college at 12 km/h and returns at 6 km/h. What is his average speed for the round trip?
cards.explain: Total distance 24 km; time = 1 h + 2 h = 3 h. Average = 24/3 = 8 km/h (or 2·12·6/18 = 8).

cards.q: A can paint a house in 10 days and B in 15 days. Working together, how long do they take?
A 200 m long train moving at 72 km/h passes a signal pole. How long does it take?

notes.p:
Rates connect three quantities: how fast, how long, how much. **Distance = Rate × Time** for travel, **Work = Rate × Time** for jobs, **Output = Rate × Time** for machines. If you know two, you know the third.

The insight that unlocks hard problems: **rates add, times do not**. Two people working together add their rates (jobs per hour), never their times. Two vehicles approaching each other add their speeds.

points: **RTD table:** one row per traveller or worker, columns Rate, Time, Distance/Work. Write the relationship between rows (same time, same distance, total work = 1).
**Average speed** = total distance / total time. For two equal legs: 2ab/(a + b), which is always below the simple average.
**Relative speed:** opposite directions add; same direction subtract.
**Work rate:** a job done in t hours has rate 1/t. Combined rate = sum of rates; combined time = 1 / combined rate. For two workers: ab/(a + b).
**Pipes and drains:** filling rates positive, draining rates negative.
**Units:** km/h → m/s multiply by 5/18; m/s → km/h multiply by 18/5. Minutes and hours must match.

notes.p:
**Question.** A delivery van leaves a warehouse at 9:00 a.m. at 40 km/h. A car leaves the same warehouse at 10:30 a.m. on the same road at 60 km/h. At what time does the car catch the van?

**Step 1.** Head start: the van drives 1.5 h × 40 = 60 km before the car leaves.
**Step 2.** Same direction, so the gap closes at 60 − 40 = 20 km/h.
**Step 3.** Time to close 60 km = 60/20 = 3 h after 10:30 → **1:30 p.m.**
**Check:** by 1:30 the van has driven 4.5 h × 40 = 180 km; the car 3 h × 60 = 180 km. ✓

notes.h: Worked problem 2: combined work with a late joiner
notes.p:
**Question.** Machine A can print an order in 6 hours, machine B in 12 hours. A starts alone; after 2 hours B joins. How long does the whole job take?

**Step 1.** A's rate = 1/6 per hour. In 2 hours A completes 2/6 = 1/3 of the job. Remaining = 2/3.
**Step 2.** Combined rate = 1/6 + 1/12 = 3/12 = 1/4 per hour.
**Step 3.** Time for 2/3 at 1/4 per hour = (2/3) ÷ (1/4) = 8/3 h = 2 h 40 min.
**Total = 2 h + 2 h 40 min = 4 h 40 min.**

Sanity check: A alone needs 6 h, both from the start need 4 h, so an answer between 4 and 6 h makes sense.

**Question.** A cab drives from Mumbai to Pune (150 km) at 50 km/h and back at 75 km/h. What is its average speed?

**Step 1.** Time out = 150/50 = 3 h. Time back = 150/75 = 2 h.
**Step 2.** Average = 300 km / 5 h = **60 km/h** (not 62.5).
**Shortcut:** 2 × 50 × 75 / 125 = 7,500/125 = 60. ✓ The slower leg takes more time, so it gets more weight.

points: Averaging speeds instead of dividing total distance by total time.
Adding times when people work together (6 h + 12 h ≠ anything useful).
Mixing minutes and hours, or km/h and m/s.
Forgetting the train's own length when it crosses a platform or bridge.
Using the wrong relative speed sign (approaching vs chasing).

notes.h: How it shows up in the exam and real jobs
notes.p: Rates questions are a GMAT staple in Problem Solving, and Data Insights often wraps them in Two-Part Analysis ('choose the rate for machine X and machine Y'). In operations, rates are capacity: an Amazon fulfilment centre's throughput in parcels per hour, a Maruti Suzuki assembly line's cars per shift, or a call centre's tickets per agent-hour. 'If we add one more line, how much faster do we clear the backlog?' is a combined-work question. Logistics firms like Delhivery plan routes with average-speed logic — and know that slow city stretches dominate total time.

points: D = R × T and W = R × T; build a table.
Average speed = total distance / total time; equal legs → 2ab/(a + b).
Toward each other: add speeds. Same direction: subtract.
Work rates add: together time = 1/(1/a + 1/b) = ab/(a + b).
Drains subtract from fill rates.
km/h × 5/18 = m/s; include the train's own length.
Sanity-check: combined time is less than the fastest individual time.

cards.title: Simple interest
cards.body:
**SI = P × R × T / 100**. Interest is earned only on the original principal.
₹1,00,000 at 10% for 2 years → SI = **₹20,000**. Amount = ₹1,20,000. Grows in a straight line.

cards.title: Compound interest
cards.body:
**A = P(1 + r/n)ⁿᵗ** (r as a decimal, n compoundings per year).
₹1,00,000 at 10% compounded annually for 2 years → 1,00,000 × 1.1² = **₹1,21,000**. Interest earns interest, so growth curves upward.

cards.title: CI − SI shortcut (2 years)
cards.body:
For 2 years, annual compounding: **CI − SI = P × (r)²** with r as a decimal.
₹1,00,000 at 10%: 1,00,000 × 0.01 = **₹1,000** — exactly the interest on the first year's interest.

cards.title: Profit, loss and markup
cards.body:
**Profit % = Profit / Cost × 100** — cost is the base.
Marked price = cost × (1 + markup). Selling price = marked × (1 − discount).
Buy at ₹800, mark up 25% to ₹1,000, give 10% off → sell at ₹900 → profit **12.5%**.

cards.title: Effective annual rate
cards.body: 8% p.a. compounded half-yearly = 4% per half-year → 1.04² = 1.0816 → **8.16%** effective. More frequent compounding means a slightly higher effective rate. Banks quote both; compare loans using the effective rate.

cards.title: Rule of 72
cards.body: Money roughly **doubles in 72 ÷ rate** years at compound interest. At 8% → about 9 years; at 12% → about 6. Great for estimating and eliminating answer choices fast.

cards.q: What is the simple interest on ₹5,000 at 6% per annum for 3 years?
cards.explain: SI = 5,000 × 6 × 3 / 100 = ₹900. (₹955.08 would be the compound interest.)

cards.q: What is the difference between compound interest (compounded annually) and simple interest on ₹20,000 for 2 years at 5% per annum?
A trader sells two phones at ₹1,200 each. On one he gains 20%; on the other he loses 20%. Overall he makes:

notes.p:
Interest is the **price of money over time**; profit is the **reward for selling above cost**. Both are percentage problems with a specific base. Simple interest always uses the original principal as base; compound interest updates the base every period. Profit percentage always uses **cost** as the base unless the question explicitly says 'profit as a percent of selling price'.

Einstein almost certainly never called compound interest 'the eighth wonder of the world' (the quote is unverified), but the idea behind it is real: growth on growth becomes powerful over long periods.

points: **Simple interest:** SI = PRT/100; amount = P + SI. Linear growth.
**Compound interest:** A = P(1 + r/n)^(nt). CI = A − P. Exponential growth.
**Two-year shortcut:** CI − SI = P·r² (annual compounding).
**Effective annual rate** = (1 + r/n)ⁿ − 1.
**Profit % = (SP − CP)/CP × 100. Loss % = (CP − SP)/CP × 100.**
**Markup and discount** chain as multipliers: SP = CP × (1 + m) × (1 − d).
**Rule of 72:** doubling time ≈ 72 / rate in percent.

notes.p:
**Question.** Neha invests ₹1,00,000 for 2 years at 10% per annum. How much more does she earn with annual compounding than with simple interest?

**Simple:** 1,00,000 × 10 × 2 / 100 = ₹20,000.
**Compound:** Year 1 interest = ₹10,000 → balance ₹1,10,000. Year 2 interest = ₹11,000 → balance ₹1,21,000. CI = ₹21,000.
**Difference = ₹1,000**, which is 10% of the first year's ₹10,000 interest — 'interest on interest'. Shortcut: P·r² = 1,00,000 × 0.01 = ₹1,000. ✓

notes.h: Worked problem 2: markup, discount and profit
notes.p:
**Question.** A shopkeeper buys a mixer for ₹800, marks it 25% above cost and then offers a 10% discount on the marked price. What is the profit percentage?

**Step 1.** Marked price = 800 × 1.25 = ₹1,000.
**Step 2.** Selling price = 1,000 × 0.90 = ₹900.
**Step 3.** Profit = ₹100 on a cost of ₹800 → **12.5%**.
**Multiplier check:** 1.25 × 0.90 = 1.125 → 12.5% profit. ✓

notes.h: Worked problems 3 & 4: half-yearly compounding; Rule of 72 and margin vs markup
notes.p:
**Question.** ₹10,000 is deposited at 8% per annum compounded half-yearly. What is the balance after 1 year, and what is the effective annual rate?

**Step 1.** Rate per half-year = 4%; periods = 2.
**Step 2.** A = 10,000 × 1.04² = 10,000 × 1.0816 = **₹10,816**.
**Step 3.** Effective annual rate = 816 / 10,000 = **8.16%**.

At 8% compounded annually she would have ₹10,800; the extra ₹16 comes from earning interest on the first half-year's ₹400.

**Question.** Rahul invests ₹5 lakh at 9% compounded annually. Roughly when does it double? Separately, a retailer prices a jacket at a 25% markup on cost of ₹2,400. What is the margin on selling price?

**Part 1.** Rule of 72: 72 / 9 ≈ **8 years**. Exact check: 1.09⁸ ≈ 1.993, so after 8 years the balance is about ₹9.96 lakh — very close to double.
**Part 2.** Selling price = 2,400 × 1.25 = ₹3,000. Profit = ₹600. Markup on cost = 600/2,400 = 25%, but **margin on price = 600/3,000 = 20%**.

The same ₹600 is 25% or 20% depending on the base. Always ask which base a quoted percentage uses.

points: Using selling price as the base for profit %.
Adding markup and discount percentages (25% − 10% ≠ 15% profit).
Forgetting to divide the rate and multiply the periods for half-yearly or quarterly compounding.
Assuming equal % gain and loss at the same selling price cancel out — they produce a net loss.
Mixing up 'amount' (principal + interest) with 'interest'.

notes.h: How it shows up in the exam and real jobs
notes.p: Expect interest questions framed as loans, deposits and investments, and profit questions framed as retail pricing. In MBA courses this is the seed of **time value of money**, which underlies NPV, bond pricing, EMIs and valuation. In jobs: a banker at SBI comparing a fixed deposit compounded quarterly against one compounded annually, a credit-card team explaining why 3% per month is far more than 36% a year effective (1.03¹² − 1 ≈ 42.6%), or a retailer like Tanishq or Croma designing a festive discount that still protects margin. Marketers and finance teams argue over markup vs margin constantly — a 25% markup is only a 20% margin on selling price.

points: SI = PRT/100 (linear); CI: A = P(1 + r/n)^(nt) (exponential).
2-year CI − SI = P·r².
Effective rate = (1 + r/n)ⁿ − 1; 8% half-yearly → 8.16%.
Profit % is on cost; markup and discount multiply.
Same SP with x% gain and x% loss → net loss of x²/100 %.
Rule of 72: doubling time ≈ 72/rate.
25% markup on cost = 20% margin on price.

cards.title: Word problems are translation
cards.body: Most GMAT Quant questions are word problems. The maths is often easy; the skill is **turning English into equations** without error. Define variables clearly ('let c = number of children'), write one equation per fact, then solve.

cards.title: The translation dictionary
cards.body:
'is / was / will be' → **=**
'of' → **×**
'more than' → **+**; 'less than' → **−** (reversed order: '5 less than x' = x − 5)
'per' → **÷**
'twice as many A as B' → **A = 2B**

cards.title: Two unknowns need two equations
cards.body: With two variables you usually need **two independent equations**. Solve by **substitution** (express one variable, plug in) or **elimination** (add/subtract equations to cancel a variable). If one equation is a multiple of the other, there are infinitely many solutions.

cards.title: Ages in one line
cards.body: A father is 3 times his son's age. In 12 years he will be twice the son's age. F = 3S and F + 12 = 2(S + 12) → 3S + 12 = 2S + 24 → **S = 12, F = 36**. Check: in 12 years, 48 = 2 × 24. ✓

cards.title: Solve for what is asked
cards.body: If a question asks for x + y, look for a shortcut. 2x + y = 11 and x + 2y = 13: adding gives 3x + 3y = 24, so **x + y = 8** — without ever finding x or y.

cards.title: Backsolve from the choices
cards.body: When the answer choices are numbers, **plug them in**, starting from the middle choice (C). If C is too large, the answer is A or B; if too small, D or E. This often beats setting up the algebra.

cards.q: Five less than twice a number is 17. What is the number?
Pens cost ₹15 and notebooks ₹40. Riya buys 12 items for ₹305 in total. How many notebooks did she buy?
cards.explain: p + n = 12 and 15p + 40n = 305. Substituting p = 12 − n: 180 + 25n = 305 → n = 5. Check: 7 pens (₹105) + 5 notebooks (₹200) = ₹305.

cards.q: If 3x + 2y = 18 and x − y = 1, what is x + y?

notes.p:
Word problems test **modelling**: taking a messy description of the real world and writing a precise mathematical statement. That is exactly what managers do when they turn 'we want break-even by March with two products' into a spreadsheet. The GMAT keeps the algebra simple (mostly linear equations) so that the translation is the real test.

A reliable process beats cleverness: **define → translate → solve → check**.

points: **Define** each unknown in words: 'a = number of adult tickets', not just 'a'.
**Translate** one sentence at a time using the dictionary: is → =, of → ×, more than → +, less than → − (order flips), per → ÷, 'A is twice B' → A = 2B.
**Count** unknowns and independent equations; you usually need as many equations as unknowns.
**Solve** by substitution or elimination. Elimination is faster when coefficients line up.
**Check** the answer against the original words, not your equations — a translation error survives an algebra check.

notes.p:
**Question.** A cinema in Bengaluru sells adult tickets at ₹300 and child tickets at ₹180. One show sells 40 tickets for ₹9,600. How many child tickets were sold?

**Define:** a = adult tickets, c = child tickets.
**Translate:** a + c = 40; 300a + 180c = 9,600.
**Solve:** substitute c = 40 − a → 300a + 7,200 − 180a = 9,600 → 120a = 2,400 → a = 20, so **c = 20**.
**Check:** 20 × 300 + 20 × 180 = 6,000 + 3,600 = ₹9,600. ✓

**Shortcut thinking:** if all 40 were child tickets, revenue would be ₹7,200. Each swap to an adult ticket adds ₹120. The extra ₹2,400 needs 20 swaps — so 20 adults.

notes.h: Worked problem 2: ages with a twist
notes.p:
**Question.** Five years ago, Meera was 4 times as old as her daughter. In 5 years, she will be twice as old as her daughter. How old is Meera now?

**Define:** M and D = current ages.
**Translate:** M − 5 = 4(D − 5) and M + 5 = 2(D + 5).
**Simplify:** M = 4D − 15 and M = 2D + 5.
**Solve:** 4D − 15 = 2D + 5 → 2D = 20 → D = 10, **M = 25**.
**Check:** five years ago 20 and 5 (4×) ✓; in five years 30 and 15 (2×) ✓.

notes.h: Worked problem 3: when you cannot solve — and do not need to
notes.p:
**Question.** A café sells tea and samosas at fixed prices. Ankit buys 2 teas and 3 samosas; Bina buys 4 teas and 6 samosas. Can you find the price of a samosa from 'Ankit paid ₹85 and Bina paid ₹170'?

No new information: Bina's order is exactly double Ankit's, so 4t + 6s = 170 is just 2 × (2t + 3s = 85). Two equations, but they are **not independent** — infinitely many (t, s) pairs fit. This idea is central to **Data Sufficiency** in the Data Insights section: two statements that say the same thing do not give a unique answer.

points: Reversing 'less than': '7 less than y' is y − 7, not 7 − y.
Writing 'there are 3 times as many boys as girls' as 3B = G (correct: B = 3G). Test with numbers: 30 boys, 10 girls.
Solving for x when the question asked for x + y, or for the number of children when it asked for adults.
Not checking whether the second equation is truly new information.
Skipping the check against the original words.

notes.h: How it shows up in the exam and real jobs
notes.p: Translation is the backbone of GMAT Quant — ratios, rates, interest and sets problems all start with it. In Data Insights, Two-Part Analysis questions often ask you to pick two values that jointly satisfy a word constraint. In jobs, every pricing or capacity model is a system of equations: a D2C brand deciding how many units of two products to produce given a budget and a warehouse limit, or a consultant solving for the price at which a client breaks even. Clear variable definitions are also the first habit of good spreadsheet modelling.

points: Define → translate → solve → check.
is → =, of → ×, more than → +, less than → − (order flips), per → ÷.
Test translations of 'times as many' with sample numbers.
n unknowns usually need n independent equations.
Multiples of the same equation add no information.
Backsolve from the middle answer choice when options are numbers.
Answer the question asked (x + y, not x).

cards.title: Factoring quadratics
cards.body:
x² + bx + c = 0: find two numbers that **multiply to c and add to b**.
x² − 5x − 14 = 0 → −7 and +2 → (x − 7)(x + 2) = 0 → **x = 7 or −2**.
Always set the equation to zero first.

cards.title: Three identities to know cold
cards.body:
(a + b)² = a² + 2ab + b²
(a − b)² = a² − 2ab + b²
**a² − b² = (a + b)(a − b)**
99² − 1 = 98 × 100 = 9,800. The GMAT disguises these constantly.

cards.title: Sum and product of roots
cards.body:
For ax² + bx + c = 0: **sum of roots = −b/a**, **product = c/a**.
For 2x² − 6x + 4 = 0: sum = 3, product = 2 (roots 1 and 2). Useful when you need a combination of roots, not the roots themselves.

cards.title: Functions are machines
cards.body: f(x) = 2x² − 3 means 'square the input, double it, subtract 3'. f(a + 1) = 2(a + 1)² − 3. For **composite** functions f(g(x)), work from the inside out: compute g first, then feed it to f.

cards.title: Hidden quadratic
cards.body: If x + 1/x = 5, find x² + 1/x². Square both sides: x² + 2 + 1/x² = 25 → **x² + 1/x² = 23**. Squaring a sum to reach a sum of squares is a classic GMAT move.

cards.title: Never divide by a variable
cards.body: x² = 3x does **not** mean x = 3. Divide by x and you lose x = 0. Instead: x² − 3x = 0 → x(x − 3) = 0 → **x = 0 or 3**.

cards.q: What is the product of the roots of x² + x − 12 = 0?
cards.explain: Product = c/a = −12. (Roots are 3 and −4; 3 × −4 = −12.)

cards.q: If f(x) = x² − 2x and g(x) = x + 3, what is f(g(1))?
If a² + b² = 29 and ab = 10, what is (a − b)²?

notes.p:
A **quadratic** is any expression where the highest power of the variable is 2. Quadratics model anything with a peak or a trough: revenue as price rises, area for a fixed fence, profit as output grows. On the GMAT, they appear as equations to factor, as identities in disguise, and as functions.

The skill is **pattern recognition**: seeing that 49 − x² is (7 − x)(7 + x), or that a question about x² + 1/x² is really about (x + 1/x)².

points: **Standard form:** ax² + bx + c = 0. Move everything to one side first.
**Factoring:** find two numbers with product c and sum b (when a = 1).
**Quadratic formula** (rarely needed): x = [−b ± √(b² − 4ac)] / 2a. The discriminant b² − 4ac tells you the number of real roots: positive → 2, zero → 1, negative → 0.
**Sum of roots = −b/a; product = c/a.**
**Identities:** (a ± b)² and a² − b² = (a + b)(a − b).
**Functions:** substitute the whole input in brackets; composite functions work inside out. A **domain** issue appears when a function has a square root (input ≥ 0) or a denominator (≠ 0).
**Maximum/minimum:** y = −(x − h)² + k peaks at x = h with value k; a parabola opening downward (a < 0) has a maximum at x = −b/2a.

notes.p:
**Question.** The product of two consecutive positive even integers is 168. What is their sum?

**Step 1.** Let them be n and n + 2: n(n + 2) = 168 → n² + 2n − 168 = 0.
**Step 2.** Two numbers multiplying to −168 and adding to 2: 14 and −12 → (n + 14)(n − 12) = 0.
**Step 3.** n = 12 (positive), so the integers are 12 and 14 and their sum is **26**.
**Check:** 12 × 14 = 168. ✓ (Faster: √168 ≈ 13, so try 12 × 14.)

**Question.** If x² − y² = 48 and x + y = 12, what is x?

**Step 1.** x² − y² = (x + y)(x − y) → 48 = 12(x − y) → x − y = 4.
**Step 2.** Add the equations: 2x = 16 → **x = 8** (and y = 4).
**Check:** 64 − 16 = 48 ✓.

The question looked like it needed squares; the identity reduced it to a linear system.

**Question.** An online course platform estimates monthly enrolments E = 1,000 − 5p, where p is the price in rupees. At what price is revenue maximised, and what is the maximum revenue? (Illustrative model.)

**Step 1.** Revenue R = p × E = p(1,000 − 5p) = 1,000p − 5p².
**Step 2.** A downward parabola peaks at p = −b/2a = −1,000 / (2 × −5) = **₹100**.
**Step 3.** E = 1,000 − 500 = 500 enrolments; R = 100 × 500 = **₹50,000**.
**Check:** at ₹90, R = 90 × 550 = 49,500; at ₹110, R = 110 × 450 = 49,500. Symmetric around 100. ✓

points: Dividing both sides by a variable and losing the root x = 0.
Forgetting the negative root when solving x² = 25 (x = ±5).
Writing (a + b)² = a² + b² — the 2ab term is the most common algebra error on the test.
Substituting into a function without brackets: f(a + 1) for f(x) = x² is (a + 1)², not a + 1².
Not rejecting roots that break a condition (negative lengths, non-integers when integers are required).

notes.h: How it shows up in the exam and real jobs
notes.p: GMAT questions favour identities and factoring over heavy formula work, and often ask for an expression (x + y, ab, x² + 1/x²) rather than a single variable. In MBA economics, quadratics are the shape of revenue and profit curves: the price that maximises revenue sits where marginal revenue is zero — the same −b/2a point. Pricing teams at airlines, ride-hailing apps and streaming services estimate demand curves and look for exactly this peak, though real demand is rarely a perfect straight line.

points: Set to zero, then factor: product c, sum b.
(a + b)² = a² + 2ab + b²; (a − b)² = a² − 2ab + b²; a² − b² = (a + b)(a − b).
Sum of roots −b/a; product c/a; discriminant decides number of real roots.
Never divide by a variable that could be zero.
x² = k gives ±√k.
Composite functions: inside first.
Parabola vertex at x = −b/2a (max when a < 0).

cards.title: Inequalities behave like equations — almost
cards.body: You can add, subtract, multiply or divide both sides as usual, with one exception: **multiplying or dividing by a negative flips the sign**. −3x > 12 → x < −4. Never multiply by a variable unless you know its sign.

cards.title: Absolute value = distance
cards.body:
|x| is the distance of x from 0. **|x − a| is the distance between x and a.**
|x − 4| < 3 → x is within 3 of 4 → **1 < x < 7**.
|x − 4| > 3 → **x < 1 or x > 7**.

cards.title: Solving |expression| = k
cards.body:
