Split into two cases: expression = k or expression = −k.
|2x − 3| = 7 → 2x − 3 = 7 (x = 5) or 2x − 3 = −7 (x = −2).
If k is negative, there is **no solution**.

cards.title: Compound inequalities
cards.body: Treat all three parts together: −3 < 2x + 1 ≤ 7 → subtract 1: −4 < 2x ≤ 6 → divide by 2: **−2 < x ≤ 3**. Integer solutions: −1, 0, 1, 2, 3 — five of them.

cards.title: Sign logic
cards.body: If xy > 0, x and y have the **same** sign. If xy < 0, **opposite** signs. If x² > x, then x > 1 or x < 0. Between 0 and 1, powers shrink: for 0 < x < 1, **x³ < x² < x < √x**.

cards.title: Test zones with numbers
cards.body: For 'which must be true' questions, test a number from each zone: negative, between 0 and 1, greater than 1, and the boundaries 0 and 1. Fractions and negatives are where intuition fails.

cards.q: How many integers x satisfy |x + 2| ≤ 3?
If −2x + 5 > 11, which must be true?
cards.explain: −2x > 6. Dividing by −2 flips the sign: x < −3.

cards.q: If 0 < x < 1, which of these is greatest?
cards.explain: Between 0 and 1, higher powers get smaller and roots get larger. E.g. x = 0.25: √x = 0.5 > 0.25 > 0.0625 > 0.0156.

notes.p:
An equation pins a variable to a value; an **inequality** describes a range. Business constraints are almost always inequalities: budget ≤ ₹50 lakh, delivery time < 30 minutes, margin ≥ 15%. **Absolute value** captures distance or tolerance: a part must be within 0.5 mm of spec, a forecast within 10% of actuals.

Two rules carry most of the chapter: **flip the sign when multiplying or dividing by a negative**, and **read |x − a| as 'distance from a'**.

points: **Operations:** add/subtract freely; multiply/divide by a positive freely; by a negative, flip the sign.
**Never multiply both sides by a variable of unknown sign** — split into cases or move everything to one side.
**|x − a| < k** ⇔ a − k < x < a + k (inside the band).
**|x − a| > k** ⇔ x < a − k or x > a + k (outside the band).
**|expr| = k:** two cases, expr = k or expr = −k; always check solutions in the original.
**Combining inequalities:** you may add inequalities pointing the same way (a > b and c > d → a + c > b + d). Do not subtract or divide them.
**Number line zones:** x < −1, −1 < x < 0, 0 < x < 1, x > 1 behave differently for powers and reciprocals.

notes.h: Worked problem 1: range of a combination
notes.p:
**Question.** If 2 ≤ a ≤ 5 and −3 ≤ b ≤ 1, what are the greatest and least possible values of a − b?

**Step 1.** a − b is largest when a is largest and b is smallest: 5 − (−3) = **8**.
**Step 2.** a − b is smallest when a is smallest and b is largest: 2 − 1 = **1**.
**So 1 ≤ a − b ≤ 8.**

The safe method for products (ab) is to test all four corner combinations: 2×(−3) = −6, 2×1 = 2, 5×(−3) = −15, 5×1 = 5 → −15 ≤ ab ≤ 5.

**Question.** What is the sum of all solutions of |3x − 6| = 2x + 1?

**Case 1:** 3x − 6 = 2x + 1 → x = 7. Check: |21 − 6| = 15 and 2(7) + 1 = 15 ✓.
**Case 2:** 3x − 6 = −(2x + 1) → 5x = 5 → x = 1. Check: |3 − 6| = 3 and 2(1) + 1 = 3 ✓.
**Sum = 7 + 1 = 8.**

The check matters: when the right side contains x, a case can produce a value that makes the right side negative, which an absolute value can never equal. Here both survive.

**Question.** A bottling plant fills bottles with a target of 500 ml. Bottles are rejected if the fill f satisfies |f − 500| > 6. Which fill is accepted: 493, 494.5, 507, 506.5 ml?

Accepted bottles satisfy |f − 500| ≤ 6 → 494 ≤ f ≤ 506. Only **494.5 ml** is accepted; 493 is too low, 506.5 and 507 too high. This is exactly how quality-control specs are written.

points: Forgetting to flip the sign after dividing by a negative.
Multiplying by a variable (like x) without knowing its sign.
Solving only the positive case of an absolute value.
Accepting absolute-value solutions without checking them in the original.
Assuming x² > x for every x — false for 0 < x < 1.
Subtracting inequalities as if they were equations.

notes.h: How it shows up in the exam and real jobs
notes.p: GMAT inequality questions often ask how many integers satisfy a condition, the maximum or minimum of an expression, or 'which must be true'. In Data Insights, Data Sufficiency loves inequalities ('Is x > y?') because a statement that narrows a range may still not settle the question. At work, linear programming — the tool airlines, oil refiners and logistics firms use to optimise — is built entirely from inequality constraints. Six Sigma quality programmes express specs as tolerances, which are absolute-value statements.

points: Multiply/divide by a negative → flip the sign.
|x − a| = distance from a; < k is inside the band, > k is outside.
|expr| = k → two cases; k < 0 → no solution; verify each answer.
For ranges of a ± b or ab, test the extremes (all corners for products).
Same-direction inequalities can be added, never subtracted.
For 0 < x < 1: x³ < x² < x < √x.
Test numbers from every zone: negative, 0, between 0 and 1, above 1.

cards.title: The exponent rules
cards.body:
aᵐ × aⁿ = **aᵐ⁺ⁿ**   aᵐ ÷ aⁿ = **aᵐ⁻ⁿ**
(aᵐ)ⁿ = **aᵐⁿ**   (ab)ⁿ = aⁿbⁿ
a⁰ = 1 (a ≠ 0)   a⁻ⁿ = **1/aⁿ**   a^(1/n) = ⁿ√a
These only work with the **same base** (or the same exponent).

cards.title: Make the bases match
cards.body: 4, 8, 16, 32 are powers of 2; 9, 27, 81 are powers of 3; 25, 125 are powers of 5. Rewrite everything in the smallest base, then compare exponents. 8ˣ = 4³ → 2³ˣ = 2⁶ → **x = 2**.

cards.title: Adding powers: factor out
cards.body: You cannot add exponents when adding terms: 2¹⁰ + 2¹⁰ is **not** 2²⁰. Factor instead: 2¹⁰ + 2¹⁰ = 2 × 2¹⁰ = **2¹¹**. And 5¹⁰ − 5⁸ = 5⁸(25 − 1) = 24 × 5⁸.

cards.title: Signs and sizes
cards.body: Negative base, even power → positive: (−2)⁴ = 16. Odd power keeps the sign: (−2)³ = −8. But −2⁴ = −16 (the minus is outside). √x always means the **non-negative** root. Fractions between 0 and 1 shrink when raised to powers.

cards.title: Estimate big powers
cards.body: 2¹⁰ = 1,024 ≈ 10³. So 2³⁰ ≈ 10⁹. Use this to compare quantities like 2⁵⁰ vs 10¹⁵ fast: 2⁵⁰ ≈ 10¹⁵ (actually slightly larger).

cards.q: 2¹⁰ + 2¹⁰ equals:
cards.explain: 2¹⁰ + 2¹⁰ = 2 × 2¹⁰ = 2¹¹. Adding terms does not add exponents.

cards.q: What is (9⁴ × 27²) ÷ 3¹²?
cards.explain: 9⁴ = 3⁸ and 27² = 3⁶. So 3¹⁴ ÷ 3¹² = 3² = 9.
√72 = 6√2 and √32 = 4√2, so the difference is 2√2. (√40 is the trap: you cannot subtract under the root.)

notes.p:
Exponents are repeated multiplication, and roots undo them. The GMAT uses them to test whether you can **simplify before you calculate**. A question with 3²⁰ in it is never asking you to compute 3²⁰ — it is asking you to factor, match bases or cancel.

Two instincts solve most problems: **rewrite in a common base**, and **factor out the smallest power** when terms are added or subtracted.

points: **Product rule:** aᵐ·aⁿ = aᵐ⁺ⁿ. **Quotient rule:** aᵐ/aⁿ = aᵐ⁻ⁿ. **Power rule:** (aᵐ)ⁿ = aᵐⁿ.
**Zero and negative exponents:** a⁰ = 1; a⁻ⁿ = 1/aⁿ, so (1/2)⁻³ = 8.
**Fractional exponents:** a^(m/n) = (ⁿ√a)ᵐ; 8^(2/3) = (∛8)² = 4.
**Common base:** express 4, 8, 16, 32, 64 as powers of 2; 9, 27, 81, 243 as powers of 3.
**Factoring sums:** 3²⁰ + 3²⁰ + 3²⁰ = 3 × 3²⁰ = 3²¹. 7⁵ − 7³ = 7³(49 − 1) = 48 × 7³.
**Root simplification:** pull out perfect squares; add only like surds; rationalise with the conjugate.
**Equations:** if aˣ = aʸ (a ≠ 0, ±1), then x = y.

notes.p:
**Question.** If 2ˣ × 4ˣ⁺¹ = 2,048, what is x?

**Step 1.** 4ˣ⁺¹ = (2²)ˣ⁺¹ = 2²ˣ⁺², and 2,048 = 2¹¹.
**Step 2.** 2ˣ × 2²ˣ⁺² = 2³ˣ⁺² = 2¹¹ → 3x + 2 = 11 → **x = 3**.
**Check:** 2³ × 4⁴ = 8 × 256 = 2,048. ✓

Memorising powers of 2 up to 2¹² (4,096) and powers of 3 up to 3⁶ (729) makes this kind of question instant.

notes.h: Worked problem 2: factor the smallest power
notes.p:
**Question.** What is (5¹⁰ − 5⁸) / (5⁹ + 5⁸)?

**Step 1.** Numerator: 5⁸(5² − 1) = 24 × 5⁸.
**Step 2.** Denominator: 5⁸(5 + 1) = 6 × 5⁸.
**Step 3.** Ratio = 24/6 = **4**.

Without factoring, you would be subtracting numbers in the millions. With it, the 5⁸ cancels and the question becomes 24 ÷ 6.

notes.h: Worked problems 3 & 4: roots and rationalising; comparing huge numbers
notes.p:
**Question.** Simplify (√50 + √18) / √2 and then 4/(√7 + √3).

**Part 1.** √50 = 5√2, √18 = 3√2; sum = 8√2; divided by √2 = **8**.
**Part 2.** Multiply by the conjugate: 4(√7 − √3) / (7 − 3) = 4(√7 − √3)/4 = **√7 − √3**.

The conjugate works because (a + b)(a − b) = a² − b², which kills the roots in the denominator — the difference of squares identity from the quadratics chapter.

**Question.** Which is larger, 2⁴⁰ or 3²⁵?

**Step 1.** Find a common exponent. 40 and 25 share a factor of 5.
**Step 2.** 2⁴⁰ = (2⁸)⁵ = 256⁵ and 3²⁵ = (3⁵)⁵ = 243⁵.
**Step 3.** 256 > 243, so **2⁴⁰ is larger**.

When bases differ and the numbers are far too big to compute, rewrite both with the **same exponent** (then compare bases) or the **same base** (then compare exponents). One of these two moves almost always works.

points: Adding exponents when adding terms (2³ + 2³ = 2⁴, not 2⁶).
Multiplying bases: 2³ × 3³ = 6³ is fine (same exponent), but 2³ × 3² cannot be combined.
Splitting a root over addition: √(a + b) ≠ √a + √b.
Losing the sign: −3² = −9 but (−3)² = 9.
Assuming a larger exponent always gives a larger number — not for bases between 0 and 1 or for negative bases.

notes.h: How it shows up in the exam and real jobs
notes.p: Exponent questions appear in pure algebra, in units-digit and divisibility questions, and in growth problems ('a population triples every 4 years'). In Data Insights you may meet scientific notation in tables. In finance, exponents are compounding: (1 + r)ⁿ drives every valuation model, and Reliance Jio's subscriber base climbing from zero to hundreds of millions within a few years of its 2016 launch is an exponential-growth story. Data teams think in orders of magnitude (10³, 10⁶, 10⁹) when sizing markets, and 2¹⁰ ≈ 10³ is how engineers relate kilobytes to thousands.

points: Same base: multiply → add exponents; divide → subtract; power of power → multiply.
Rewrite 4, 8, 16, 32 in base 2; 9, 27, 81 in base 3.
Adding/subtracting powers: factor out the smallest power.
√(ab) = √a√b; add only like surds; rationalise with the conjugate.
(−a)ⁿ is positive for even n; −aⁿ is always negative for a > 0.
2¹⁰ ≈ 10³ for quick estimates.

cards.title: Arithmetic sequences
cards.body:
Constant difference d: 7, 11, 15, 19…
**nth term = a + (n − 1)d**
**Sum = n × (first + last) / 2**
Sum of 1 to 100 = 100 × 101/2 = **5,050** (the story attributed to young Gauss).

cards.title: Counting terms
cards.body:
Number of terms from a to b with step d = **(b − a)/d + 1**.
Multiples of 7 from 105 to 196: (196 − 105)/7 + 1 = **14** terms. Forgetting the '+1' is the fence-post error.

cards.title: Geometric sequences
cards.body:
Constant ratio r: 3, 6, 12, 24…
**nth term = a × rⁿ⁻¹**
Sum of first n terms = a(rⁿ − 1)/(r − 1). Compound growth is a geometric sequence.

cards.title: Recursive definitions
cards.body: The GMAT often defines each term from the previous one: a₁ = 2, aₙ = 3aₙ₋₁ − 1. Just **compute term by term**: 2, 5, 14, 41… If many terms are needed, look for a pattern after 4–5 terms.

cards.title: Repeating patterns
cards.body: Letters repeat ABCDEABCDE… What is the 2,026th letter? Divide by the cycle length 5: 2,026 = 5 × 405 + 1. Remainder 1 → **A**. Remainder 0 would mean the last letter of the cycle (E).

cards.title: Write it out
cards.body: When a sequence rule looks abstract, list the first few terms. Patterns — cycles, constant differences, doubling — become obvious on paper long before they do in your head.

cards.q: What is the 20th term of 7, 11, 15, 19, …?
What is the sum of the first 50 positive even integers?
A sequence has a₁ = 1 and aₙ = aₙ₋₁ + n for n ≥ 2. What is a₅?

notes.p:
A sequence is an ordered list built by a rule. The GMAT tests three kinds: **arithmetic** (add the same amount each time), **geometric** (multiply by the same amount) and **recursive or patterned** (a custom rule, often repeating). The test rarely needs advanced formulas; it rewards you for **finding the structure** — the constant difference, the ratio, or the cycle.

The arithmetic-series idea is old and lovely: pair the first and last terms, the second and second-last, and every pair has the same sum. That is why sum = number of terms × average of first and last.

points: **Arithmetic:** aₙ = a₁ + (n − 1)d; Sum = n(a₁ + aₙ)/2. Average of an arithmetic sequence = average of first and last term.
**Number of terms:** (last − first)/step + 1.
**Geometric:** aₙ = a₁rⁿ⁻¹; Sum = a₁(rⁿ − 1)/(r − 1) for r ≠ 1.
**Recursive:** compute directly; look for a cycle or simple formula after a few terms.
**Cycles:** find the cycle length L; the nth item matches position (n mod L), with remainder 0 meaning the last item of the cycle.
**Useful sums:** 1 + 2 + … + n = n(n + 1)/2; sum of first n odd numbers = n²; sum of first n even numbers = n(n + 1).

notes.p:
**Question.** A sequence is defined by a₁ = 2 and aₙ = 3aₙ₋₁ − 1. What is a₅ − a₄?

**Compute:** a₂ = 3(2) − 1 = 5; a₃ = 3(5) − 1 = 14; a₄ = 3(14) − 1 = 41; a₅ = 3(41) − 1 = 122.
**Answer:** 122 − 41 = **81**.
**Pattern spotted:** the differences are 3, 9, 27, 81 — powers of 3. That is no accident: aₙ − aₙ₋₁ = 3(aₙ₋₁ − aₙ₋₂), so differences form a geometric sequence.

notes.h: Worked problem 3: a business growth sequence
notes.p:
**Question (illustrative).** A cloud-kitchen brand opens 4 outlets in month 1 and each month opens 3 more than the month before (4, 7, 10, …). How many outlets has it opened in total after 12 months?

**Step 1.** Arithmetic with a = 4, d = 3. Month 12: 4 + 11 × 3 = 37.
**Step 2.** Total = 12 × (4 + 37)/2 = 12 × 20.5 = **246 outlets**.

Compare with geometric growth: if outlets doubled each month starting at 4, month 12 alone would see 4 × 2¹¹ = 8,192 openings — which is why 'linear' and 'exponential' growth assumptions give wildly different business plans.

points: The fence-post error: counting terms as (last − first)/step and forgetting +1.
Using n instead of n − 1 in the nth-term formula.
Assuming 'between 100 and 200' includes the endpoints without checking.
Getting the cycle position wrong when the remainder is 0.
Trying to find a general formula for a recursive sequence when computing five terms would take 30 seconds.

notes.h: How it shows up in the exam and real jobs
notes.p: Sequence questions appear as pure number puzzles, as patterns (repeating colours, days of the week) and as growth stories. Day-of-week questions are cycles of length 7. In finance, an annuity or EMI schedule is a geometric series, and a salary with fixed annual increments is an arithmetic one. Strategy teams at startups model expansion as arithmetic (add a fixed number of cities a year) or geometric (grow a fixed percentage) — the difference compounds into very different capital needs.

points: Arithmetic: aₙ = a + (n − 1)d; sum = n(first + last)/2.
Number of terms = (last − first)/step + 1.
Geometric: aₙ = arⁿ⁻¹; sum = a(rⁿ − 1)/(r − 1).
1 + … + n = n(n + 1)/2; first n odds sum to n².
Recursive: compute term by term, look for a pattern.
Cycles: use the remainder; remainder 0 = last item in the cycle.
Arithmetic sequence average = (first + last)/2.

cards.title: The multiplication principle
cards.body: If one choice can be made in m ways and a second in n ways, together they can be made in **m × n** ways. 4 shirts and 3 trousers → 12 outfits. Every counting formula is built from this one idea.

cards.title: Permutations: order matters
cards.body:
Arranging r of n distinct items: **ⁿPᵣ = n! / (n − r)!**
President, VP and treasurer from 8 people: 8 × 7 × 6 = **336**.
All n items in a row: **n!** (5 people → 120).

cards.title: Combinations: order does not
cards.body:
Choosing r of n: **ⁿCᵣ = n! / [r!(n − r)!]**
A team of 3 from 8: 336 / 3! = **56**.
Ask: if I swap two chosen items, is it a different outcome? Yes → permutation. No → combination.

cards.title: Repeated items
cards.body:
Arrangements of n items with repeats a, b, …: **n! / (a! b! …)**
LEVEL: 5! / (2! × 2!) = 120 / 4 = **30**.
The division removes arrangements that look identical.

cards.title: Restrictions
cards.body: **Must be together:** glue them into one block, arrange, then multiply by internal arrangements. **Must be apart:** total − together. **At least one:** total − none. Handle the most restricted position first.

cards.title: Write slots
cards.body: Draw blanks for each position and fill the number of options in each: _8_ × _7_ × _6_. Restricted slots first. This prevents most counting errors and is faster than recalling formulas.

cards.q: In how many ways can a president, a vice-president and a treasurer be chosen from 8 club members?
cards.explain: Order matters (different roles): 8 × 7 × 6 = 336.

cards.q: How many distinct arrangements are there of the letters in BANANA?
cards.explain: 6 letters with A repeated 3 times and N twice: 6! / (3! × 2!) = 720 / 12 = 60.

cards.q: At a meeting, each of 10 people shakes hands with every other person exactly once. How many handshakes are there?
cards.explain: A handshake is an unordered pair: ¹⁰C₂ = 10 × 9 / 2 = 45.

notes.p:
Counting problems ask 'how many ways?' and the answer is almost never found by listing. You build it from one principle — **multiply independent choices** — and one question: **does order matter?** If it does, you are counting arrangements (permutations). If it does not, you are counting selections (combinations), which is the permutation count divided by the number of ways to order the chosen items.

Counting is also the foundation of probability: most probability questions are 'favourable outcomes ÷ total outcomes', and both are counting problems.

points: **Multiplication principle:** sequential independent choices multiply.
**Addition principle:** mutually exclusive cases add (e.g. 'a committee with exactly 1 woman OR exactly 2 women').
**Permutations:** ⁿPᵣ = n!/(n − r)!.
**Combinations:** ⁿCᵣ = n!/[r!(n − r)!]; note ⁿCᵣ = ⁿCₙ₋ᵣ (choosing 3 to include = choosing 5 to exclude from 8).
**Repeats:** n!/(a!b!…).
**Circular arrangements:** (n − 1)! — rotations of the same seating are identical.
**Complement:** 'at least one' = total − none.

notes.p:
**Question.** A 3-person committee is chosen from 5 men and 4 women. How many committees include at least one woman?

**Step 1.** Total committees: ⁹C₃ = 9 × 8 × 7 / 6 = 84.
**Step 2.** Committees with no woman (all men): ⁵C₃ = 10.
**Step 3.** At least one woman = 84 − 10 = **74**.
**Check by cases:** 1 woman: ⁴C₁ × ⁵C₂ = 4 × 10 = 40; 2 women: ⁴C₂ × ⁵C₁ = 6 × 5 = 30; 3 women: ⁴C₃ = 4. Total 74. ✓

**Question.** Six friends, including Aman and Bela, sit in a row for a photo. In how many arrangements do Aman and Bela sit next to each other? In how many are they apart?

**Together:** glue Aman and Bela into one block. Now arrange 5 units: 5! = 120. Inside the block they can sit as AB or BA: × 2 = **240**.
**Total arrangements:** 6! = 720.
**Apart:** 720 − 240 = **480**.

The 'apart = total − together' move is far safer than counting apart directly.

notes.h: Worked problems 3 & 4: codes with restrictions; circular seating and selection
notes.p:
**Question.** A bank issues 4-digit PINs using digits 0–9 with no digit repeated, and the PIN cannot start with 0. How many PINs are possible?

**Slots:** first digit — 9 options (1–9). Second — 9 (any remaining digit, now including 0). Third — 8. Fourth — 7.
**Total = 9 × 9 × 8 × 7 = 4,536.**

Starting with the restricted slot (the first digit) keeps the count clean. If repeats were allowed and 0 could lead, there would be 10⁴ = 10,000 PINs.

**Question.** Six board members sit around a round table. In how many distinct ways can they sit? If a 2-person audit sub-committee is then chosen from them, how many choices are there?

**Part 1.** Around a circle, rotating everyone one seat gives the same arrangement. Fix one person's seat and arrange the other 5 in a line: 5! = **120**. (In a row it would be 6! = 720, which counts each circular seating 6 times.)
**Part 2.** Order does not matter: ⁶C₂ = 6 × 5 / 2 = **15**.

Two questions about the same six people, two different tools — the deciding factor is always whether order (or position) matters.

points: Using permutations when order does not matter (teams, committees, handshakes) — overcounting by r!.
Forgetting to multiply by the internal arrangements of a glued block.
Adding when you should multiply (sequential choices) or multiplying when you should add (separate cases).
Counting 'at least one' case by case and missing or double-counting a case.
Ignoring identical items (letters like the As in BANANA).

notes.h: How it shows up in the exam and real jobs
notes.p: Counting questions are among the hardest-looking Quant questions, yet most reduce to 2–3 lines once you identify order and restrictions. They are also a natural place to apply your 3-minute cut-off. In business, combinations size possibility spaces: how many product bundles can a telecom like Airtel create from 6 add-ons (2⁶ = 64 subsets, including the empty one), how many A/B test variants a product team must run, or how many password combinations make a system secure. Consulting case interviews sometimes ask quick 'how many combinations' questions to test structured thinking.

points: Multiply sequential choices; add separate cases.
Order matters → ⁿPᵣ = n!/(n − r)!; order irrelevant → ⁿCᵣ = n!/[r!(n − r)!].
Repeated items: divide by the factorial of each repeat count.
Together: glue, arrange, multiply by internal order. Apart: total − together.
At least one = total − none.
Circular seating: (n − 1)!.
Fill restricted slots first.

cards.title: The basic definition
cards.body: **P(event) = favourable outcomes / total equally likely outcomes**. Always between 0 (impossible) and 1 (certain). Two dice have 36 outcomes; a sum of 7 happens 6 ways → P = 6/36 = **1/6**.

cards.title: AND: multiply (independent)
cards.body:
For independent events, **P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B)**.
Two heads in two coin tosses: 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4.
Without replacement, update the second probability: two reds from 5 red + 3 blue = 5/8 × 4/7 = **5/14**.

cards.title: OR: add, then subtract overlap
cards.body:
**P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A and B)**.
If A and B cannot happen together (mutually exclusive), the overlap is 0 and you simply add. Drawing a king or a heart: 4/52 + 13/52 − 1/52 = **16/52 = 4/13**.

cards.title: The complement trick
cards.body: **P(at least one) = 1 − P(none)**. At least one head in 3 tosses = 1 − (1/2)³ = **7/8**. Whenever you see 'at least', flip to the complement — it is usually one calculation instead of several.

cards.title: Independent vs mutually exclusive
cards.body: **Independent:** one happening does not change the other's probability (two coin tosses). **Mutually exclusive:** they cannot both happen (rolling a 2 and a 5 on one die). Mutually exclusive events with non-zero probabilities are never independent.

cards.title: Sanity checks
cards.body: Probabilities above 1 or below 0 mean an error. 'At least one' should be larger than any single case. If an answer choice equals what you would get by adding probabilities of overlapping events, it is probably a trap.

cards.q: A fair coin is tossed 4 times. What is the probability of getting at least one tail?
cards.explain: P(no tails) = (1/2)⁴ = 1/16. So P(at least one tail) = 1 − 1/16 = 15/16.

cards.q: Independent events A and B have P(A) = 0.5 and P(B) = 0.4. What is P(A or B)?
A box has 4 white and 6 black balls. Two are drawn without replacement. What is the probability both are white?
cards.explain: 4/10 × 3/9 = 12/90 = 2/15. (4/25 would be the answer with replacement.)

notes.p:
Probability puts a number on uncertainty. On the GMAT it is essentially **counting with a fraction bar**: count what you want, count everything possible, divide. Three rules then do the heavy lifting: **AND multiplies, OR adds (minus overlap), and 'at least one' is 1 minus 'none'**.

Managers live in uncertainty — will a product launch succeed, will a supplier deliver, will a borrower default — so probability is the language of every risk discussion you will have after the MBA.

points: **Definition:** P = favourable / total, when outcomes are equally likely.
**Complement:** P(not A) = 1 − P(A).
**Multiplication rule:** P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B | A). For independent events, P(B | A) = P(B).
**Addition rule:** P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A and B).
**Without replacement:** the total (and possibly the favourable count) shrinks after each draw.
**Using combinations:** P = (ways to choose favourable items) / (ways to choose any items). Two whites from 4 white, 6 black: ⁴C₂ / ¹⁰C₂ = 6/45 = 2/15.
**Exactly k successes in n independent trials:** ⁿCₖ × pᵏ × (1 − p)ⁿ⁻ᵏ.

notes.p:
**Question.** A bag holds 5 red and 3 blue tokens. Two are drawn without replacement. What is the probability that they are of different colours?

**Method 1 (sequences):** red then blue = 5/8 × 3/7 = 15/56; blue then red = 3/8 × 5/7 = 15/56. Total = **30/56 = 15/28**.
**Method 2 (combinations):** favourable = ⁵C₁ × ³C₁ = 15; total = ⁸C₂ = 28 → **15/28**. ✓

The common error is to compute only one order (15/56) and forget that blue-then-red is a separate way to get one of each.

**Question.** A quality team at an electronics plant knows each unit independently has a 10% chance of a defect. If 3 units are tested, what is the probability that at least one is defective?

**Step 1.** P(a unit is fine) = 0.9.
**Step 2.** P(all three fine) = 0.9³ = 0.729.
**Step 3.** P(at least one defective) = 1 − 0.729 = **0.271**.

Doing this by cases (exactly 1, exactly 2, exactly 3) gives 0.243 + 0.027 + 0.001 = 0.271 — same answer, three times the work.

notes.h: Worked problems 3 & 4: exactly k successes; conditional probability from a table
notes.p:
**Question.** A salesperson closes a deal on any given call with probability 0.2, independently. What is the probability of exactly 2 closes in 4 calls?

**Step 1.** Number of ways to choose which 2 calls succeed: ⁴C₂ = 6.
**Step 2.** Each such pattern has probability 0.2² × 0.8² = 0.04 × 0.64 = 0.0256.
**Step 3.** P = 6 × 0.0256 = **0.1536** (about 15%).

Forgetting the ⁴C₂ factor gives 0.0256 — a classic trap answer.

**Question (illustrative data).** A lender reviews 400 past borrowers: 150 self-employed and 250 salaried. 100 borrowers defaulted, of whom 60 were self-employed. What is the probability of default for a self-employed borrower, and for a salaried one?

**Step 1.** P(default | self-employed) = 60 / 150 = **0.40**.
**Step 2.** Salaried defaulters = 100 − 60 = 40, so P(default | salaried) = 40 / 250 = **0.16**.
**Step 3.** Overall default rate = 100/400 = 0.25, which sits between the two group rates — a weighted average again.

'Given that' means **shrink the denominator** to the group you are told about. This is exactly how Data Insights table questions on rates by segment work.

points: Adding probabilities of events that can happen together, without subtracting the overlap.
Treating draws without replacement as independent.
Counting only one order when the question does not care about order.
Confusing 'mutually exclusive' with 'independent'.
Forgetting the combination factor for 'exactly k successes'.
Gambler's fallacy: after five heads, the sixth toss is still 1/2.

notes.h: How it shows up in the exam and real jobs
notes.p: GMAT probability questions are usually short but need careful reading of 'and', 'or', 'at least' and 'without replacement'. In Data Insights you may estimate probabilities from tables of counts. In jobs: credit teams at banks like HDFC or ICICI estimate default probabilities; insurers price policies on claim probabilities; product teams interpret A/B tests; supply-chain managers estimate the chance that at least one of several suppliers fails. MBA decision analysis courses build decision trees by multiplying probabilities along branches — exactly the AND rule.

points: P = favourable / total for equally likely outcomes.
AND → multiply (adjust for no replacement).
OR → add, subtract the overlap.
At least one = 1 − P(none).
Exactly k of n: ⁿCₖ pᵏ(1 − p)ⁿ⁻ᵏ.
Mutually exclusive ≠ independent.
Sanity check: 0 ≤ P ≤ 1.

cards.title: Two-set formula
cards.body:
**Total = A + B − Both + Neither**
120 students: 70 take Finance, 50 take Marketing, 20 take both. Neither = 120 − (70 + 50 − 20) = **20**. You subtract 'both' because those students were counted twice.

cards.title: The double-set matrix
cards.body: When items are classified two ways (engineer / non-engineer × remote / office), draw a **2 × 2 table with totals**. Every row and column must add up. Fill in what you know; the blanks fall out by subtraction. This is the fastest tool for most set questions.

cards.title: Three-set formula
cards.body:
**Total = A + B + C − (exactly two) − 2 × (all three) + Neither**
Or, with pairwise overlaps that include the triple:
**Total = A + B + C − (AB + BC + CA) + ABC + Neither**
Know which kind of overlap the question gives you.

cards.title: Maximum and minimum overlap
cards.body: With A = 30 and B = 25 in a group of 50: **maximum** both = 25 (the smaller set fits inside the larger). **Minimum** both = 30 + 25 − 50 = **5** (if negative, minimum is 0). Questions asking 'at least' or 'at most' are testing these extremes.

cards.title: Matrix in action
cards.body: 200 employees, 60% engineers, 40% of engineers remote, 50 non-engineers remote. Engineers = 120; remote engineers = 48; office engineers = 72. Non-engineers = 80; office non-engineers = 30. **Office total = 102.**

cards.title: Percent sets
cards.body: When a question gives only percentages, set the total to **100**. Then all the numbers are counts and the matrix or formula works directly.

cards.q: Of 50 employees, 30 speak Hindi, 25 speak Tamil and 10 speak both. How many speak neither?
cards.explain: Speak at least one = 30 + 25 − 10 = 45. Neither = 50 − 45 = 5.

cards.q: In a group of 50, 30 like cricket and 25 like football. What is the minimum number who like both?
cards.explain: Minimum overlap = 30 + 25 − 50 = 5 (assuming everyone could like at least one).

cards.q: Each of 60 people likes at least one of tea, coffee and juice: 35 tea, 30 coffee, 20 juice, and 3 like all three. How many like exactly two?
cards.explain: 60 = 85 − (exactly two) − 2 × 3 + 0 → exactly two = 85 − 6 − 60 = 19.

notes.p:
Overlapping sets questions are about **not double counting**. When some people belong to two groups, adding the groups counts them twice. Every formula in this chapter is a careful way of correcting that.

The visual tools — **Venn diagrams** for one classification of overlapping groups and the **double-set matrix** for two yes/no classifications — make these questions mechanical. Pick the tool before you start computing.

points: **Two sets:** Total = A + B − Both + Neither.
**Double-set matrix:** rows for one attribute (yes/no), columns for another, plus totals. Each row and column sums to its total; the grand total sits in the corner.
**Three sets (exactly-two version):** Total = A + B + C − (exactly two) − 2(all three) + Neither.
**Three sets (pairwise version):** Total = A + B + C − (|A∩B| + |B∩C| + |C∩A|) + |A∩B∩C| + Neither, where each pairwise count includes those in all three.
**Extremes:** max overlap = smaller set (if it fits); min overlap = A + B − Total (or 0).
**Percentages only:** take the total as 100.

notes.h: Worked problem 1: Venn with two sets
notes.p:
**Question.** In an MBA class of 120, 70 students take the Finance elective and 50 take Marketing. 20 take neither. How many take both?

**Step 1.** Total = A + B − Both + Neither → 120 = 70 + 50 − Both + 20.
**Step 2.** 120 = 140 − Both → **Both = 20**.
**Step 3.** Finance only = 50, Marketing only = 30, Both = 20, Neither = 20 → 50 + 30 + 20 + 20 = 120. ✓

**Question.** A firm has 200 employees. 60% are engineers. 40% of engineers work remotely. 50 non-engineers work remotely. How many employees work from the office?

Build the table (rows: engineer / non-engineer; columns: remote / office):
points: Engineers: total 120 → remote 0.4 × 120 = 48, office 72.
Non-engineers: total 80 → remote 50, office 30.
Column totals: remote 98, office **102**; grand total 200. ✓
Any unknown in a matrix is found by subtraction along its row or column — no formula to remember.

notes.p:
**Question.** A fintech surveys 100 customers about payment methods. 50 use UPI, 40 use cards and 30 use cash. 20 use exactly two methods and 5 use all three. How many use none of the three?

**Step 1.** A + B + C = 120. This counts exactly-one users once, exactly-two users twice and all-three users three times.
**Step 2.** Users of at least one = 120 − 20 − 2 × 5 = 90.
**Step 3.** None = 100 − 90 = **10**.
**Check:** exactly-one users = 120 − 2(20) − 3(5) = 65; 65 + 20 + 5 = 90. ✓ (Numbers are illustrative.)

points: Forgetting the 'neither' group.
Mixing 'exactly two' with pairwise overlaps that include the triple — they need different formulas.
Subtracting the triple overlap only once in the exactly-two formula (it must be subtracted twice).
Assuming the minimum overlap is 0 when A + B exceeds the total.
Using a Venn diagram when the question is really a 2 × 2 classification — the matrix is cleaner.

notes.h: How it shows up in the exam and real jobs
notes.p: Set questions appear in Quant as survey and class-enrolment problems, and in Data Insights as cross-tabulated tables. In business, overlap is everywhere: marketers measure audience overlap between channels (how many customers see both the TV ad and the Instagram ad), so adding reach figures double-counts. Banks cross-sell — the overlap between credit-card and home-loan customers is a set problem. A product manager estimating total users across an app and a website must remove users counted on both.

points: Two sets: Total = A + B − Both + Neither.
Two yes/no classifications → use a 2 × 2 matrix with totals.
Three sets: Total = A + B + C − (exactly two) − 2(all three) + Neither.
Pairwise-overlap version: − (sum of pairwise) + (all three).
Max overlap = smaller set; min overlap = A + B − Total (or 0).
Percent-only questions: set the total to 100.
Always check the 'neither' group.

cards.title: What the Verbal section is now
cards.body: In the **GMAT Focus Edition**, Verbal Reasoning has **23 questions in 45 minutes**, and only two types: **Reading Comprehension (RC)** and **Critical Reasoning (CR)**. Sentence Correction was removed. So Verbal is now a pure reasoning test: can you follow an argument, see its structure and spot what it does and does not prove?

cards.title: Read for structure, not facts
cards.body: An RC passage is 200–350 words on business, science or the humanities. You are not tested on remembering details — you can always look back. You are tested on **why** each paragraph exists. Read to answer three questions: What is the **main point**? What is the **author's attitude**? What job does **each paragraph** do?

cards.title: The passage map
cards.body: As you read, write a 3–5 line map on your noteboard, one line per paragraph, in your own words: e.g. 'P1: old view — price wars kill margins. P2: author: not always — new data. P3: one exception (telecom).' Then a last line: **Main point** and **tone**. Total time: about 2–3 minutes for the first read.

cards.title: Keywords are road signs
cards.body: Pivot words show the author changing direction: **however, but, yet, nevertheless**. Continuation words add support: **moreover, furthermore, similarly**. Evidence words: **for example, because, since**. Conclusion words: **thus, therefore, hence**. Opinion words — **surprisingly, unfortunately, merely, compelling** — reveal the author's own view. Slow down at every one of them.

cards.title: Mapping in action
cards.body: P1: 'Economists long assumed loyalty programmes simply bought repeat purchases.' P2: '**However**, recent studies suggest they mainly change *which* store loyal customers visit first.' P3: 'This **may** explain why airline programmes outlast retail ones.' Map: P1 old view; P2 author's new view; P3 tentative application. Main point: loyalty programmes shift order of choice, not total loyalty.

cards.title: Timing rule of thumb
cards.body: Budget roughly **2 minutes per question** across Verbal. For an RC set, that means about 2.5–3 minutes reading and then 1–1.5 minutes per question. Do not reread the whole passage for each question — use your map to jump to the right paragraph.

cards.title: The 'old view vs new view' template
cards.body: Most GMAT passages follow one of a few shapes: **old view → author challenges it**; **phenomenon → competing explanations → author picks one**; **problem → proposed solution → limitations**. Spot the shape in the first paragraph and the rest of the passage becomes predictable.

cards.q: A paragraph begins: 'Critics argue that the merger will raise prices. **Yet** the evidence from earlier mergers in the sector is mixed.' What is the author most likely doing?
options: Introducing doubt about the critics' claim
cards.explain: 'Yet' is a pivot: the author is pushing back on the critics' claim, not agreeing with it.

cards.q: What should a good passage map contain?
options: Every number and name from the passage
Only the first sentence of each paragraph, copied word for word
One short line per paragraph on its purpose, plus main point and tone
cards.explain: A map records each paragraph's role in your own words, plus the main point and the author's tone. Details can be found later by looking back.

cards.q: Which word most strongly signals the author's own opinion?
cards.explain: 'Regrettably' is an attitude word: it shows the author judges something as bad. The others are continuation, evidence or factual markers.

notes.h: The core idea: RC is an argument test in disguise
notes.p:
Most test-takers treat Reading Comprehension as a memory test: read slowly, try to hold every fact, then hunt for the answer. That is exactly backwards. The GMAT lets you look back at the passage as often as you like, so **recall is never the bottleneck**. What it tests is whether you understand the **architecture** of the text: what the author is claiming, what the evidence is, who disagrees, and how strongly the author holds the view.

In the GMAT Focus Edition, Verbal Reasoning has **23 questions in 45 minutes**, made up only of Reading Comprehension and Critical Reasoning. Sentence Correction no longer exists. Roughly half of Verbal comes from RC passages, each followed by several questions, so a good reading method pays off several times per passage.

notes.h: The framework: read for purpose, map, then answer
notes.p:
A reliable method has three steps.

**1. First read (about 2–3 minutes).** Read actively for structure. After each paragraph, pause for two seconds and ask: why did the author write this paragraph? Is it giving background, stating a view, attacking a view, giving evidence, or adding a qualification?

**2. Write the map.** One line per paragraph in your own shorthand, then **MP:** (main point) and **T:** (tone). For example: 'P1 trad view: CEO pay = performance. P2 auth: weak link, luck. P3 eg oil cos. MP: much CEO pay rewards luck. T: critical but measured.'

**3. Answer from the map, verify in the text.** Predict the answer from your map, then go back to the exact lines to confirm. Never pick an answer just because it 'sounds familiar'.
points: Background or context → usually P1
Author's thesis → often after a pivot word
Evidence and examples → middle paragraphs
Qualification or limitation → often the last paragraph

notes.h: Keywords: the road signs of the passage
notes.p: Authors leave signals. Learning to see them is the single biggest speed gain in RC.
points: **Contrast / pivot:** however, but, yet, although, nevertheless, on the other hand — the important idea usually follows
**Continuation:** moreover, also, furthermore, likewise — more of the same; skim faster
**Evidence:** because, since, for example, as shown by — support for a claim
**Conclusion:** therefore, thus, consequently, hence — the claim being supported
**Emphasis and attitude:** surprisingly, crucially, unfortunately, merely, admittedly — the author's voice
**Hedging:** may, might, some, suggests, in part — the claim is limited, and correct answers will be equally limited

notes.h: Worked example: mapping a business passage
notes.p:
Consider this short original passage.

*P1: For decades, management writers argued that diversified conglomerates destroy value, because investors can diversify more cheaply on their own. P2: Yet in emerging markets such as India, business groups like the Tata group have often thrived. One explanation is that, where capital markets and talent markets are thin, a group can play the role those markets would otherwise play — lending its reputation, capital and managers to new ventures. P3: This advantage may shrink as markets deepen; it does not, by itself, justify diversification everywhere.*

A good map:

P1: Old view — conglomerates destroy value.
P2: Author: but in emerging mkts groups fill 'missing markets' (Tata eg).
P3: Limit — advantage may fade as mkts develop.
MP: Diversified groups can create value where markets are weak, but this is context-dependent.
T: Balanced, mildly sceptical of the old view.

This argument echoes the **institutional voids** idea developed by Tarun Khanna and Krishna Palepu at Harvard. Notice how much of the right answer to a 'main point' question is already sitting in that map — including the qualification in P3, which wrong answers love to ignore.

points: **Reading too slowly for detail.** Spending five minutes memorising numbers leaves no time for questions. Details are only needed when a question asks.
**Skipping the map.** Without it you reread the passage for every question and lose two or three minutes per set.
**Ignoring hedges.** If the author says 'may partly explain', an answer saying 'proves' is wrong.
**Confusing a cited view with the author's view.** 'Some economists argue…' is not the author speaking.
**Bringing outside knowledge.** Even if you know the industry, answer only from the passage.

notes.h: How it shows up in interviews, exams and real jobs
notes.p:
In the exam, every RC question type — main idea, detail, inference, function — becomes faster once you have a map. In MBA classrooms, you will read 20-page Harvard cases overnight; students who read for structure ('What decision does the protagonist face? What are the options? What evidence matters?') finish in an hour and speak sharply in class.

In consulting and investment roles, the same skill is called **synthesis**: reading a 60-page industry report and telling a partner the three things that matter. Interviewers at firms like McKinsey or BCG, and in Indian banking and strategy roles, often hand you an exhibit or a paragraph and ask, 'What is the so-what?' That is a main-point question, asked out loud.

points: Verbal (Focus Edition) = 23 questions, 45 minutes, only RC and CR — no Sentence Correction
You can always look back: read for **structure and purpose**, not facts
Write a map: one line per paragraph + main point + tone
Pivot words (however, yet, but) usually introduce the author's real view
Hedges (may, some, suggests) limit the claim — correct answers match that strength
Common passage shapes: old view → challenge; phenomenon → explanations; problem → solution → limits
Answer from the map, then verify in the exact lines

chapters.title: Reading Comprehension: the six question types

cards.title: Know the question before you hunt
cards.body: RC questions fall into six families: **main idea**, **detail** (stated facts), **inference** (what must be true), **function/structure** (why a sentence or paragraph is there), **tone/attitude**, and **application** (which situation is most similar). Each family has its own trap answers, so classify the question first.

cards.title: Main idea and detail
cards.body: **Main idea:** the answer must cover the whole passage, not one paragraph, and match the author's strength. Too narrow or too broad is wrong. **Detail** ('According to the passage…'): the answer is stated almost directly in the text. Find the line, then match a paraphrase. Watch for answers that reuse words but twist the meaning.

cards.title: Inference: the smallest safe step
cards.body: On the GMAT, 'infer' means **must be true based on the passage**, not 'could be true'. The right answer is usually a modest, almost boring restatement of something combined from one or two sentences. Extreme words — always, never, only, all — are red flags unless the passage uses them too.

cards.title: Function and structure
cards.body: 'The author mentions X **in order to**…' asks why, not what. Look at the sentence before and after X. If X follows 'for example', its function is to support the previous claim. If it follows 'however', it probably challenges something. Answer with a verb: illustrate, challenge, qualify, contrast, explain.

cards.title: Tone and application
cards.body: **Tone** answers are usually moderate: 'cautiously optimistic', 'qualified support', 'measured scepticism'. GMAT authors are rarely 'outraged' or 'indifferent'. **Application** asks you to find the situation with the same **logical structure** as one in the passage — match the relationship, not the topic.

cards.title: Inference worked through
cards.body: Passage: 'Unlike most retailers, which raise prices during festivals, the firm kept prices flat in Diwali 2024 and still saw record footfall.' Which can be inferred? (a) Flat prices caused record footfall. (b) Most retailers raised prices at Diwali 2024. (c) The firm did not raise prices during Diwali 2024. **(c)** — it is directly supported. (a) assumes causation; (b) over-reads 'most retailers raise prices' as a statement about that specific year.

cards.title: Wrong-answer patterns
cards.body: Learn the five classic traps: **out of scope** (topic never discussed), **too extreme** ('proves', 'all'), **distortion** (right words, wrong relationship), **half right, half wrong**, and **true but irrelevant** (true per passage, but doesn't answer this question). Eliminating traps is often faster than finding the answer.

cards.q: A question asks: 'The author mentions the Tokyo subway primarily in order to…' What type is this?
cards.explain: 'In order to' asks for the purpose of a reference in the argument — a function question.

cards.q: Passage: 'Some analysts believe the policy will lower inflation; the evidence so far is inconclusive.' Which is the best description of the author's attitude to the analysts' belief?
cards.explain: 'Evidence is inconclusive' shows neither support nor rejection — a reserved, wait-and-see stance.

cards.q: Which answer choice is MOST likely to be correct on an inference question?
options: A modest statement directly supported by one or two sentences
A bold prediction about the future of the industry
A claim using 'always' when the passage says 'often'
A true fact about the world that the passage doesn't mention
cards.explain: Inference answers must be true given the passage, so they tend to be modest and closely tied to the text.

notes.h: The core idea: classify first, then use the right test
notes.p:
Every RC question is one of six types, and each type has a different standard of proof. A **detail** answer must be stated. An **inference** answer must be guaranteed. A **main idea** answer must cover the whole passage. A **function** answer must explain *why* something is there. Mixing up these standards is the main reason good readers miss RC questions.

So train a reflex: read the question stem, name the type in one word, and only then go to the passage.

points: **Main idea / primary purpose:** 'The primary purpose of the passage is to…'. Start with a verb that fits the whole passage: argue, challenge, explain, compare, describe. Eliminate answers that fit only one paragraph (too narrow) or go beyond the passage (too broad).
**Detail:** 'According to the passage…', 'The passage states that…'. Go to the line, read one sentence before and after, match a paraphrase.
**Inference:** 'It can be inferred…', 'The author would most likely agree…', 'The passage suggests…'. The answer must be true if the passage is true. Usually a small step from one or two sentences.
**Function / structure:** 'in order to', 'serves to', 'primarily functions to', 'Which best describes the organisation of the passage?'. Look at context, not content.
**Tone / attitude:** Find the attitude words. Most correct answers are moderate and mixed.
**Application / analogy:** 'Which of the following is most similar to…'. Strip the topic away and describe the logical relationship, then find the same relationship in a different setting.
A seventh, rarer type asks which statement would **strengthen or weaken** a claim in the passage — handle it with Critical Reasoning tools.

notes.h: Worked example: one passage, four questions
notes.p:
*Passage (original): Behavioural economists have documented that people value an item more once they own it — the **endowment effect**, associated with experiments by Richard Thaler, Daniel Kahneman and Jack Knetsch. Retailers exploit this through free trials: once customers 'own' a product for 30 days, cancelling feels like a loss. Some researchers, however, find the effect weakens sharply among experienced traders, suggesting it may reflect inexperience rather than a fixed feature of human preference.*

**Q1 (main idea).** Best: 'to describe a behavioural effect, its commercial use, and evidence that limits its generality'. Wrong: 'to prove that free trials always increase sales' (too extreme, too narrow).

**Q2 (detail).** 'According to the passage, the effect weakens among whom?' Experienced traders — stated directly.

**Q3 (inference).** 'The passage suggests that a retailer selling to first-time buyers…' Safe answer: 'may benefit more from a free trial than one selling to experienced traders.' It combines the last two sentences with a hedge.

**Q4 (function).** 'The free-trial example serves to…' illustrate a practical application of the effect. It follows the definition and shows it in use.
GMAT wrong answers are built from a small set of recipes. Name the recipe and you can cross out a choice in seconds.
points: **Out of scope:** introduces something the passage never discusses (e.g. 'pricing in luxury markets')
**Extreme language:** always, never, only, prove, all, completely — wrong unless the passage is equally strong
**Distortion:** uses passage words but reverses cause and effect, or swaps who believes what
**Half right:** first half matches, second half adds an unsupported claim
**True but irrelevant:** accurate per passage but answers a different question
**Opposite:** the reverse of what the author says — common on tone questions
Treating 'infer' as 'probably true'. If you need an extra assumption to make the answer work, it is wrong.
Choosing the most interesting answer. The right answer is often dull and modest.
On function questions, explaining **what** the sentence says instead of **why** it is there.
On main-idea questions, choosing the answer that matches the last paragraph only.
Answering tone questions from your feelings about the topic rather than the author's words.

notes.h: How it shows up in interviews, exams and real jobs
notes.p:
On the GMAT, RC sets reward speed with accuracy: if your map is good, detail and function questions should take about a minute each, leaving time for harder inference questions.

The same distinctions matter at work. When a financial analyst reads an annual report, they separate what the company **states** (detail), what you can **safely conclude** (inference), and the **tone** of management commentary — confident or defensive? Equity research analysts covering firms like Infosys or HDFC Bank listen to earnings calls exactly this way. In case interviews, 'What is the key takeaway from this exhibit?' is a main-idea question, and 'Why do you think the client mentioned X?' is a function question.

points: Six types: main idea, detail, inference, function, tone, application
Main idea must cover the whole passage at the author's level of certainty
Detail = stated; inference = must be true; neither allows outside knowledge
Function questions ask **why** — answer with a verb (illustrate, challenge, qualify)
Tone answers are usually moderate
Application = same logical relationship, different topic
Five trap types: out of scope, extreme, distortion, half right, true but irrelevant

chapters.title: Critical Reasoning: argument anatomy and assumptions

cards.title: What a CR question is
cards.body: Critical Reasoning gives a short argument (30–100 words) and one question. It tests whether you can see **how an argument works and where it is weak**. Nearly every CR question becomes easy once you split the argument into three parts: **conclusion**, **evidence (premises)**, and the unstated **assumption** that links them.

cards.title: Find the conclusion first
cards.body: The conclusion is the claim the author wants you to accept. Signals: **therefore, thus, so, clearly, hence, it follows that**, or recommendations with **should**. Test it: ask 'Why?' after the sentence. If another sentence answers the 'Why?', you have found conclusion and evidence.

cards.title: The argument equation
cards.body: **Evidence + Assumption = Conclusion.** The assumption is the gap — something the author must believe for the evidence to lead to the conclusion, but never says. Common gaps: **cause vs correlation**, **sample vs whole population**, **past vs future**, **plan will work**, **no other explanation**, and **comparison is fair**.

cards.title: Spotting the gap
cards.body: 'Stores that installed self-checkout kiosks saw sales rise 12% last year. Therefore our chain should install kiosks to boost sales.' Evidence: kiosk stores grew. Conclusion: kiosks will lift **our** sales. Assumptions: the kiosks **caused** the rise (not, say, store renovations done at the same time), and our stores are **similar** to those stores.

cards.title: Necessary vs sufficient assumptions
cards.body: Most GMAT 'assumption' questions want a **necessary** assumption: something that must be true for the argument to hold. 'Justify' questions ("Which, if assumed, allows the conclusion to be properly drawn?") want a **sufficient** one: an assumption strong enough to make the conclusion certain.

cards.title: The negation test
cards.body: To check a necessary assumption, **negate** it. If the negated version destroys the argument, it was necessary. 'Kiosks caused at least some of the rise' → negation 'Kiosks caused none of the rise' — the argument collapses. Correct. Answers that are 'nice to have' survive negation and are wrong.

cards.title: Pre-think before options
cards.body: Read the stem first, then the argument, and **predict the gap in your own words** before reading the choices. GMAT answer choices are written to sound plausible; arriving with a prediction protects you from being talked into the wrong one.

cards.q: 'Cities with more coffee shops have higher average incomes. So opening coffee shops will raise a city's income.' The main flaw is assuming that…
options: Correlation between coffee shops and income reflects causation from shops to income
cards.explain: The evidence is a correlation; the conclusion claims cause. Higher income could just as easily attract coffee shops.

cards.q: Which statement is the CONCLUSION? 'The new metro line will reduce traffic on MG Road. Most commuters on MG Road travel between the two stations the line will connect, and surveys show they would switch if fares are low.'
options: Most commuters travel between the two stations
The new metro line will reduce traffic on MG Road
cards.explain: Ask 'why?' after the first sentence — the next two sentences answer it. So the first sentence is the conclusion.

cards.q: Argument: 'Our online ads reached 2 million people, so sales will rise.' You negate a candidate assumption: 'None of the people reached are likely buyers of our product.' The argument collapses. This means the original assumption was…
cards.explain: If negating a statement destroys the argument, the argument depends on it — so it is a necessary assumption.

notes.h: The core idea: every argument has a hidden bridge
notes.p:
Critical Reasoning questions give you a short argument — a few sentences that try to persuade — and ask you to do something to it: find its assumption, strengthen it, weaken it, spot the flaw, or resolve a puzzle. All of these depend on one skill: **seeing the gap between what the author proves and what the author claims.**

The evidence (premises) is taken as true; the GMAT will not ask you to doubt the facts. Your job is to examine the **leap** from those facts to the conclusion. The unstated belief that makes the leap work is the **assumption**. Once you can name the assumption, strengthen answers support it, weaken answers attack it, and flaw answers describe it.

notes.h: The framework: anatomy in four steps
notes.p:
**Step 1 — Read the question stem first.** It tells you what to do (assumption? weaken? inference?) and therefore how to read.

**Step 2 — Find the conclusion.** Look for 'therefore, so, thus, hence, clearly, consequently', or a recommendation ('should', 'ought'). Use the **'Why?' test**: the conclusion is the sentence that the others explain.

**Step 3 — List the evidence.** Facts, data, examples, survey results.

**Step 4 — Name the gap.** Compare the language of the conclusion with the language of the evidence. Any new term in the conclusion is a clue. If the evidence is about 'sales in Mumbai' and the conclusion is about 'sales across India', the gap is representativeness.
points: **Causal gap:** A and B occur together, so A causes B (ignores reverse causation, a third factor, coincidence)
**Sampling gap:** a group studied represents the whole
**Analogy gap:** what worked there will work here
**Time gap:** the past trend will continue
**Plan gap:** the plan is feasible and has no fatal side effects
**Alternative-explanation gap:** no other cause explains the evidence
**Numbers gap:** percentages vs absolute numbers, rates vs totals

notes.h: Worked example: a full assumption question
notes.p:
*Argument (original): Last year, a quick-commerce company cut its delivery promise in Bengaluru from 30 minutes to 10 minutes, and its average order frequency per customer rose 25%. The company therefore plans to introduce 10-minute delivery in Pune, expecting a similar rise in order frequency.*

**Conclusion:** 10-minute delivery will raise Pune order frequency by a similar amount.
**Evidence:** In Bengaluru, after the change, frequency rose 25%.
**Gaps:** (1) The faster promise caused the rise, rather than, say, a discount campaign that ran simultaneously. (2) Pune customers will respond like Bengaluru customers. (3) The company can actually deliver in 10 minutes in Pune (dark-store density, traffic).

Now test a candidate answer: 'Pune customers are not much less sensitive to delivery speed than Bengaluru customers.' **Negate it:** 'Pune customers are much less sensitive to delivery speed.' The plan's expected result now looks doubtful — the argument is badly hurt. So this is a **necessary assumption**. Compare: 'Pune has more young professionals than Bengaluru.' Negating it changes little — not necessary.

notes.h: Necessary vs sufficient: two different questions
notes.p:
An **assumption question** ('The argument depends on which of the following?', 'relies on the assumption that') wants a **necessary** condition: a minimum requirement. Correct answers are often worded weakly — 'at least some', 'not all', 'not significantly' — because a weak statement is easier to be necessary.

A **justify / sufficient** question ('Which, if assumed, enables the conclusion to be properly drawn?') wants an answer strong enough to make the conclusion follow with certainty. Correct answers are often strong — 'all', 'any', 'only'.

The **negation test** is your tool for necessary assumptions: flip the answer to its logical opposite (not to its extreme). The negation of 'some customers will switch' is 'no customers will switch'; the negation of 'all will switch' is 'at least one will not switch'.

points: Attacking the evidence ('maybe the 25% figure is wrong'). Premises are accepted as true.
Choosing an answer that strengthens the argument but isn't required — fails the negation test.
Negating too strongly: 'not all' is the negation of 'all', not 'none'.
Getting pulled in by an answer that repeats the conclusion's words but adds nothing.
Reading the options before predicting the gap.

notes.h: How it shows up in interviews, exams and real jobs
notes.p: Assumption and its cousins make up a large share of CR. But the bigger payoff is outside the exam. Every business plan is an argument: 'competitor X grew with this product, so we will too'. Investment committees at private equity funds, and boards at companies like Tata Sons or Reliance, spend their time asking **what has to be true** for a plan to work — a phrase popularised by Roger Martin and A.G. Lafley in *Playing to Win*. Consultants call it **hypothesis-driven** thinking: state the answer, list the assumptions it rests on, then test the riskiest ones first. In case interviews, saying 'This recommendation assumes customers in the new city behave like our current ones — I'd want to check that' is a signal of structured thinking.

points: Evidence + Assumption = Conclusion; the assumption is the unstated bridge
Find the conclusion with signal words and the 'Why?' test
Premises are always taken as true — attack the leap, not the facts
Classic gaps: cause, sample, analogy, time, plan feasibility, alternatives, numbers
Assumption questions want **necessary**; justify questions want **sufficient**
Negation test: if negating the answer breaks the argument, it is necessary
Predict the gap before reading options

cards.title: Same skill, two directions
cards.body: Strengthen and weaken questions are the most common CR types. Both target the **assumption**. A strengthener makes the assumption more likely to be true; a weakener makes it less likely. Neither has to prove or destroy the argument — just **shift the odds**. 'Most strengthens' means 'moves the conclusion the most'.

cards.title: New information is allowed
cards.body: Unlike inference questions, strengthen/weaken answers **bring in new facts**. That is their job. So don't reject an answer for 'not being in the passage'. Reject it if it is **irrelevant to the gap** between evidence and conclusion, or if it pushes the wrong way.

cards.title: The causal toolkit
cards.body: When the conclusion says **A causes B**, weaken by showing: (1) an **alternative cause** C; (2) **reverse causation** — B causes A; (3) **A without B** or **B without A** in a comparable case. Strengthen by ruling these out, or by showing a **mechanism** or a **dose-response** (more A, more B).

cards.title: Weakening a causal claim
cards.body: 'Employees who attended the leadership course were promoted at twice the rate of others. So the course boosts promotion.' Best weakener: '**Managers nominate their highest performers for the course.**' Now high performance could explain both attendance and promotion — an alternative cause (selection bias).

cards.title: Plans and predictions
cards.body: If the conclusion is 'Plan X will achieve goal Y', weaken by showing X **can't be implemented**, has a **side effect that defeats Y**, or that Y **won't follow** even if X happens. Strengthen by removing an obvious obstacle. Note the goal precisely: 'raise revenue' differs from 'raise profit'.

cards.title: Watch for the scope trap
cards.body: Wrong answers often talk about the right topic but the wrong **group, time, or measure**. If the argument is about **profit**, an answer about **sales volume** may be irrelevant. If it is about **urban** customers, data about rural customers doesn't touch it. Match the exact terms of the conclusion.

cards.title: EXCEPT questions
cards.body: 'All of the following weaken the argument EXCEPT' — four answers weaken; the right answer either **strengthens or is irrelevant**. Label each option W, S or 0, and pick the odd one out. Don't hunt for a strengthener only — an irrelevant option is just as correct.

cards.q: 'Since the city introduced a congestion charge, air pollution has fallen 15%. So the charge reduced pollution.' Which most WEAKENS this?
options: The charge raised ₹200 crore in its first year
In the same period, the state shut down two large coal power plants upwind of the city
Pollution also fell 15% in the city's charged zone
cards.explain: Closing coal plants is an alternative cause for the pollution fall, which weakens the claim that the charge caused it.

cards.q: 'Restaurants that listed calorie counts saw diners order lower-calorie meals. So listing calories changes choices.' Which most STRENGTHENS this?
options: Health-conscious diners were already more likely to visit those restaurants
At the same restaurants, before calorie listing began, diners ordered higher-calorie meals
Many diners say they ignore menus
cards.explain: A before/after comparison at the same restaurants removes a selection explanation and links the change to the listing.

cards.q: A company plans to raise profit by cutting prices 10% to win volume. Which most WEAKENS the plan?
options: Competitors have no capacity to match the cut
Customers say they like lower prices
The cut will increase volume by 5%, below the roughly 11% needed for revenue to break even, while costs per unit stay the same
cards.explain: With a 10% price cut, volume must rise about 11% (1/0.9 ≈ 1.11) just to keep revenue flat; a 5% rise means revenue falls while unit costs are unchanged, so profit falls.

notes.h: The core idea: shift the probability
notes.p:
A strengthen or weaken answer is a new piece of evidence that makes the conclusion **more or less likely**. It does not have to settle the matter. That is why the question says 'most strengthens' — you are ranking options by how hard they push on the argument's **central gap**.

The winning habit: before reading the choices, say to yourself in one line, 'This argument assumes ___.' Then the strengthener is the answer that supports that blank, and the weakener is the answer that attacks it. Everything else is noise.

notes.h: The framework: argument patterns and their levers
notes.p: Most GMAT arguments fall into a few patterns. Each has standard ways to strengthen and weaken.
points: **Causal (A causes B):** weaken with an alternative cause, reverse causation, or a case where A occurs without B. Strengthen by eliminating alternatives, showing a mechanism, or showing that removing A removes B.
**Plan / recommendation:** weaken with an obstacle to implementation, a self-defeating side effect, or evidence the goal won't follow. Strengthen by removing the biggest obstacle.
**Prediction from trend:** weaken by showing conditions are changing. Strengthen by showing they are stable.
**Analogy / comparison:** weaken by showing the two cases differ in a relevant way. Strengthen by showing they are similar in that way.
**Survey / sample:** weaken with bias in who answered or how. Strengthen by showing the sample is representative.
**Numbers (percent vs total):** weaken by showing the base changed — e.g. accidents fell in percentage terms but total driving fell more.

notes.h: Worked example: a pricing plan with numbers
notes.p:
*Argument (original): A regional dairy brand sells 1,00,000 litres a month at ₹60 per litre. Its variable cost is ₹45 per litre and fixed costs are ₹10 lakh a month. To fight a national rival, management proposes cutting the price to ₹54, arguing that the higher volume will raise monthly profit.*

Current profit = (60 − 45) × 1,00,000 − 10,00,000 = 15,00,000 − 10,00,000 = **₹5 lakh**.

After the cut, contribution per litre falls from ₹15 to ₹9. To keep total contribution at ₹15 lakh, volume must reach 15,00,000 ÷ 9 ≈ **1,66,667 litres** — a rise of about **67%**.

So a strong **weakener** would be: 'Market research suggests volume would rise by about 20% at ₹54.' Then contribution = 9 × 1,20,000 = ₹10.8 lakh, and profit = 10.8 − 10 = **₹0.8 lakh**, far below today. A **strengthener**: 'At ₹54, the brand would win a supermarket contract that alone adds 80,000 litres a month' — then volume is 1,80,000 and profit = 9 × 1,80,000 − 10,00,000 = ₹6.2 lakh, above today.

The lesson: in plan arguments, the hidden assumption is often quantitative. A price cut needs a much larger proportional volume increase than people intuitively think when margins are thin.

The most common weakener on the GMAT is the **alternative explanation**, and its most elegant version is **selection bias**: the people who received a treatment were different to begin with. Employees who take a course, customers who join a loyalty programme, students who use a coaching institute — all chose to do so, and the qualities that made them choose may explain the outcome.

The gold-standard fix, as any statistician will tell you, is a **randomised controlled trial**. On the GMAT, strengthening answers often mimic this: 'participants were assigned at random', or 'before the programme, the two groups performed equally'.

points: Rejecting a correct answer because it introduces new information — that is allowed here.
Picking an answer that is relevant to the topic but not to the gap (scope trap).
Confusing the goal: an answer that raises sales doesn't help a plan to raise profit if costs rise faster.
Choosing the answer that would weaken a stronger conclusion than the one actually stated.
On EXCEPT questions, looking only for the opposite direction and missing an irrelevant answer.

notes.h: How it shows up in interviews, exams and real jobs
notes.p:
On the GMAT, strengthen and weaken are among the most frequent CR types, and the causal toolkit alone solves a large share of them.

At work, this is how good managers read a dashboard. When a marketing team says 'the campaign lifted sales 18%', a sharp manager asks: 'Was there a festival that month? Did a competitor stock out? Did we run discounts at the same time?' Companies like Amazon and Netflix built cultures around A/B testing precisely to kill these alternative explanations before acting. In interviews, a consultant who says 'before we credit the campaign, let's rule out seasonality and a competitor's supply problem' is doing a weaken question out loud.

points: Strengtheners make the assumption more likely; weakeners make it less likely
New information is allowed — judge relevance to the gap
Causal claims: attack with alternative cause, reverse causation, A without B
Plans: attack with feasibility, side effects, or goal not following
Watch scope: same group, time and measure as the conclusion
With thin margins, a price cut needs a big volume rise to keep profit
EXCEPT questions: the answer can be a strengthener or irrelevant

cards.title: Evaluate the argument
cards.body: 'Which would be **most useful to know** in evaluating the argument?' The right answer is a question whose answer **could go either way** — and one answer strengthens, the other weakens. If both possible answers leave the argument unchanged, the question is irrelevant.

cards.title: The two-sided test
cards.body: For each option, imagine a 'yes' answer and a 'no' answer. 'Whether the stores that installed kiosks also renovated' → Yes: alternative cause, weakens. No: removes alternative, strengthens. **Both sides matter → correct.** 'Whether kiosks are made in India' → neither answer affects sales → wrong.

cards.title: Flaw questions
cards.body: 'The reasoning is **flawed** because it…' or '…is **vulnerable to criticism** on the grounds that it…'. You describe the gap in abstract language: 'fails to consider an alternative explanation', 'takes for granted that…', 'treats a correlation as causation'. Predict the gap first, then match the abstract wording.

cards.title: Classic flaws to recognise
cards.body: **Correlation → causation.** **Unrepresentative sample.** **Necessary vs sufficient** confusion. **Part-to-whole** (each part is X, so the whole is X). **Percent vs number.** **Ad hominem** (attacking the person, not the claim). **Circular reasoning.** **Equivocation** (a word shifts meaning). **False dilemma** (only two options presented).

cards.title: Necessary vs sufficient flaw
cards.body: 'Every successful start-up had strong founders. Meera's start-up has strong founders, so it will succeed.' Flaw: strong founders are **necessary** (per the evidence) but treated as **sufficient**. Many start-ups with strong founders also fail.

cards.title: Percent vs number flaw
cards.body: 'Brand A's share of the smartphone market fell from 20% to 15%, so it sold fewer phones.' If the market grew from 10 crore to 15 crore units, A sold 2 crore before and 2.25 crore after — **more phones**. The argument confuses share with volume.

cards.title: Read flaw answers literally
cards.body: Flaw answers are abstract and dense. Translate each into plain words and check it against the argument: 'presumes, without justification, that X'. Is X really assumed? Is it really unjustified? Many wrong answers describe a flaw that sounds smart but simply **isn't in this argument**.

cards.q: Argument: 'Sales rose after the new logo launched, so the logo boosted sales.' Which is MOST useful to evaluate it?
options: Whether the designer was well known
Whether any other major change, like a price cut, happened at the same time
cards.explain: If yes, there is an alternative cause (weakens); if no, the logo becomes a likelier cause (strengthens). Both answers matter.

cards.q: 'Each member of the committee is an expert economist, so the committee will produce an expert economic report.' This argument mainly…
options: Attacks a person rather than a claim
Assumes that what is true of each part is true of the whole
cards.explain: It is a part-to-whole flaw: expert individuals don't guarantee an expert collective output.

cards.q: Brand X's market share fell from 25% to 20% while the market grew from 40 lakh to 60 lakh units. How did X's unit sales change?
cards.explain: Before: 25% × 40 lakh = 10 lakh. After: 20% × 60 lakh = 12 lakh. Sales rose by 2 lakh units despite the lower share.

notes.h: The core idea: name the weakness precisely
notes.p:
Evaluate and flaw questions are two ways of asking the same thing: **where exactly is this argument weak?** A flaw question asks you to **describe** the weakness in abstract terms. An evaluate question asks you to identify **the piece of information** that would tell you whether the weakness is fatal.

Both depend on predicting the gap before reading the options — the same habit you built for assumptions.

An evaluate question's right answer is usually phrased as 'whether…' or 'what percentage…'. Its defining feature: different possible answers move the argument in **different directions**.

Use the **two-sided (variance) test**: plug in an extreme answer on each side. If one side strengthens and the other weakens, you have a strong candidate. If both sides leave the argument where it was, cross it out.

Typical correct evaluate answers ask about an **alternative cause**, a **comparison group** ('Did sales also rise at stores without kiosks?'), **representativeness** of a sample, or **feasibility** of a plan.

notes.h: Flaw questions: a catalogue of classic errors
notes.p: GMAT flaw answers reuse a small vocabulary. Learn it once and you will recognise it everywhere.
points: **Correlation as causation:** 'treats a correlation as evidence of a causal link'
**Overlooks alternatives:** 'fails to consider other possible explanations'
**Unrepresentative sample:** 'draws a general conclusion from a sample that may not be typical'
**Necessary vs sufficient:** 'treats a condition required for X as enough to guarantee X'
**Part to whole / whole to part:** 'assumes that a property of each member belongs to the group' (or vice versa)
**Percent vs number / rate vs total:** 'confuses a proportion with an absolute quantity'
**Ad hominem:** 'attacks the source of a claim rather than the claim itself'
**Circular reasoning:** 'assumes what it sets out to prove'
**Equivocation:** 'uses a key term in two different senses'
**False dilemma:** 'presents two options as the only ones possible'
**Absence of evidence:** 'treats lack of proof that X is true as proof that X is false'

notes.h: Worked example: market share vs volume
notes.p:
*Argument (original): Five years ago, Brand P held 30% of India's two-wheeler market. Today it holds 24%. Clearly, fewer Indians are buying Brand P's two-wheelers than five years ago.*

Let the market have been 1.6 crore units then and 2.0 crore units now (illustrative numbers).

Then: 30% × 1.6 crore = **48 lakh** units.
Now: 24% × 2.0 crore = **48 lakh** units.

Sales are **identical** even though share fell 6 percentage points. If the market had grown to 2.2 crore, P would sell 52.8 lakh — more than before.

**Flaw:** the argument 'fails to consider that the total market may have grown'. **Evaluate:** 'How has the total number of two-wheelers sold in India changed over five years?' — if it shrank or stayed flat, the conclusion holds; if it grew by more than 25%, the conclusion fails. (Break-even: 0.30 × M₀ = 0.24 × M₁ → M₁ = 1.25 M₀.)

This exact confusion appears in real business reporting: a company can lose share while growing strongly in an expanding market, as many Indian incumbents did when new competitors entered fast-growing sectors.

points: On evaluate questions, choosing a question whose answer only helps one side.
Choosing a flaw answer that describes a real fallacy that is not present in this argument.
Treating 'the argument fails to consider X' as correct when X would not affect the conclusion anyway.
Confusing 'necessary' and 'sufficient' — the GMAT's favourite formal-logic trap.
Rushing: flaw answers are wordy, so translate each one into plain English before judging.

notes.h: How it shows up in interviews, exams and real jobs
notes.p:
Evaluate questions train the most valuable habit in a manager: **asking the question that would change your mind**. In consulting, this is the 'key question' that a work plan is built around. In a product review at a firm like Flipkart or Zomato, the analyst who asks 'Did conversion also rise in cities where we *didn't* launch the feature?' saves the company from a false conclusion.

Flaw vocabulary also helps in group discussions and interviews for Indian B-schools and in boardrooms: calmly naming 'that's a correlation, not proof of cause' or 'we're comparing share, not volume' earns credibility quickly.

points: Evaluate: the right question has answers that would push the argument both ways
Use the two-sided test: imagine a 'yes' and a 'no'
Flaw: describe the gap in abstract terms; predict it first
Key flaws: correlation/causation, sampling, necessary/sufficient, part/whole, percent/number
Share can fall while volume rises if the market grows
Wrong flaw answers often name a real fallacy that just isn't in this argument

cards.title: Inference flips the direction
cards.body: In most CR questions the passage is an argument and you attack or support it. In **inference** ('must be true', 'most strongly supported') the passage is a set of **facts**, and you find the answer those facts **prove**. Here, new information is **not** allowed. The correct answer is supported by the statements, often by combining two of them.

cards.title: Small, safe, combined
cards.body: Good inference answers are **modest** and **combine** facts.
