If the passage says 'All premium plans include insurance' and 'Riya's plan has no insurance', you can infer 'Riya's plan is not premium'. You cannot infer 'Riya chose the cheapest plan'. Check every word of the answer against the text.

cards.title: Conditional logic in 30 seconds
cards.body: 'If A then B' (A → B) allows the **contrapositive**: not B → not A. It does **not** allow B → A (reversal) or not A → not B (negation). 'Only if' reverses direction: 'A only if B' means A → B. 'Unless' means 'if not': 'A unless B' means not B → A.

cards.title: Boldface / role questions
cards.body: A boldface question puts one or two sentences in **bold** and asks what **role** each plays. Roles: the **main conclusion**; an **intermediate conclusion** (supported, then used to support the main one); **evidence** for the main conclusion; a **position the author opposes**; evidence for that opposing position; or **background**.

cards.title: Boldface worked through
cards.body: '**Some analysts predict that the new tax will cut alcohol sales.** But such taxes usually lead to more smuggling, not less drinking. **Therefore, the tax is unlikely to reduce consumption much.**' First bold: a **prediction the author argues against**. Second bold: the **author's main conclusion**.

cards.title: Label first, then match
cards.body: For boldface, label every sentence on your noteboard: **C** (author's conclusion), **E** (evidence for C), **OC** (opposing conclusion), **OE** (evidence for the opposing side), **BG** (background). Then compare labels with the answer choices. Do not read the answers first — they're designed to blur.

cards.title: 'Most strongly supported' still means proof
cards.body: Even when the stem softens to 'most strongly supported', treat it as near-certain. Eliminate any answer that needs an outside fact, extends a 'some' into a 'most', or predicts the future from a description of the past.

cards.q: Facts: 'Every employee in the analytics team knows Python. Arjun does not know Python.' What must be true?
options: Arjun is not in the analytics team
Everyone who knows Python is in analytics
cards.explain: Contrapositive: not knowing Python → not in analytics. The other options are reversals or outside speculation.

cards.q: 'The loan will be approved only if the applicant has a credit score above 750.' Which follows?
options: If the score is above 750, the loan is approved
If the loan is not approved, the score is below 750
If the score is not above 750, the loan is not approved
cards.explain: 'Approved only if score > 750' means approved → score > 750; the contrapositive is score not > 750 → not approved.

cards.q: In a boldface question, a sentence is supported by evidence and then itself used to support the author's main conclusion. Its role is…
cards.explain: A claim that is both supported and supporting is an intermediate (sub-) conclusion.

notes.h: The core idea: from attacking to deducing
notes.p:
Inference and boldface questions are different from the strengthen/weaken family. You are not judging whether an argument is good. You are either **deducing** what the facts guarantee (inference) or **describing the structure** of the argument (boldface).

Both reward careful, literal reading. Both punish imagination. If you catch yourself thinking 'well, that's probably true in real life', you are about to choose a wrong answer.

Treat the passage as true and ask which answer **must** follow. Three habits help:

**1. Look for combinations.** The best answers often link two separate statements. If the passage says 'Plant X uses only solar power' and later 'All facilities using only solar power received the green certificate', then 'Plant X received the certificate' is a combined inference.

**2. Respect quantity words.** 'Some' is at least one. 'Most' is more than half. 'Many' is vague. You can go from 'all' to 'some', never from 'some' to 'most'.

**3. Respect time and scope.** Facts about last year do not prove anything about next year. Facts about urban customers say nothing about rural ones.
points: Allowed: 'If A then B' + 'not B' → 'not A' (contrapositive)
Not allowed: 'If A then B' + 'B' → 'A' (affirming the consequent)
Not allowed: 'If A then B' + 'not A' → 'not B' (denying the antecedent)
'A only if B' = A → B
'A unless B' = if not B, then A
'No A is B' = A → not B, and B → not A

notes.p:
*Facts (original): In 2025, a hospital chain's revenue per bed increased compared with 2024. The number of beds stayed the same. However, the chain's total revenue from inpatient services fell.*

Wait — if beds are constant and revenue per bed rose, total bed revenue must have risen. So how can inpatient revenue fall? Only if **'revenue per bed' includes something other than inpatient services** (say, day-care procedures or outpatient services billed to bed units), or if the two measures are defined differently.

A well-built GMAT inference answer would be: 'Revenue counted in the per-bed figure includes revenue from sources other than inpatient services.' That **must** be true for all three facts to hold together.

Check the arithmetic: say 100 beds, per-bed revenue ₹40 lakh in 2024 → total ₹40 crore; ₹44 lakh in 2025 → total ₹44 crore. If inpatient revenue fell from ₹35 crore to ₹33 crore, then non-inpatient revenue inside the per-bed figure rose from ₹5 crore to ₹11 crore. The numbers only reconcile if something besides inpatient services is in the per-bed figure.

notes.h: Boldface: describe the role, not the content
notes.p:
Boldface questions ask what part a sentence plays. Build the argument's skeleton first.

**Find the author's main conclusion.** Often after 'but', 'however', 'therefore', or in the final sentence.

**Label everything else** relative to it. Is it evidence for the conclusion? A claim the author disputes? Evidence that the opposing side would use? Background that neither supports nor opposes?

**Watch for intermediate conclusions.** 'Since X, Y; and because Y, Z.' Here Y is supported by X and supports Z.

Answer choices use phrases like 'the first is a judgement the argument opposes; the second is evidence offered in support of that judgement'. Check each half separately — many wrong answers get one bold right and the other wrong.

points: Choosing an inference that is plausible but needs one outside fact.
Reversing a conditional: 'only premium plans include insurance' does not mean 'all premium plans include insurance'.
Upgrading quantity words: 'some' to 'most', 'often' to 'always'.
On boldface, confusing evidence for the opposing view with evidence for the author's view.
Reading boldface answers before labelling — the abstract wording is confusing on purpose.

notes.h: How it shows up in interviews, exams and real jobs
notes.p:
Conditional logic is everywhere in business rules: credit policies at banks like HDFC ('approved only if CIBIL score above a threshold'), compliance rules, contract clauses. Misreading 'only if' as 'if' can cost real money.

Boldface thinking is how good lawyers, analysts and editors read: they ask what each sentence is **doing**. In case interviews and consulting memos, the classic **pyramid principle** (Barbara Minto) asks you to separate the main conclusion from supporting arguments and evidence — the same skeleton boldface questions test.

points: Inference: the answer must be true given the facts — no new information
Prefer modest answers that combine two statements
A → B allows not B → not A; never B → A or not A → not B
'Only if' marks the necessary condition; 'unless' means 'if not'
Boldface roles: main conclusion, intermediate conclusion, evidence, opposing view, its evidence, background
Label every sentence before reading answer choices

chapters.title: Critical Reasoning: paradox, plan and method

cards.title: Paradox (explain the discrepancy)
cards.body: 'Which **most helps to explain** the apparent discrepancy?' The passage gives two facts that seem to conflict. You need a new fact that lets **both** be true at once. You are not choosing which fact is wrong — both stay true. The right answer usually reveals a **difference** between the two situations.

cards.title: A classic paradox
cards.body: 'After a city added more cycle lanes, the number of cycling accidents **rose**, yet officials say cycling became **safer**.' Resolution: 'The number of people cycling tripled.' More cyclists can mean more total accidents but **fewer accidents per kilometre cycled**. Rate vs total — the GMAT's favourite paradox.

cards.title: Plan / goal questions
cards.body: Some questions ask which fact best shows that a **plan will succeed**, or which is the best **reason to doubt** it. Write the goal in your own words first. Then check: Can the plan be implemented? Will it actually achieve **this** goal? Are there side effects that cancel the benefit?

cards.title: Method of reasoning
cards.body: 'The argument proceeds by…' or 'X responds to Y by…'. Describe **how** the argument works, not what it says. Typical answers: 'offering a counter-example', 'pointing out that the evidence supports an alternative conclusion', 'arguing by analogy', 'questioning the reliability of a source'.

cards.title: Paradox checklist
cards.body: When two facts clash, test these resolutions: **rate vs total** (bigger base); **different groups** (the facts describe different people); **time lag**; **hidden cost or benefit**; **substitution** (customers moved to another product); **measurement change** (the definition changed). One of them usually unlocks the question.

cards.title: Sales up, profit down
cards.body: 'A smartphone brand's unit sales rose 30% after it entered the budget segment, but its profit fell.' Resolution: 'Budget phones carry much lower margins, and many existing customers switched from premium models to the budget ones.' That is **cannibalisation** — both facts now fit.

cards.title: Avoid the 'one side' trap
cards.body: Wrong paradox answers often explain **only one** fact ('Budget phones are popular' explains rising sales but not falling profit) or **deepen** the puzzle. The right answer bridges both. Ask: after reading this answer, am I still surprised?

cards.q: A town's total road deaths rose after a new highway opened, but officials claim roads became safer. Which best resolves this?
options: Road deaths in other towns fell
Total vehicle-kilometres driven in the town more than doubled after the highway opened
cards.explain: If travel more than doubled while deaths rose less, deaths per vehicle-km fell — so total deaths can rise even as roads get safer.

cards.q: 'Ravi says remote work cuts productivity, citing a firm whose output fell after going remote. Meena replies that the firm also lost its two largest clients that year.' Meena's response…
options: Offers an alternative explanation for the evidence Ravi cites
cards.explain: Meena does not dispute the data; she gives another reason the output might have fallen.

cards.q: A chain plans to cut queues by adding self-checkout kiosks. Which most suggests the plan will FAIL?
options: Some stores have spare floor space
Most customers buy alcohol or loose produce, which still require staff assistance at kiosks
cards.explain: If most transactions still need staff help, kiosks won't speed up checkout — the plan won't achieve its goal.

notes.h: The core idea: make the facts fit together
notes.p:
Paradox questions present two true facts that seem to contradict each other. Your task is to find a third fact that makes both **comfortable to believe at the same time**. This is not about choosing a side — the GMAT will never ask you to doubt the facts in the passage.

Plan and method questions are the practical cousins. **Plan** questions ask whether a course of action will reach its goal. **Method** questions ask you to describe how an argument or a rebuttal works. All three reward one habit: stating the situation in your own words before looking at the answers.
Most paradoxes on the GMAT fall into a handful of patterns. Run through them when you are stuck.
points: **Rate vs total:** totals rise because the base grew, while the rate falls (accidents, defaults, crimes)
**Different populations:** the two facts describe different groups (new vs old customers, urban vs rural)
**Substitution / cannibalisation:** sales moved from one product or channel to another
**Hidden cost or revenue:** a cost increase or a one-off charge explains falling profit
**Time lag:** effects show up later than expected
**Measurement or definition change:** the thing counted changed
**Selection effect:** who is observed changed (e.g. weaker students dropped out, so the average rose)

notes.h: Worked example: revenue up, profit down
notes.p:
*Facts (original): A food-delivery platform's gross order value rose from ₹1,000 crore to ₹1,300 crore in a year. Yet its operating profit fell from ₹40 crore to ₹10 crore.*

Which would explain this? Suppose the platform earns a **take rate** (commission) of 20% and spends on delivery and discounts.

Year 1: revenue = 20% × 1,000 = ₹200 crore. Costs = ₹160 crore. Profit = ₹40 crore.
Year 2: suppose it cut its take rate to 18% to win restaurants: revenue = 18% × 1,300 = ₹234 crore. If costs rose to ₹224 crore because of heavy customer discounts and more delivery staff in new cities, profit = 234 − 224 = **₹10 crore**.

So a good resolving answer would be: 'To expand into new cities, the platform lowered commissions and funded large customer discounts.' It explains both the growth **and** the profit fall. A one-sided answer such as 'More restaurants joined the platform' explains only growth.

This pattern — growth bought with margin — is familiar from Indian consumer internet companies such as Zomato and Swiggy in their expansion years, which is why analysts look at **unit economics**, not just GMV.

**Plan questions.** Write the goal precisely (reduce queues? reduce costs? raise profit?). The plan fails if it **can't be implemented**, if it **doesn't affect** the cause of the problem, or if it creates a **side effect** that defeats the goal. A plan succeeds when the main obstacle is removed.

**Method questions.** The answer describes a technique. Common ones:
points: Offering a **counter-example** to a general claim
Providing an **alternative explanation** for the same evidence
Arguing by **analogy**
Showing that the opponent's argument leads to an **absurd or contradictory** result
Questioning the **reliability or representativeness** of evidence
Distinguishing two **meanings** of a key term
Choosing an answer that explains one fact but not the other.
Choosing an answer that makes the discrepancy deeper.
On plan questions, confusing the plan's goal with a related goal (revenue vs profit, footfall vs sales).
On method questions, describing the content of the argument rather than its technique.
Doubting one of the facts — the GMAT treats them as true.

notes.h: How it shows up in interviews, exams and real jobs
notes.p:
Paradoxes are the bread and butter of case interviews: 'Revenue grew 20% but profit fell — why?' The structured answer is the paradox checklist: mix shift, price cuts, cost increases, one-off charges, cannibalisation. Interviewers at consulting firms and at Indian conglomerates such as the Aditya Birla Group or Tata group test exactly this in profitability cases.

Plan evaluation is what boards do: before approving a new plant or a price cut, they ask about feasibility, the causal link to the goal, and side effects. Method awareness makes you a better negotiator and debater — you can see *how* the other side is arguing, not just what they're saying.

points: Paradox: find a fact that lets both facts be true
Top resolutions: rate vs total, different groups, cannibalisation, hidden cost, time lag, measurement change
Wrong answers explain only one side or deepen the puzzle
Plans: check feasibility, causal link to the goal, side effects
Method: describe the technique (counter-example, alternative explanation, analogy)
Revenue up + profit down usually means mix shift, price cuts or rising costs

cards.title: The Data Insights section
cards.body: In the GMAT Focus Edition, **Data Insights** has **20 questions in 45 minutes** and an **on-screen calculator**. Five formats: **Data Sufficiency**, **Table Analysis**, **Graphics Interpretation**, **Two-Part Analysis** and **Multi-Source Reasoning**. Some questions have several parts, and you get credit only if **every part is right**.

cards.title: Sufficiency, not solving
cards.body: A Data Sufficiency (DS) question gives a question and **two statements**. You don't find the answer. You decide **whether the information is enough** to find exactly one answer. 'What is x?' is answered only if x has a single value. Stop calculating the moment you know sufficiency.

cards.title: The five fixed answer choices
cards.body: **A:** Statement (1) alone is sufficient, (2) alone is not. **B:** (2) alone is sufficient, (1) alone is not. **C:** Both together are sufficient, neither alone is. **D:** Each alone is sufficient. **E:** Even together, not sufficient. These never change — memorise them so you never read them in the exam.

cards.title: The AD / BCE grid
cards.body: Judge statement (1) alone first. If (1) is sufficient, the answer is **A or D** — now check (2) alone. If (1) is not sufficient, the answer is **B, C or E** — check (2) alone: sufficient → **B**; not → combine: sufficient → **C**, not → **E**. Write 'AD' or 'BCE' on your noteboard and cross out as you go.

cards.title: A C-answer
cards.body: What was the shop's profit in March? (1) Revenue was ₹5 lakh. (2) Costs were 80% of revenue. (1) alone: no costs → not sufficient → BCE. (2) alone: no revenue → not sufficient → CE. Together: profit = 5 − 4 = ₹1 lakh → **C**. Note we needed only to know a single value exists.

cards.title: A D-answer
cards.body: What is the value of x? (1) 3x − 7 = 11. (2) x² = 36 and x > 0. (1): 3x = 18, x = 6 — sufficient → AD. (2): x = 6 or −6, but x > 0 → x = 6 — sufficient. Each alone works → **D**.

cards.title: Forget statement (1) when judging (2)
cards.body: The most common DS error is **leaking** information: you learn something from (1), then unconsciously use it while judging (2) alone. Judge each statement as if the other doesn't exist. Only combine at the C/E step.

cards.q: You decide statement (1) alone is NOT sufficient. Which answers are still possible?
cards.explain: If (1) fails, A and D are out. B, C and E remain.

cards.q: What is the price of one pen? (1) 3 pens and 2 pencils cost ₹50. (2) 6 pens and 4 pencils cost ₹100.
cards.explain: (2) is just (1) multiplied by 2 — the same equation. Two unknowns, one independent equation, even together → E.

cards.q: What is the value of n? (1) n² = 9. (2) n > 0.
cards.explain: (1): n = 3 or −3, not sufficient. (2): any positive n, not sufficient. Together: n = 3 → C.

notes.h: The core idea: is the information enough?
notes.p:
Data Sufficiency is the most distinctive question type on the GMAT, and since the Focus Edition it sits in the **Data Insights** section rather than Quant. Data Insights has **20 questions in 45 minutes**, with an **on-screen calculator** available (the Quant section does not allow one). DS questions are a large share of the section and are mostly quantitative, though some test pure logic.

The central shift: **you are a manager deciding whether you have enough data, not an analyst computing the answer.** A manager asked 'Can we work out next quarter's break-even volume from these two reports?' does not need to compute it — just to know that it can be computed uniquely. That is why DS is fast for people who stop early and slow for those who solve everything.

notes.h: The framework: AD/BCE step by step
notes.p: The five answer choices are fixed. Memorise them word for word.
points: **A** — Statement (1) ALONE is sufficient, but statement (2) alone is not
**B** — Statement (2) ALONE is sufficient, but statement (1) alone is not
**C** — BOTH statements TOGETHER are sufficient, but NEITHER alone is
**D** — EACH statement ALONE is sufficient
**E** — Statements (1) and (2) TOGETHER are NOT sufficient

notes.p:
**Step 1. Understand the question stem.** Simplify it. 'What is 2x + y?' only needs the value of the expression, not x and y separately. 'Is n odd?' is a yes/no question.

**Step 2. Judge statement (1) alone.** Sufficient → write **AD**. Not → write **BCE**.

**Step 3. Judge statement (2) alone,** forgetting (1) completely.
From AD: (2) sufficient → **D**; not → **A**.
From BCE: (2) sufficient → **B**; not → go to step 4.

**Step 4. Combine.** Sufficient → **C**; not → **E**.

The grid also helps when you are stuck. If you can't decide on (1) but are sure (2) alone is sufficient, the answer is B or D — a 50% guess, not 20%.

**Example 1 — needs the expression, not each variable.**
What is the value of 2a + b?
(1) 4a + 2b = 30.
(2) a − b = 3.
(1): divide by 2 → 2a + b = 15. Sufficient → AD.
(2): many pairs (a, b) satisfy a − b = 3, giving different 2a + b (a = 3, b = 0 → 6; a = 4, b = 1 → 9). Not sufficient → **A**.

**Example 2 — business framing.**
A retailer sold only shirts and trousers last month. How many shirts did it sell?
(1) It sold 400 items in total.
(2) Revenue was ₹3,20,000; shirts sell at ₹600 and trousers at ₹1,000.
(1): no split → BCE. (2): 600s + 1,000t = 3,20,000 has many non-negative integer solutions (s = 200, t = 200; or s = 400, t = 80) → not sufficient. Together: s + t = 400 and 600s + 1,000t = 3,20,000. Substitute t = 400 − s: 600s + 4,00,000 − 1,000s = 3,20,000 → 400s = 80,000 → s = 200. Unique → **C**. (In the exam, you'd stop as soon as you see two independent linear equations — no need to solve.)

**Example 3 — linear equations rule.** Two different linear equations in two unknowns usually give one solution, **unless** they are multiples of each other (same line) or contradictory (parallel). Always glance for that before choosing C.

points: **Solving fully.** Once you know a unique answer exists, move on. Time saved here funds harder questions.
**Leaking** facts from (1) into your judgement of (2) alone.
**Rushing to C.** When both together clearly work, check again whether one statement alone already does — the 'C trap'.
**Assuming integers or positives** that the question doesn't state.
**Counting equations blindly.** Two equations may be the same equation in disguise (answer E), and one equation can be sufficient if it gives the needed expression directly.

notes.h: How it shows up in interviews, exams and real jobs
notes.p: DS trains the habit consultants call **'what data do we need?'** Before a team at a firm like McKinsey, Bain or an Indian strategy unit commissions an expensive survey, someone asks whether the existing numbers already pin down the answer. Product managers at companies like Flipkart ask the same question before running a new experiment. In case interviews, when you're given a fact and asked to estimate something, saying 'I'd also need the average order value to compute this — do we have it?' is a DS move, and it signals structured thinking.

points: Data Insights: 20 questions, 45 minutes, on-screen calculator allowed
DS asks whether data is sufficient for one answer — don't solve fully
A: (1) only; B: (2) only; C: together only; D: each alone; E: not even together
Grid: (1) sufficient → AD; not → BCE
Judge (2) as if (1) didn't exist
Two identical equations = one equation; two independent linear equations in two unknowns = unique solution
A value question needs exactly one value; a yes/no question needs a definite yes or a definite no

chapters.title: Data Sufficiency: traps and hidden constraints

cards.title: Yes/No questions
cards.body: For 'Is x > 5?', a statement is sufficient if it gives a **definite answer** — either **always yes** or **always no**. 'Always no' counts as sufficient! Only 'sometimes yes, sometimes no' is insufficient. Test by trying numbers that could flip the answer.

cards.title: A definite 'no' is sufficient
cards.body: Is x > 10? (1) x < 7. (2) x² = 144. (1): x is always below 7, so the answer is always **no** → sufficient. (2): x = 12 (yes) or −12 (no) → not sufficient. Answer **A**.

cards.title: Pick smart numbers
cards.body: To test sufficiency, deliberately try **0, 1, negatives, fractions, and large numbers**. These are the cases that break careless reasoning. 'Is x² > x?' — x = 2: yes; x = ½: no; x = −1: yes; x = 0 or 1: no. If you only try 2 and 3, you'll wrongly call it sufficient.

cards.title: Integer constraints change everything
cards.body: If the unknowns must be **whole numbers** (people, cars, tickets), one equation with two unknowns can still have **only one solution**. Pens at ₹5, notebooks at ₹8, at least one of each, total ₹31: 5p + 8n = 31 → only n = 2, p = 3 works. **Always test the integer cases** before calling it insufficient.

cards.title: Hidden constraints
cards.body: Real-world quantities carry silent rules: lengths and prices are **positive**, people are **integers**, percentages are **between 0 and 100** for parts of a whole, ages are positive. Geometry figures are **not necessarily drawn to scale** in DS. Use the real-world rules; ignore the picture's look.

cards.title: The C trap
cards.body: When the two statements together obviously work, the test-maker is often hoping you pick C without noticing that **one statement alone already works** (A, B or D). When C seems too easy, recheck each statement alone carefully.

cards.title: The E trap
cards.body: The opposite trap: a question that looks unsolvable but has a hidden way through — integer constraints, a simplified expression in the stem, or a **ratio question** that needs no absolute numbers. Before choosing E, ask: what exactly does the question need?

cards.q: Is the integer k divisible by 6? (1) k is divisible by 3. (2) k is divisible by 4.
cards.explain: (1): k = 3 (no) or 6 (yes) — insufficient. (2): k = 4 (no) or 12 (yes) — insufficient. Together k is divisible by 12, so by 6 → yes → C.
(1): x could be 2 or −2 → insufficient. (2): a cube is positive only if x is positive → definite yes → B.

cards.q: A shop sells pens at ₹7 and notebooks at ₹11. Riya spent exactly ₹100 on pens and notebooks. How many pens did she buy? (She bought whole items.) Is the information sufficient?
options: Yes — only 8 pens and 4 notebooks fits
No — she could have bought 3 pens
cards.explain: 7p + 11n = 100 with whole numbers: trying n = 0 to 9, only n = 4 gives a multiple of 7 (100 − 44 = 56 = 7 × 8). Unique, so sufficient.

notes.h: The core idea: the test-maker's favourite tricks
notes.p: Once you know the AD/BCE method, most DS mistakes come not from weak maths but from a small set of **predictable traps**. The question writers know that people assume numbers are positive integers, that people stop testing after one or two examples, and that people grab C when both statements are needed 'obviously'. Learning these traps is the fastest way to raise a Data Insights score.

In a yes/no question, sufficiency means **certainty**, not 'yes'. A statement that guarantees 'no' every time is just as sufficient as one that guarantees 'yes'.

Method: try to make the answer 'yes' with one number and 'no' with another, while obeying the statement. If you can do both, the statement is insufficient. If you can't, it's sufficient.
points: Is x > 10? (1) x < 7 → always no → sufficient
Is n even? (1) n = 2m for some integer m → always yes → sufficient
Is n even? (1) n = 2m for some number m → n could be 3 (m = 1.5) → insufficient
Is p prime? (1) p is odd → 3 (yes), 9 (no) → insufficient

notes.h: Trap 2: number properties and picking numbers
notes.p:
Many statements look decisive but fail for special values. Build a reflex testing list: **0, 1, −1, a fraction like ½, a negative fraction, a big number**.

For instance: 'Is x² > x?' Statement: 'x > 0'. With x = 2 → 4 > 2 (yes). With x = ½ → ¼ > ½ (no). Insufficient. Statement: 'x < 0'. Any negative x gives a positive square, which is greater than x → always yes → sufficient.

Inequalities need care: multiplying both sides by a negative number flips the sign. Square roots are non-negative by definition (√9 = 3), but x² = 9 has two solutions (3 and −3).

When the unknowns count real things, they must be non-negative whole numbers, and that can make one equation sufficient.

**Worked example.** A ticket counter sells adult tickets at ₹7 and child tickets at ₹11 (illustrative prices). A family spent exactly ₹100. How many adult tickets?

We need 7a + 11c = 100 with a, c ≥ 0 integers. Try each c from 0 up to 9 (since 11 × 10 > 100):
c = 0 → 100, not divisible by 7
c = 1 → 89, no
c = 2 → 78, no
c = 3 → 67, no
c = 4 → 56 = 7 × 8 ✔ (a = 8)
c = 5 → 45, no
c = 6 → 34, no
c = 7 → 23, no
c = 8 → 12, no
c = 9 → 1, no
Exactly one solution: **8 adults, 4 children** → sufficient.

Contrast: with prices ₹2 and ₹3 and total ₹12, solutions are (6, 0), (3, 2), (0, 4) → several → insufficient. The general signal: **large, awkward coefficients with a small total** often give a unique integer answer; small coefficients usually don't. Use the calculator if it saves time — it's allowed in Data Insights.

notes.h: Trap 4: the C trap and the E trap
notes.p:
**C trap.** Statement (1) gives 'x + y = 10'; statement (2) gives 'x = 2y'. Together, obviously sufficient. But if the question asks 'What is x + y?', (1) alone answers it — the answer is A (or D if (2) also works, which it doesn't here). Always restate what the question actually needs.

**E trap.** A question asking for a **ratio** or **percentage** may be answerable without absolute numbers. 'What percentage of the class are girls? (1) There are 3 girls for every 2 boys.' Sufficient alone: 60%. People who think 'I need the class size' pick E or C wrongly.

**Same-information trap.** If (2) is just (1) rearranged or multiplied, combining adds nothing — the answer is A, D or E, never C.

points: Treating a definite 'no' as insufficient
Testing only positive integers
Ignoring that counts of people or items must be whole numbers
Trusting the figure's proportions — DS figures are not necessarily drawn to scale
Choosing C without checking each statement alone again
Choosing E for ratio questions that don't need totals

notes.h: How it shows up in interviews, exams and real jobs
notes.p: These traps mirror real analytical errors. Assuming all values are positive is how forecasting models break when a quarter has negative growth. Ignoring integer constraints is how planners propose hiring '2.6 engineers'. The 'ratio vs absolute' trap appears when executives demand a full census when a sample proportion would answer the question. Testing extreme cases — the habit of trying 0, negatives and fractions — is exactly what good software engineers and risk managers at banks like HDFC or ICICI do when they stress-test a model.

points: Yes/no: 'always no' is sufficient; 'sometimes yes, sometimes no' is not
Test 0, 1, negatives, fractions and large numbers
x² = 9 gives ±3; √9 = 3 only
Integer constraints can make one equation sufficient — test cases
Real quantities: positive, whole numbers, within 0–100% for parts
C trap: recheck each statement alone; E trap: ratios may not need totals
Statements that repeat the same information never produce C

cards.title: What Table Analysis looks like
cards.body: You see a table of data (often 6–25 rows) that you can **sort by any column**. Then come typically **three statements**, each with two choices such as **True/False** or **Yes/No**. You must get **all three** right to earn credit for the question. The on-screen calculator is available.

cards.title: Sort before you calculate
cards.body: Most statements are about **ranks, medians, maxima or counts**. Sorting the right column turns a 2-minute calculation into a 10-second glance. Read each statement, decide which column matters, sort, then answer.

cards.title: Stats you'll need
cards.body: **Mean** = sum ÷ count. **Median** = middle value when sorted; for an even count, the average of the two middle values. **Range** = max − min. **Percentage change** = (new − old) ÷ old × 100. **Ratio** comparisons: compute or estimate per-unit values (per employee, per sq ft).

cards.title: Estimate first
cards.body: Many statements only ask 'more than' or 'at least'. Rough estimates often decide them: 135/9 = 15 is clearly bigger than 150/12 = 12.5. Use the calculator only for close calls, and double-check boundary cases like '**more than**' vs '**at least**'.

cards.title: Read the statement literally
cards.body: 'More than half of the stores' with 6 stores means **4 or more**, not 3. 'Above ₹6,000' excludes exactly ₹6,000. A large share of Table Analysis errors come from boundary words, not arithmetic.

cards.title: Some statements are not maths
cards.body: Statements can be logical: 'If the table is sorted by area, the store with the largest area also has the highest revenue.' Or they can ask whether the data is **consistent with** a claim. 'Consistent with' means the data doesn't contradict it — a weaker test than 'proves'.

cards.q: Using the mini table (revenue: A 120, B 90, C 150, D 75, E 110, F 135), the median revenue is:
cards.explain: Sorted: 75, 90, 110, 120, 135, 150. Two middle values 110 and 120 → median 115.

cards.q: Areas (sq ft): A 2,000, B 1,500, C 2,500, D 1,200, E 1,800, F 2,200, with revenues as above (₹ lakh). True or false: more than half the stores earn more than ₹6,000 per sq ft.
options: False — only 3 stores (D, E, F) do
cards.explain: A, B and C earn exactly ₹6,000/sq ft (e.g. 120 lakh ÷ 2,000). D ≈ 6,250, E ≈ 6,111, F ≈ 6,136. Three of six is not more than half.

cards.q: A Table Analysis question has three statements. You get two right and one wrong. What credit do you get?
cards.explain: Multi-part Data Insights questions are scored as a whole: all parts must be correct to get credit.

notes.h: The core idea: a sortable spreadsheet and three verdicts
notes.p:
Table Analysis is the closest thing on the GMAT to a real analyst's day: a spreadsheet, a few claims from a manager, and the question 'Are these right?' The table can be sorted by clicking a column heading. Below it are usually **three statements**, each needing a binary verdict (True/False, Yes/No, Consistent/Inconsistent, Inferable/Not inferable). You must get **all of them** right to earn the question.

The skill being tested is not heavy arithmetic. It is choosing the **right column**, the **right summary statistic**, and reading the statement **literally**.

**1. Skim the table (20–30 seconds).** Read column headings and units (₹ lakh? thousands? percent?). Note any footnotes. Don't study the numbers yet.

**2. Read statement 1 and classify it.** Is it about a maximum/minimum, a rank, a median or mean, a count above a threshold, a ratio, or a logical relationship between two columns?

**3. Sort and compute only what's needed.** Sort by the relevant column. Estimate first; use the calculator for close calls.

**4. Check the boundary words.** 'More than half', 'at least', 'exactly', 'greater than', 'all', 'each'. Then repeat for the next statement.
points: Mean = sum ÷ count
Median = middle value (or average of middle two)
Percentage change = (new − old) ÷ old × 100
Percentage points ≠ percent: 10% → 12% is +2 points, +20%
Per-unit ratios: revenue ÷ staff, revenue ÷ area
Correlation in a table: when sorted by one column, does the other mostly rise too?

notes.p:
*Table (illustrative data): Store, City, Revenue (₹ lakh), Staff, Area (sq ft)*
A — Pune — 120 — 10 — 2,000
B — Jaipur — 90 — 8 — 1,500
C — Kochi — 150 — 12 — 2,500
D — Indore — 75 — 6 — 1,200
E — Lucknow — 110 — 11 — 1,800
F — Nagpur — 135 — 9 — 2,200

**Statement 1:** 'The median revenue is greater than ₹110 lakh.' Sort by revenue: 75, 90, 110, 120, 135, 150. Median = (110 + 120) ÷ 2 = 115 → **True**.

**Statement 2:** 'The store with the highest revenue per staff member is in Nagpur.' A 12.0, B 11.25, C 12.5, D 12.5, E 10.0, F 15.0 → F, Nagpur → **True**.

**Statement 3:** 'More than half of the stores generate more than ₹6,000 of revenue per sq ft.' Convert: ₹1 lakh = ₹1,00,000. A: 1,20,00,000 ÷ 2,000 = 6,000. B: 90,00,000 ÷ 1,500 = 6,000. C: 1,50,00,000 ÷ 2,500 = 6,000. D: 75,00,000 ÷ 1,200 = 6,250. E: 1,10,00,000 ÷ 1,800 ≈ 6,111. F: 1,35,00,000 ÷ 2,200 ≈ 6,136. Only D, E, F exceed 6,000 — 3 of 6, not more than half → **False**.

Statement 3 is a deliberate boundary trap: three stores sit exactly on ₹6,000.

points: Ignoring units: mixing ₹ lakh and ₹ crore, or thousands and units
Computing the mean when the statement asks for the median
Treating 'percent' and 'percentage points' as the same
Reading 'more than half' as 'half or more'
Calculating everything instead of sorting first
Treating 'consistent with the data' as 'proved by the data'

notes.h: How it shows up in interviews, exams and real jobs
notes.p: This is everyday work in an MBA job. A category manager at a retailer like DMart or Reliance Retail looks at a store table and asks which outlets are most productive per square foot — a key retail metric. A private equity associate screens a list of companies by revenue growth and margin. In consulting case interviews, you are often handed a table and asked 'What stands out?' The right instinct is the same as here: choose the metric that matters (per staff, per sq ft, growth), sort, and look at the extremes and the median rather than the noise.

points: Sortable table + usually three binary statements; all must be right for credit
Classify the statement, sort the right column, compute only what's needed
Median for an even count = average of the two middle values
Per-unit ratios (per staff, per sq ft) reveal productivity
Watch boundary words: more than, at least, exactly
Percent change ≠ percentage-point change
Check units before every calculation

cards.title: The format
cards.body: You get one graph — bar chart, line chart, scatter plot, pie chart, bubble chart, timeline or flow diagram — and usually **two sentences with drop-down blanks**. Pick the option that makes each sentence true. Both blanks must be right for credit. The calculator is available, but most blanks can be settled by careful reading and estimation.

cards.title: Read the frame before the data
cards.body: Spend the first 20 seconds on **title, axis labels, units, scale and legend**. Is the y-axis in lakh or crore? Does it start at zero? Is it a **percentage** or an **absolute** value? Are there two y-axes? Most wrong answers come from misreading the frame, not the bars.

cards.title: Key calculations
cards.body: **% change** = (new − old) ÷ old × 100. **Slope** of a line = change in y ÷ change in x. **Share** of a pie slice = slice ÷ total. **CAGR** (n years) = (end ÷ start)^(1/n) − 1. 'Closest to' blanks reward estimation: round sensibly and compare options.

cards.title: Line chart example
cards.body: An app's subscribers (lakh): Jan 40, Apr 46, Jul 55, Oct 66. 'Growth from Jul to Oct was closest to [10% / 20% / 30% / 40%].' (66 − 55) ÷ 55 = 11 ÷ 55 = **20%**. 'The quarter with the highest % growth was [Jan–Apr / Apr–Jul / Jul–Oct].' 15%, ≈19.6%, 20% → **Jul–Oct**.

cards.title: Scatter plots and trend lines
cards.body: Scatter plots show the **relationship** between two variables. Upward cloud = positive correlation; downward = negative; shapeless = none. A **line of best fit** lets you predict. Remember: correlation in a scatter plot does **not** prove causation — a favourite trap in the answer options.

cards.title: Reading a trend line
cards.body: A scatter plot of price (₹) vs units sold has a trend line through (₹100, 300 units) and (₹200, 100 units). Slope = (100 − 300) ÷ (200 − 100) = **−2 units per ₹1**. Predicted sales at ₹150: 300 − 2 × 50 = **200 units**.

cards.title: Truncated axes exaggerate
cards.body: If the y-axis starts at 90 instead of 0, a move from 92 to 96 looks enormous but is only about **4%**. Always compute from the axis values, not from how tall the bars look. The GMAT uses this to test whether you read numbers or pictures.

cards.q: A bar chart shows sales of ₹80 crore in 2024 and ₹100 crore in 2025. The increase was:
cards.explain: (100 − 80) ÷ 80 = 20 ÷ 80 = 25%. Dividing by the new value (giving 20%) is the classic error.

cards.q: A trend line passes through (x = 2, y = 10) and (x = 6, y = 30). What is its slope?
A scatter plot shows that cities with more gyms have lower average blood pressure. Which statement is best supported?
options: Higher blood pressure causes cities to close gyms
Gyms have no link to health
In these cities, number of gyms and average blood pressure are negatively correlated
cards.explain: A scatter plot supports a correlation claim. Causal claims in either direction need more evidence.

notes.h: The core idea: read the picture as numbers
notes.p:
Graphics Interpretation questions test whether you can turn a chart into correct statements. You get a single graphic and, usually, two sentences with drop-down menus. Each blank has three to five options. Credit requires both blanks right.

The GMAT uses a wide range of graphics: bar and stacked-bar charts, line graphs, scatter plots with trend lines, pie charts, bubble charts, Venn diagrams, timelines and organisation or process flowcharts. The underlying skill is the same: **understand the frame, extract the right values, do a simple calculation, and match the wording precisely.**

notes.h: The framework: frame, extract, compute, match
notes.p:
**1. Frame (20–30 seconds).** Title, axes, units, scale (linear or not), where the axis starts, legend, footnotes. Ask: what does one unit on each axis mean?

**2. Read the blanks.** Identify exactly which quantity each blank needs — a value, a difference, a % change, a ratio, a slope, a count of points satisfying a condition.

**3. Extract and compute.** Read values off the graph as accurately as the gridlines allow. Estimate first. If answer choices are far apart, rough numbers are enough; if close, compute carefully, using the calculator if useful.

**4. Match the language.** 'Closest to', 'at least', 'approximately', 'the greatest'. 'Positive/negative/no' correlation. 'Increase' vs 'percent increase'.
points: % change = (new − old) ÷ old
Slope = rise ÷ run (change in y ÷ change in x)
Pie share = part ÷ whole; a 90° slice = 25%
Stacked bars: each segment's length, not its top edge, is its value
CAGR = (end ÷ start)^(1/n) − 1
Percentage points vs percent: 20% → 25% is +5 points, +25%

notes.h: Worked example: subscriber growth and a CAGR blank
notes.p:
*Graphic (illustrative): a line chart titled 'Paid subscribers, streaming app X (lakh)'. Points: Jan 40, Apr 46, Jul 55, Oct 66.*

**Blank 1:** 'Subscribers grew by approximately ___ between January and October.' Change = 66 − 40 = 26 lakh. Percent = 26 ÷ 40 = **65%**.

**Blank 2:** 'The three-month period with the largest percentage growth was ___.'
Jan–Apr: 6 ÷ 40 = 15.0%
Apr–Jul: 9 ÷ 46 ≈ 19.6%
Jul–Oct: 11 ÷ 55 = 20.0%
Answer: **Jul–Oct**, by a hair. Notice the trap: Apr–Jul and Jul–Oct look similar on a chart. The question is designed so that only computation separates them.

**CAGR variant.** If a bar chart showed revenue of ₹100 crore in 2022 and ₹144 crore in 2024, the two-year CAGR is (144 ÷ 100)^(1/2) − 1 = 1.2 − 1 = **20%** per year — not 22%, which is the simple average of the total 44% rise.

Scatter plots are common in Graphics Interpretation. Learn the standard vocabulary: **positive** correlation (points rise left to right), **negative** (they fall), **none** (no pattern), **strong** (points hug the trend line) vs **weak** (widely scattered). The **slope** of the trend line tells you how much y changes per unit of x.

A classic GMAT blank offers 'The data show that X causes Y' alongside 'X and Y are positively correlated'. Only the second is supported by a scatter plot. This connects directly to Critical Reasoning: correlation, by itself, does not establish cause.

points: Ignoring a y-axis that does not start at zero
Dividing by the new value instead of the old in % change
Reading the top of a stacked segment as its value
Treating a simple average of growth rates as a CAGR
Inferring causation from a scatter plot
Mixing up the two y-axes on a dual-axis chart

notes.h: How it shows up in interviews, exams and real jobs
notes.p: Every board deck, investor presentation and consulting report is a stack of graphics. Annual reports of companies like Asian Paints or Infosys present multi-year revenue and margin charts; analysts must read them precisely and spot when a chart's design flatters the story (a truncated axis, a cherry-picked time range). In case interviews, candidates are handed exhibits and asked for the takeaway in 30 seconds. The same discipline — frame first, then numbers, then one clear sentence — wins both on the exam and in the room.

points: One graphic, usually two drop-down blanks; both must be right
Read title, axes, units, scale and legend before any data
% change divides by the old value
Slope = rise ÷ run; use it to predict from a trend line
CAGR is not the simple average of growth
Truncated axes exaggerate differences
Scatter plots show correlation, not causation

cards.title: The format
cards.body: A problem (quantitative or verbal) asks you to pick **two answers** from one shared list of about 5–6 options, shown as a table with two selection columns. Each column has its own condition. The **same option can be correct for both columns**. You need both right for credit.

cards.title: Two flavours
cards.body: **Quant:** e.g. choose values for two variables that satisfy given equations or constraints. **Verbal/logic:** e.g. choose the statement that **most strengthens** and the one that **most weakens** an argument, or a cause and an effect, or a premise and a conclusion. Same skills as CR and algebra, new layout.

cards.title: Quant example
cards.body: A café sold 100 teas and 50 coffees for ₹6,000. Coffee costs exactly twice tea. Pick tea price and coffee price from: ₹20, 25, 30, 40, 50, 60. 100t + 50(2t) = 200t = 6,000 → t = **₹30**, c = **₹60**. Both appear in the list — select one per column.

cards.title: Link the two columns
cards.body: Usually the two answers **depend on each other**: once you find one, the other follows. Look for the column with the tighter constraint and solve it first, or test the options in pairs. Read the stem slowly — the relationship between the columns is the heart of the problem.

cards.title: Verbal example
cards.body: Claim: 'A four-day week raises productivity — a pilot team's output per hour rose 10%.' Options include: (a) the pilot team was made of volunteers already among the top performers; (b) the team's output per hour before the pilot was measured the same way and was lower. **Weakens most: (a)** (selection bias). **Strengthens most: (b)** (same-team comparison).

cards.title: Test options, don't solve blind
cards.body: With only 5–6 options, **plugging in** is often faster than algebra. If x + y = 10 and xy = 21 with options 1, 3, 5, 7, 9: try 3 and 7 → sum 10, product 21. Done. Use the calculator for ugly numbers — it's available in Data Insights.

cards.title: Same option, both columns
cards.body: Test-takers often assume the two answers must differ. They needn't. If x = y is allowed by the conditions, the same option is correct in both columns. Check the stem: if it doesn't forbid it, consider it.

cards.q: Select x and y from {1, 3, 5, 7, 9} such that x + y = 10 and x − y = 4.
In Two-Part Analysis, can the same option be the correct choice for both columns?
options: Yes, if it satisfies both conditions
Only if the stem says so explicitly
cards.explain: Both columns draw from the same list, and one option may satisfy both conditions.

cards.q: A trader buys an item at cost C and sells it at price P for a 25% profit on cost. If P = ₹500, choose C and the profit from {₹100, ₹125, ₹375, ₹400}.

notes.h: The core idea: two linked decisions from one list
notes.p:
Two-Part Analysis presents a problem and a table: a list of options in the middle, with two columns of radio buttons, each column headed by a different requirement. You pick one option per column. Credit comes only when **both** are right.

The content can be anything the GMAT tests — algebra, rates, profit, logic, argument analysis. What's new is the format: two answers that are usually **connected**, so solving one helps with the other. Think of it as a mini-negotiation: you're choosing a pair that satisfies two conditions at once.

notes.h: The framework: decode, link, solve, verify
notes.p:
**1. Decode each column's requirement.** Write them on your noteboard: 'Col 1: price of tea. Col 2: price of coffee.' Or: 'Col 1: most strengthens. Col 2: most weakens.'

**2. Find the link.** Is there an equation joining them? A logical relationship (cause/effect, claim/evidence)? A constraint like 'the total is fixed'?

**3. Solve or plug in.** Start with the more constrained column. With few options, test them directly.

**4. Verify the pair.** Plug both answers back into the stem. Many traps are options that satisfy one condition but not the other.
points: Quant Two-Part: often two unknowns, two conditions — systems of equations, rates, mixtures, profit
Verbal Two-Part: strengthen/weaken, assumption/conclusion, cause/effect, plan/obstacle
The same option may answer both columns
Both columns must be right for credit

notes.p:
*An online seller offers a product at list price L and gives a discount d (in ₹) so that the selling price is ₹1,200. The seller wants the discount to be exactly 20% of the list price. Select L and d from: ₹240, ₹300, ₹960, ₹1,200, ₹1,440, ₹1,500.*

Selling price = L − d = L − 0.2L = 0.8L = 1,200 → L = 1,200 ÷ 0.8 = **₹1,500**.
d = 0.2 × 1,500 = **₹300**.
Check: 1,500 − 300 = 1,200 ✔, and 300 ÷ 1,500 = 20% ✔.

Trap options: ₹1,440 (adding 20% to ₹1,200 — wrong base) and ₹240 (20% of the selling price rather than the list price). The test-maker anticipates the 'wrong base' error, which is also the most common mistake in real-world discount and markup calculations.

*A city council argues: 'Our new free-parking zone near the market will increase shop sales, because the market lost customers when parking fees were introduced three years ago.'*

Column 1: the statement that **most strengthens**. Column 2: the statement that **most weakens**.

Options (abridged):
(a) Surveys at the time showed most lost customers cited parking fees as their reason for leaving.
(b) The market's sales fall every monsoon.
(c) Three years ago, a large mall with free parking opened nearby and has kept attracting shoppers.
(d) The council's budget is under pressure.
(e) Most market shoppers arrive by bus.

**Strengthens:** (a) — it links the earlier loss directly to parking fees.
**Weakens:** (c) is the best — an alternative cause for the lost customers that free parking won't fix. (e) also weakens (parking may matter little), but (c) attacks the causal claim the argument is built on.

points: Solving each column independently and missing the link
Assuming the two answers must be different
Using the wrong base for percentages (discount on list vs selling price)
On verbal Two-Part, picking a 'weakener' that only addresses the topic, not the logic
Not verifying the pair against every condition

notes.h: How it shows up in interviews, exams and real jobs
notes.p: Business decisions are rarely single numbers. A pricing team sets list price **and** discount together; a supply planner chooses order quantity **and** reorder point; a marketing head weighs the strongest argument for and against a campaign. Two-Part Analysis mirrors these paired choices. In e-commerce companies such as Amazon or Flipkart, getting the base of a discount wrong on a festival sale can cost crores in margin — exactly the trap in example 1.

points: One option list, two columns, one pick per column
Both must be right for credit
Find the link between columns; solve the tighter one first
Plug in options — the list is short
The same option can be right in both columns
Watch percentage bases: discount on list price vs selling price
Verbal version uses CR skills: strengthen, weaken, assumption

cards.title: The format
cards.body: You get **two or three tabs** of information — emails, memos, tables, charts, articles — and several questions about them. Questions are either standard multiple choice or a set of **Yes/No (or True/False) statements** where all must be right. The key skill: knowing **which tab holds which fact** and combining them.

cards.title: First pass: build a tab map
cards.body: Spend 2–3 minutes skimming every tab and write one line per tab: 'T1 email: rules — 1 supplier, ≤5 days delivery, < ₹30L/yr, 1.2L boxes. T2 table: supplier price/delivery. T3 memo: CFO approval > ₹25/box; volume +10% next year.' Then let the questions send you back for details.

cards.title: Combining two tabs
cards.body: T1: need 1,20,000 boxes/yr, delivery ≤ 5 days, annual cost < ₹30 lakh. T2: P ₹22, 4 days; Q ₹24, 3 days; R ₹20, 7 days; S ₹26, 5 days. Annual cost: P ₹26.4L, Q ₹28.8L, R ₹24L, S ₹31.2L. **Qualifying: P and Q** (R too slow; S too costly).

cards.title: Adding the third tab
cards.body: T3 says volume will rise 10% next year to 1,32,000 boxes. P: 22 × 1,32,000 = ₹29.04 lakh — still under ₹30L. Q: 24 × 1,32,000 = ₹31.68 lakh — over. So **only P** satisfies the email's cost rule next year. Note: S also needs CFO approval (above ₹25/box).

cards.title: Watch for conflicts and updates
cards.body: Sources may **disagree** or **update** each other: a later email may change a rule in an earlier memo; a table may cover only some regions. Questions often hinge on which source governs. Note dates, authors and scope in your tab map.

cards.title: Answer from the sources only
cards.body: As in RC, outside knowledge is a trap. 'Can be inferred' means the tabs **together** guarantee it. If a statement needs information no tab provides, the answer is No / Cannot be determined — even if it's probably true in real life.

cards.title: Time management
cards.body: An MSR set has several questions on the same tabs, so the first-pass investment pays back. Typically spend more on the first question (learning the sources) and less on later ones. If one question is a calculation sink, guess and move on — it's one question.

cards.q: Using the supplier example, which supplier meets BOTH the 5-day delivery rule and the under-₹30-lakh annual cost at 1,20,000 boxes, AND needs no CFO approval (price ≤ ₹25/box)?
cards.explain: P (₹22, 4 days, ₹26.4L) and Q (₹24, 3 days, ₹28.8L) both pass all three rules. S exceeds ₹25 and ₹30L; R is too slow.

cards.q: At 1,32,000 boxes next year, what is Q's annual cost?
A memo dated March says 'travel must be booked 14 days ahead'. An email dated June from the same manager says 'from July, 7 days ahead is enough'. For an August trip, which rule applies?
options: 7 days, because the later email updates the rule from July
cards.explain: The later communication from the same authority explicitly updates the rule for dates from July onward.

notes.h: The core idea: an analyst's inbox
notes.p:
Multi-Source Reasoning (MSR) simulates a real workday: an email from your boss, a spreadsheet from operations, a memo from finance. Each contains part of the picture. The questions test whether you can **find the right fact in the right tab** and **combine sources** without importing assumptions.

MSR appears in the Data Insights section of the GMAT Focus Edition. Each set has two or three tabs and several questions. Some are standard five-option multiple choice; others present several Yes/No or True/False statements that all need to be correct for credit.

notes.h: The framework: map, locate, combine, verify
notes.p:
**1. Map the tabs (2–3 minutes on the first question).** For each tab note: type (email, table, chart, article), author/date, and its key content in one line. For tables, note column headings and units.

**2. Locate.** For each question, decide which tab(s) it needs. Many questions need just one; the harder ones need two or three.

**3. Combine.** Apply rules from one tab to data in another. Watch for conflicts and updates.

**4. Verify.** For Yes/No statements, check each against the exact wording of the sources. 'Can be inferred' requires certainty.
points: Text tabs usually hold **rules, goals and context**
Table/chart tabs usually hold **data**
Later dated sources may **override** earlier ones
Footnotes often contain the decisive exception
Calculator is available; units (lakh, crore, thousands) still trip people up

notes.h: Worked example: choosing a packaging supplier
notes.p:
*Tab 1 — Email from the Head of Operations:* 'We will select one packaging supplier for the next 12 months. Requirements: delivery within 5 days of order, and total annual cost under ₹30 lakh. Our forecast demand is 1,20,000 boxes a year.'

*Tab 2 — Table of quotes (illustrative):*
P — ₹22 per box — 4-day delivery
Q — ₹24 per box — 3-day delivery
R — ₹20 per box — 7-day delivery
S — ₹26 per box — 5-day delivery

*Tab 3 — Memo from Finance:* 'Any quote above ₹25 per box requires CFO approval. Sales expects volume to rise 10% next year.'

**Step 1 — annual cost at 1,20,000:** P = 22 × 1,20,000 = ₹26,40,000 (₹26.4 lakh). Q = ₹28.8 lakh. R = ₹24 lakh. S = ₹31.2 lakh.

**Step 2 — apply Tab 1 rules:** R fails delivery (7 days). S fails cost (₹31.2L > ₹30L) and also needs CFO approval per Tab 3. **P and Q qualify.**

**Step 3 — next year, 1,32,000 boxes:** P = 22 × 1,32,000 = ₹29.04 lakh (still under ₹30L). Q = 24 × 1,32,000 = ₹31.68 lakh (over).

Sample Yes/No statements:
'Supplier R is the cheapest but does not meet the delivery requirement.' → **Yes.**
'If the 10% volume forecast is correct, only one supplier meets the email's cost rule next year among those meeting the delivery rule.' → Among P, Q, S (delivery OK): P ₹29.04L ✔, Q ₹31.68L ✘, S 26 × 1,32,000 = ₹34.32L ✘ → **Yes.**
'Supplier Q's quote requires CFO approval.' → ₹24 ≤ ₹25 → **No.**

points: Answering from one tab when the question needs two
Missing a rule hidden in a memo or footnote
Ignoring dates — an older source may have been superseded
Treating 'probably true' as 'can be inferred'
Unit errors: per box vs per thousand boxes, lakh vs crore
Re-reading every tab for every question instead of using a tab map

notes.h: How it shows up in interviews, exams and real jobs
notes.p: MSR is the most 'job-like' GMAT format. Procurement managers at manufacturers like Tata Motors or Maruti Suzuki compare quotes against delivery, cost and approval rules every week. Consultants combine client data, interview notes and industry reports into one recommendation. In MBA case competitions, teams get a data pack of exhibits and must find the two facts that, combined, change the answer. The discipline is the same: map sources, find the binding constraint, compute, and check what has been updated.

points: Two or three tabs: text usually gives rules, tables give data
Build a one-line-per-tab map on the first question
Decide which tab(s) each question needs
Combine rules and data; recompute when assumptions change (e.g. +10% volume)
Later sources from the same authority can override earlier ones
Yes/No sets: every statement must be right for credit
Only the sources count — no outside knowledge

chapters.title: GMAT vs CAT vs GRE: which test, which door

cards.title: Three tests, three doors
cards.body: **CAT** is the entrance test for the IIMs' flagship **two-year** MBA/PGP and many Indian B-schools; most takers are freshers or have a few years' work experience. **GMAT** and **GRE** are used by global MBAs and by Indian programmes for experienced professionals, such as **ISB's PGP** and the IIMs' **one-year executive MBAs** (e.g. IIM Ahmedabad's PGPX).

cards.title: GMAT Focus Edition in one card
cards.body: Three sections — **Quantitative Reasoning** (21 Q), **Verbal Reasoning** (23 Q), **Data Insights** (20 Q) — each **45 minutes**, about **2 hours 15 minutes** in total. Total score **205–805**; each section 60–90. You choose the **section order**, can **bookmark** and change up to **3 answers per section**. Scores stay valid for **5 years**.

cards.title: CAT in one card
cards.body: Run by one of the IIMs in rotation each year, usually in late November. In recent years: three sections — **VARC**, **DILR** and **Quant** — about **40 minutes each, 2 hours total**, with negative marking on MCQs. The result is a **percentile**, used with academics, work experience and diversity factors for IIM shortlists.

cards.title: GRE in one card
cards.body: ETS's GRE General Test (shortened in 2023 to just under **2 hours**) has Verbal, Quant and an Analytical Writing task. Many top global MBAs and ISB accept it **alongside** the GMAT. Some programmes and recruiters (notably consulting and banking) are more familiar with the GMAT — check each school's stated policy rather than assuming equivalence.

cards.title: Indian programmes for experienced candidates
cards.body: **ISB PGP** (one year, Hyderabad and Mohali) takes GMAT or GRE; most admits have several years of work experience, and ISB runs an early-entry route for students. **IIM one-year programmes** (e.g. IIM-A PGPX, IIM-B EPGP, IIM-C PGPEx) typically ask for GMAT/GRE and a higher minimum work experience. Rules change — always confirm on the official admissions page.

cards.title: Choosing your test
cards.body: Ask three questions: **(1) Which programmes am I targeting?** (CAT for 2-year IIMs; GMAT/GRE for ISB, PGPX-type and global). **(2) How much experience do I have?** **(3) Which test suits my strengths?** Take a free official practice test of each before committing months of prep.

cards.title: Score strategy
cards.body: Plan for **two attempts** with a buffer of 6–8 weeks before your first application deadline. Use the official practice exams to measure progress. Remember: the test gets you **past the screen**; essays, career progression and interviews get you **in**.

cards.q: Which test is the primary route into the IIMs' flagship two-year PGP/MBA for most Indian candidates?
cards.explain: CAT is the main entrance test for the IIMs' two-year flagship programmes. GMAT/GRE are used mainly for their one-year executive programmes and for ISB and global schools.

cards.q: In the GMAT Focus Edition, how many answers can you change per section using Question Review & Edit?
cards.explain: You can review and change up to three answers in each section.

cards.q: Which section of the GMAT Focus Edition allows an on-screen calculator?
cards.explain: The calculator is available only in Data Insights; Quant must be done without one.

notes.h: The core idea: the test is a door, not the house
notes.p:
Indian MBA aspirants face a confusing menu of tests. The simplest way to think about it: **pick the programmes first, then the test they use.** CAT, GMAT and GRE are not rivals for the same seat; they are keys to different doors.

**CAT** opens the IIMs' flagship two-year PGP/MBA and hundreds of other Indian schools. It suits freshers and people with 0–4 years of experience.

**GMAT and GRE** open global MBAs (Harvard, Wharton, INSEAD, LBS and others), **ISB's one-year PGP**, and the IIMs' **one-year programmes for experienced professionals**, such as IIM Ahmedabad's PGPX, IIM Bangalore's EPGP and IIM Calcutta's PGPEx.

Whatever you pick, the test only gets you past the first screen. Admissions committees then read your career, essays, recommendations and interview.

notes.h: The GMAT Focus Edition in detail
notes.p: The Focus Edition replaced the older GMAT and is now the GMAT. Its structure, per GMAC (mba.com):
points: **Quantitative Reasoning:** 21 questions, 45 minutes, problem solving only (arithmetic and algebra; no geometry), **no calculator**
**Verbal Reasoning:** 23 questions, 45 minutes, Reading Comprehension and Critical Reasoning only (no Sentence Correction)
**Data Insights:** 20 questions, 45 minutes, Data Sufficiency, Multi-Source Reasoning, Table Analysis, Graphics Interpretation, Two-Part Analysis; **on-screen calculator** allowed
Total time about **2 hours 15 minutes**, plus an optional break
Total score **205–805**; each section scored **60–90** and weighted equally
You **choose the section order**; you can bookmark and **change up to three answers per section**
Available at test centres and online; scores are valid for **five years**
There is no essay (AWA) section in the Focus Edition

notes.p:
**CAT** is conducted by one IIM each year in rotation (IIM Kozhikode ran CAT 2025). Recent papers have had three sections — Verbal Ability & Reading Comprehension, Data Interpretation & Logical Reasoning, and Quantitative Ability — with roughly **40 minutes per section** and about **2 hours** total, +3 for a correct answer and −1 for a wrong MCQ. You can't move between sections freely. Results come as percentiles. IIMs then build composite scores that weight CAT along with Class 10/12 marks, graduation, work experience and diversity, so a high percentile alone does not guarantee a call.

**GRE** (by ETS) is a general graduate test. Its shortened format (from September 2023) runs just under two hours. Many global MBAs and ISB accept it. If you are also considering master's programmes in economics or public policy, the GRE keeps more options open.

Rough heuristics: CAT's DILR and Quant are speed-heavy; the GMAT tests reasoning and data judgement; the GRE has a vocabulary-heavier verbal section. Take an official free practice test of each to see where you naturally score higher.

notes.h: Worked example: mapping an aspirant to a test
notes.p:
**Case 1 — Ananya, 22, final-year B.Com, no work experience.** Target: IIM two-year PGP. Test: **CAT**. She could also consider ISB's early-entry route (applying while still a student, joining after gaining work experience), which uses GMAT/GRE.

**Case 2 — Rohan, 27, software engineer, 5 years at a large IT services firm.** Targets: ISB PGP and a couple of US/European schools. Test: **GMAT** (or GRE). CAT's two-year programmes would also be possible, but at 5 years of experience the one-year route usually offers better opportunity-cost economics (see the next chapter).

**Case 3 — Priya, 32, 9 years in pharma sales management.** Targets: IIM-A PGPX, IIM-B EPGP, and INSEAD. Test: **GMAT or GRE**. Her experience is above the typical ISB class average but fits programmes built for mid-career managers. She should check whether a programme requires a **test-centre** score rather than an online one — some Indian one-year programmes have specified this in recent cycles.

points: Choosing the test before choosing schools
Assuming every school treats GMAT and GRE identically — read each policy
Booking the exam too close to deadlines, leaving no room for a retake
Over-investing in the score at the expense of essays and career story
Assuming a GMAT score helps with IIM two-year admissions — that route is CAT-based for most Indian candidates
Relying on old forum posts: rules, formats and eligibility change; verify on official sites

notes.h: How it shows up in interviews, exams and real jobs
notes.p: Interviewers rarely discuss your score unless it's notably low in one section, in which case they may probe your quantitative readiness. Some employers, especially consulting firms and investment banks, have historically asked for GMAT scores during MBA recruiting, so a strong score can have value beyond admissions. More importantly, the GMAT's skills — Critical Reasoning and Data Insights — are exactly the skills you'll use in case discussions, consulting interviews and analyst work.

points: Pick programmes first; the test follows
CAT → IIM two-year PGP and most Indian B-schools
GMAT/GRE → ISB PGP, IIM one-year programmes (PGPX, EPGP, PGPEx), global MBAs
GMAT Focus: Quant 21, Verbal 23, DI 20; 45 minutes each; 205–805
Calculator only in Data Insights; choose section order; change up to 3 answers/section
CAT: VARC, DILR, QA, ~40 minutes each, negative marking
Always confirm eligibility and test rules on official admissions pages

chapters.title: Choosing schools: 1-year vs 2-year, ROI and rankings

cards.title: One year or two?
cards.body: **Two-year MBAs** (IIM PGP, most US schools) include a summer internship — a structured chance to switch careers. **One-year MBAs** (ISB, INSEAD, IIM PGPX-type) cost less in lost salary and suit people with clear goals and more experience, but recruiting starts almost immediately and there's no full summer internship.

cards.title: The real cost of an MBA
cards.body: **Total cost = Fees + Living costs + Lost salary (opportunity cost) − Scholarships.** Lost salary is often the **biggest** item for experienced candidates. **Simple payback (years) ≈ Total cost ÷ Annual post-tax salary gain.** It's a rough lens, not a full NPV — but it forces honest numbers.

cards.title: ROI worked example
cards.body: Illustrative: pre-MBA salary ₹18 lakh; one-year programme fees + living ₹45 lakh; lost salary ₹18 lakh → total ₹63 lakh. Post-MBA salary ₹35 lakh → gain ₹17 lakh pre-tax, about ₹12 lakh post-tax (at ~30%). Payback ≈ 63 ÷ 12 ≈ **5.3 years**. A two-year route with ₹25 lakh fees + 2 years lost salary changes the picture.

cards.title: Rankings: useful, but read the method
cards.body: FT, QS, Bloomberg Businessweek, US News and India's NIRF all rank MBAs, with different weights — salary, salary increase, research, diversity, surveys. A school can move 10 places because of method changes, not quality. Use rankings to build a **long list**, then judge on **placements, fit and cost**.

cards.title: Read the placement report
cards.body: Look at the **median**, not just the highest salary. Check **which companies** hired, **how many** students they took, the **share of the class reporting**, and the split by function (consulting, finance, product, general management). One ₹1 crore offer tells you nothing about your likely outcome.

cards.title: Build a balanced list
cards.body: Apply to **5–8 schools** in three bands: **reach** (your profile is below their median), **target** (around the median), and **safer** (above it). Weigh location: recruiters hire where they know the school — ISB and IIMs for India; INSEAD, LBS for Europe/Middle East; US schools for the US.

cards.title: Fit is real
cards.body: Talk to 3–5 current students and alumni per school. Ask about class culture, how recruiting went for people **like you**, and what they'd change. A school strong in finance may be weak for product management, and a case-method school feels very different from a lecture-heavy one.

cards.q: For an experienced professional, which cost item is often the LARGEST part of an MBA's true cost?
cards.explain: Opportunity cost — the salary you give up — often exceeds fees for candidates with several years of experience.

cards.q: Total MBA cost is ₹60 lakh and the post-tax annual salary gain is ₹10 lakh. Simple payback is about:
cards.explain: 60 ÷ 10 = 6 years. This ignores salary growth and the time value of money, so treat it as a rough check.

cards.q: A school's placement report highlights a ₹1.2 crore top offer. What's the most useful figure to check next?
options: The median salary and share of class reporting
cards.explain: The median, with the reporting rate, tells you what a typical graduate earns; one top offer is an outlier.

notes.h: The core idea: an MBA is an investment decision
notes.p:
An MBA is one of the largest financial decisions most people make before buying a home. Treat it like one. You are spending money (fees and living costs) and, more importantly, **time** — the salary and career progression you give up. In return you expect a **better career path**: a switch of function or industry, a jump in level, a global network, or a move to a new country.

So the choice of school is not 'which is ranked highest?' but 'which programme gives me the best chance of my target career, at a cost I can justify?'

points: **Two-year (e.g. IIM PGP, Harvard, Wharton, Stanford, most US schools):** a summer internship between years lets you test a new career; more time for electives, clubs and recruiting; better for career switchers and people with less experience. Cost: two years of fees and lost salary.

**One-year (e.g. ISB PGP, INSEAD, IIM-A PGPX, IIM-B EPGP):** half the opportunity cost; intense pace; recruiting starts within months; typically suited to people with clearer goals and more experience. No traditional summer internship, so switching careers relies more on prior experience and networking.

**Part-time and executive MBAs:** keep your job and salary; often employer-sponsored; strong for advancing within your current company or industry; weaker for a full career switch because on-campus recruiting is limited.

notes.h: Worked example: payback on two routes
notes.p:
*All numbers illustrative.* Rohan earns **₹18 lakh** a year. He compares two options.

**Option A — one-year programme in India.**
Fees + living: ₹45 lakh
Lost salary (1 year): ₹18 lakh
Total cost: **₹63 lakh**
Expected post-MBA salary: ₹35 lakh → pre-tax gain ₹17 lakh; post-tax (assume ~30% marginal tax) ≈ **₹11.9 lakh** a year
Simple payback ≈ 63 ÷ 11.9 ≈ **5.3 years**

**Option B — two-year programme in India.**
Fees + living: ₹30 lakh
Lost salary (2 years): ₹36 lakh (ignoring raises he'd have got)
Total cost: **₹66 lakh**
Expected post-MBA salary: ₹35 lakh, same gain ≈ ₹11.9 lakh post-tax
Payback ≈ 66 ÷ 11.9 ≈ **5.5 years**, starting one year later.

The two look similar on payback, so the decision turns on other factors: Option B's summer internship helps if Rohan wants to switch from IT services to consulting; Option A is better if he's staying close to tech and values getting back to earning sooner.

Why 'simple payback' is only a first cut: it ignores salary growth, which usually favours the MBA path over many years; it ignores the **time value of money** (a proper NPV discounts future gains); and it ignores risk — the post-MBA salary is an expectation, not a promise. Use it to check that the numbers aren't absurd, then decide on career fit.

notes.h: Rankings and how to read them
notes.p:
Major rankings include the **Financial Times**, **QS**, **Bloomberg Businessweek**, **US News** (US schools) and India's government-run **NIRF**. Each uses a different recipe — alumni salary and salary increase, career progress, diversity, research output, and student or recruiter surveys. That's why a school can sit at different positions in different rankings, and why small moves year to year often reflect method or data changes.

Use rankings for **discovery and rough tiers**. Then use evidence closer to your goal: the **employment report** (median salary, percentage reporting, top employers, function split), conversations with alumni in your target role, and the school's strength in your target geography.

points: Ignoring opportunity cost and comparing fees only
Chasing the highest salary figure instead of the median for your function
Applying only to the top five schools with no target or safer options
Choosing a school without speaking to anyone who studied there
Treating rankings as precise — a 3-place difference is noise
Underestimating loan EMIs: a large education loan can limit post-MBA choices like joining a start-up

notes.h: How it shows up in interviews, exams and real jobs
notes.p: 'Why this school?' is a staple interview and essay question, and the answer should show you've done exactly this analysis: specific courses, clubs, recruiters and alumni relevant to your goal. Admissions committees can tell the difference between 'it's ranked highly' and 'its healthcare management electives and alumni at firms like Apollo Hospitals and Sun Pharma fit my plan'. The ROI method itself is core MBA finance — the same opportunity-cost and NPV logic you'll later apply to capital budgeting decisions.

points: Treat the MBA as an investment: fees + living + lost salary − scholarships
Lost salary is often the biggest cost for experienced candidates
Two-year: internship, better for switchers; one-year: lower opportunity cost, faster
Simple payback = total cost ÷ annual post-tax gain — a first cut, not an NPV
Read placement reports for the median, reporting rate and function split
Rankings use different methods; use them for tiers, not precise ordering
Apply to 5–8 schools across reach, target and safer bands

chapters.title: Essays and your story: why MBA, why now, goals

cards.title: What essays are for
cards.body: Your scores and CV show **what** you've done. Essays show **who you are** and **where you're going**. Admissions committees want three things: a credible **goal**, evidence you can **lead and contribute**, and **self-awareness**. Every essay should advance at least one of these.

cards.title: The goals logic
cards.body: **Past → Gap → MBA → Short-term goal → Long-term goal.** Your past experience leads naturally to a short-term goal (the role right after the MBA). The **gap** — skills, network, credentials you lack — is what the MBA fills. The long-term goal shows ambition and direction.

cards.title: Why MBA, why now, why here
cards.body: **Why MBA:** you need general-management skills and a network your current path won't give you. **Why now:** you've reached a natural ceiling or inflection point — you've seen enough to know what you need. **Why here:** specific courses, clubs, faculty, recruiters and alumni that serve your goal.

cards.title: A weak vs strong goal
cards.body: Weak: 'I want to become a leader in the corporate world and make an impact.' Strong: 'After the MBA, I want to join a consumer-health company in brand management, and in 10 years lead a business unit that makes preventive health products affordable in tier-2 India.' Specific role, industry, mission.

cards.title: Show, don't tell
cards.body: Not 'I'm a strong leader', but: 'When our largest client threatened to leave, I rebuilt the delivery team over two weekends and we kept the ₹4 crore contract.' Use **STAR**: **Situation, Task, Action, Result**. Spend most words on **Action**, and quantify the **Result**.

cards.title: Write in your own voice
cards.body: Committees read thousands of essays and can spot generic, over-polished prose instantly. Simple, specific sentences beat impressive vocabulary. AI tools and consultants can help you edit, but if the essay doesn't sound like you in the interview, it hurts more than it helps. Check each school's policy on AI use.

cards.title: The failure / weakness essay
cards.body: When asked about a setback, pick a **real** failure with real stakes, own your part without excuses, and spend at least half the essay on **what you learned and did differently afterwards**. Avoid fake weaknesses like 'I work too hard'.

cards.q: Which best explains 'why now' in an MBA application?
options: The school's deadline is next month
I've reached a point where my growth needs skills and exposure my current role can't provide
My friends are applying this year
cards.explain: 'Why now' should explain a career inflection point — why the MBA adds most value at this stage.

cards.q: In a STAR story, which part should usually get the most words?
cards.explain: The Action shows what you personally did and how you think; that's what committees evaluate most.

cards.q: Which is the strongest short-term goal statement?
options: Become a consultant at a top firm focused on operations in Indian manufacturing
Explore many careers during the MBA
cards.explain: It names a function, a type of employer and a focus area, and links naturally to a manufacturing background.

notes.h: The core idea: one coherent story
notes.p:
