Your application is not a collection of documents; it's **one argument**: 'Given who I've been and what I've done, here is where I'm going, here is why an MBA from this school is the right next step, and here is what I'll add to the class.' The essays are where you make that argument directly.

Admissions committees at schools like Harvard, Stanford, INSEAD, ISB and the IIMs' executive programmes read for three qualities: **direction** (credible goals), **impact** (evidence of leadership and results), and **character** (self-awareness, values, how you treat people). Your essays should give clear evidence of each.

notes.h: The framework: building your goals essay
notes.p: A strong goals essay follows a logical chain:
points: **Past:** two or three experiences that shaped you and show progression — promotions, larger responsibilities, a turning point
**Insight:** what those experiences taught you about where you want to go
**Short-term goal:** a specific post-MBA role (function + industry + type of company)
**Long-term goal:** a broader ambition 10–15 years out, consistent with the short-term role
**Gap:** the skills, knowledge, network or credibility you need and lack
**Why MBA / why now:** why this degree fills the gap better than alternatives, and why this is the right moment
**Why this school:** specific courses, centres, clubs, faculty, treks, recruiters and alumni — show you've done the research

notes.h: Worked example: a goals essay outline
notes.p:
*Illustrative candidate: Kavya, 28, five years in supply-chain operations at an Indian FMCG company.*

**Past:** Started as a management trainee in a plant; moved to regional distribution planning; led a project that cut stock-outs at kirana stores in her region. She noticed that the biggest losses came from poor demand forecasting in small towns.

**Short-term goal:** Join a consulting firm's operations practice, working on supply-chain transformation for consumer companies in India and Southeast Asia.

**Long-term goal:** Lead supply-chain strategy — and eventually a business unit — at a consumer company expanding into rural and semi-urban markets.

**Gap:** She knows operations deeply but lacks finance, strategy and the structured problem-solving that consulting firms recruit for; her network is concentrated in one company.

**Why now:** After five years she's at the ceiling of what she can learn from execution roles; the next step requires strategy and cross-functional exposure.

**Why here:** e.g. a school's operations and analytics electives, a consulting club with a strong record of placements, and alumni in consumer and operations roles whom she has already spoken to.

Notice what makes this credible: the goal grows **out of** her experience; it's specific; and the gap is honest. A committee can imagine her succeeding.
Many schools ask open questions — about what matters most to you, a time you led, a setback, or what you'd add to the class. Principles that work across all of them:
points: **Choose stories with stakes:** a real problem, a real risk, real people affected
**Use STAR** but weight it toward Action and reflection
**Quantify results** where honest: revenue, time saved, people trained, customers retained
**Show how you work with others** — credit the team, show influence without authority
**Reveal values:** why the moment mattered to you, not just what happened
**Answer the actual question** and respect word limits; the limit is part of the test
Vague goals ('make an impact', 'leadership role') with no function or industry
Goals that don't connect to past experience — e.g. a coder claiming a sudden passion for luxury fashion with no evidence
Retelling the CV instead of explaining decisions and motives
Copy-pasting 'why this school' across applications — committees notice
Over-polishing until the essay sounds like no real person
Blaming others in a failure essay

notes.h: How it shows up in interviews, exams and real jobs
notes.p: Your essays are the script for your interview: interviewers often ask you to expand on them, so everything must be true and something you can discuss comfortably for ten minutes. The same story skills matter after the MBA — in recruiting ('walk me through your CV'), in pitching an idea to a CEO, or in writing a strategy memo. Narrative structure — context, problem, action, result, lesson — is how leaders at companies from Infosys to Amazon communicate; Amazon is known for replacing slide decks with written narratives in many meetings.

points: Essays show direction, impact and character
Goals chain: past → insight → short-term → long-term → gap → why MBA/now/here
Short-term goal = function + industry + company type
Show, don't tell; use STAR and spend most words on Action
Failure essays: real stakes, ownership, what changed afterwards
Make 'why this school' specific: courses, clubs, recruiters, alumni
Keep your own voice; check each school's policy on AI tools

cards.title: The application calendar
cards.body: Most global MBAs and ISB admit in **rounds**. Typically: **Round 1** deadlines in September–October, **Round 2** in roughly December–January, and a later **Round 3** in spring. Earlier rounds generally have more seats and scholarship money; late rounds are more competitive for most international candidates. Check each school's exact dates.

cards.title: Backward plan from Round 1
cards.body: For a September deadline: **Jan–Apr**: GMAT/GRE prep and test. **May–Jun**: research schools, talk to alumni, draft your story. **Jul–Aug**: write essays, brief recommenders. **Sep**: submit. **Oct–Dec**: interviews. Leave a buffer for a retake.

cards.title: Recommendations
cards.body: Most top schools ask for **one or two** letters, usually from **current or recent supervisors**. A recommender who knows your work closely beats a senior name who barely knows you. Good letters give **specific examples** and **compare you with peers**.

cards.title: Brief your recommenders
cards.body: Give each recommender a one-page brief: your goals, why you're applying, and 3–4 projects they saw with concrete outcomes. Ask them to cover **different** strengths. Give them **4–6 weeks**. Never write the letter yourself — schools warn against it and treat it as an integrity issue.

cards.title: Interview formats
cards.body: Formats vary: **blind** interviews (the interviewer has seen only your CV) vs **application-based**; with admissions staff, alumni or students; one-on-one, panel or group exercises; in person or video. IIM programmes often include written ability tests or panel interviews; some schools add short recorded video questions.

cards.title: Questions you will be asked
cards.body: Prepare crisp answers to: **'Walk me through your CV'** (2 minutes); **'Why MBA? Why now? Why us?'**; **short- and long-term goals**; **a leadership example**; **a failure**; **a conflict at work**; **what you'll contribute**; and **'Do you have any questions for me?'** Have STAR stories ready for each.

cards.title: Practise out loud, not by memorising
cards.body: Write bullet points, not scripts. Do 3–5 mock interviews with friends, alumni or current students. Record yourself. The goal is to sound **structured and natural**. End with one or two thoughtful questions that show genuine research — not things answered on the website.

cards.q: Who is usually the BEST choice of recommender?
options: A famous CEO who met you once
A direct supervisor who has seen your work closely
Your college professor from 6 years ago
cards.explain: Schools want specific, comparative evidence of your work, which a close supervisor can provide.

cards.q: Why do many advisers recommend applying in Round 1 or Round 2 rather than Round 3?
options: Earlier rounds usually have more seats and scholarship funds available
Round 3 doesn't require a test score
cards.explain: Most of the class and much of the scholarship money is committed in the first two rounds, so later rounds are typically tighter.

cards.q: Your recommender asks you to draft the letter for them to sign. What should you do?
options: Write it — it saves them time
Ask a consultant to write it
Copy a sample from the internet
Politely decline and give them a brief with examples instead
cards.explain: Schools require letters written by the recommender; drafting them yourself risks an integrity violation. A detailed brief is the right help.

notes.h: The core idea: the last mile decides
notes.p: By the time you reach the interview stage, the school believes you're academically capable — your test score and record have passed the screen. The final decision often rests on two things you've partly outsourced — **what your recommenders say about you** — and one thing you control completely: **how you come across in conversation**. Both reward preparation far more than talent. Many strong applicants lose out here because they treat recommendations as a formality and interviews as something to wing.
Plan backwards from your first deadline. For a Round 1 deadline in September (dates illustrative — check each school):
points: **December–January:** decide on the MBA, choose GMAT or GRE, take a diagnostic
**January–April:** test preparation; first attempt by April–May, leaving room for a retake
**April–June:** research schools; talk to students and alumni; attend information sessions; shortlist 5–8 schools
**June–July:** write your story — goals, key experiences; choose and brief recommenders
**July–August:** draft, revise and tighten essays; complete forms; recommenders submit
**September:** submit Round 1 applications
**October–December:** interviews; prepare and practise
**December–January:** decisions; Round 2 applications if needed

notes.p:
A recommendation is evidence from someone who has watched you work. The best ones are **specific** ('she redesigned our dispatch schedule and cut late deliveries from 12% to 4%') and **comparative** ('one of the top two analysts I've managed in ten years'). Generic praise from a famous person counts for little.

**Choosing recommenders:** a current direct supervisor is usually ideal. If you can't tell your current boss you're applying, a former supervisor or a senior colleague who has evaluated your work is acceptable — explain briefly if the form allows.

**Briefing them:** give each a one-page document with your goals, why the MBA, and a few specific projects they witnessed with outcomes. Ask one recommender to emphasise, say, leadership and the other analytical problem-solving, so the letters don't duplicate.

**Integrity:** the letter must be written by the recommender. Schools explicitly prohibit applicants drafting their own letters and can rescind admissions over it.

notes.h: Worked example: answering 'Walk me through your CV'
notes.p:
This is usually the first question and sets the tone. Aim for about **two minutes**, structured as a story, not a list.

*Illustrative answer (Kavya, supply-chain manager):*
'I studied mechanical engineering at a state university and joined an FMCG company as a management trainee in 2021 — I wanted to see how products actually reach people. My first year was on a plant floor, where I learned how small scheduling decisions ripple into cost. I then moved to regional distribution planning for about 40 distributors. My biggest project was reducing stock-outs at small retailers: by changing how we forecast demand for slower-moving products, our region's stock-outs fell noticeably over two quarters. That project showed me that the hardest supply-chain problems are really strategy and data problems, which is why I want to move into operations consulting after the MBA, and long term lead supply-chain strategy for a consumer company expanding into smaller towns.'

Why it works: chronological, each move explained, one concrete achievement, and it **lands on the goal** — inviting the natural follow-up 'Why MBA?'.

Prepare a **story bank** of 8–10 experiences — leadership, teamwork, conflict, failure, ethical dilemma, influencing without authority, a time you changed your mind — each in STAR form. Most behavioural questions can be answered by adapting one of them.

Know your application cold: interviewers may pick any line from your essays or CV. Research the school deeply enough to ask a genuine question — about a specific programme, centre or club, or what the interviewer found most valuable.

Formats vary by school and change over time: some interviews are blind, some use your full application; some schools have used group exercises, short recorded video answers or, as Harvard has, a brief written reflection after the interview. IIMs' programmes for experienced candidates have used panel interviews and sometimes written tasks. Read the latest guidance for each school.

points: Picking recommenders for their titles, not their knowledge of your work
Giving recommenders a week's notice
Memorising scripted answers that sound robotic
A 6-minute 'walk me through your CV' that lists every job
No questions for the interviewer, or questions answered on the website
Criticising a current employer or colleagues
Leaving the test to the last minute so applications slip to a later round

notes.h: How it shows up in interviews, exams and real jobs
notes.p: The skills here never stop paying off. Post-MBA recruiting for consulting, banking and product roles opens with the same 'walk me through your CV' and behavioural questions, followed by case or technical rounds. Managing recommenders is early practice in **managing stakeholders** — briefing senior people, making their job easy, and following up graciously. And the backward-planning discipline you use for the application calendar is project management, which you'll use in every job after.

points: Rounds: R1 ~Sep–Oct, R2 ~Dec–Jan, R3 spring; earlier rounds usually have more seats and scholarships
Plan backwards ~9 months from your first deadline; leave room to retake the test
Best recommenders know your work closely; brief them 4–6 weeks ahead
Never draft your own recommendation letter
Prepare a 2-minute CV walk-through that lands on your goal
Build a story bank of 8–10 STAR examples
Formats differ and change — read each school's latest guidance
